## Variables, Emission Factors, and Outputs — Quick Reference

---

### 1 · Input Variables: What Is and Is Not Used

**Fuel variables — included in Scope 1 (direct combustion):**

| SI variable | Canonical name | Unit | Coverage | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `esoliu` | `fuel_diesel_ltr` | litre | 2000–2014 | Largest Scope 1 contributor |
| `epeliu` | `fuel_petrol_ltr` | litre | 2000–2014 | |
| `ekeliu` | `fuel_kerosene_ltr` | litre | 2000–2014 | |
| `eclkgu` | `fuel_coal_kg` | kg | 2000–2014 | No unit correction — data already in Kg (see §4.1) |
| `elpkgu` | `fuel_lpg_kg` | kg | 2006–2014 | Absent 2000–2005 (structural gap) |
| `egam3u` | `fuel_citygas_m3` | m³ | 2006–2014 | PGN piped gas; absent 2000–2005 |
| `egom3u` | `fuel_othergas_m3` | m³ | 2012–2014 | Non-PGN gas; sparse |
| `efoliu` | `fuel_fueloil_ltr` | litre | Sparse | Mostly 2000; <600 obs most years |
| `ecoiku` | `fuel_coke_kg` | kg | 2012–2014 | <0.1% of firm-years |
| `ecbkgu` | `fuel_coalbriq_kg` | kg | 2012–2014 | <0.1% of firm-years |

**Electricity variables — included in Scope 2 (indirect, purchased):**

| SI variable | Canonical name | Unit | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `eplkhu` | `elec_pln_kwh` | kWh | PLN state grid; near-continuous 2000–2014 |
| `enpkhu` | `elec_nonpln_kwh` | kWh | Non-PLN purchased; absent 2000 (structural) |
| — | `elec_purchased_kwh_strict` | kWh | PLN + non-PLN; missing if either missing *(primary)* |
| — | `elec_purchased_kwh_zero` | kWh | PLN + non-PLN; structural missing → 0 *(robustness)* |

**Variables excluded from emission conversion — and why:**

| Variable | Reason for exclusion |
|---|---|
| `eluliu` — Lubricant | Not a combustion fuel; CO₂ from lubricant oxidation negligible and not reported in IPCC manufacturing EF table |
| `ekaykgu` — Firewood; `earakgu` — Charcoal | Biogenic fuels: CO₂ from combustion is short-cycle carbon, excluded from Scope 1 per IPCC 2006 and GHG Protocol |
| `esgkhu` — Self-generated electricity | Would double-count: the fossil fuel burned to run the on-site generator is already counted in Scope 1; including kWh output as Scope 2 would count the same energy twice |
| All `*_rp` / `*vcu` variables (Rp000) | Expenditure variables — used for unit-price diagnostics only; monetary values cannot substitute for physical quantities in GJ or CO₂ conversion |

---

### 2 · Emission Conversion: Spec 1 vs Spec 2

**Scope 1 — Direct fuel combustion** uses a two-step conversion:

$$\text{physical unit} \xrightarrow{\times\,\text{NCV}} \text{GJ} \xrightarrow{\times\,\text{IPCC EF}} \text{kg CO}_2\text{e} \xrightarrow{\div\,1{,}000} \text{tCO}_2\text{e}$$

**Scope 2 — Purchased electricity** uses a single-step direct conversion:

$$\text{kWh} \xrightarrow{\times\,\text{grid EF}_{t}} \text{tCO}_2\text{e}$$

The two specifications differ only in **NCV source** (Scope 1) and **grid EF assumption** (Scope 2):

| | **Spec 1 — primary** | **Spec 2 — robustness** |
|---|---|---|
| **NCV source (Scope 1)** | BPS *Neraca Energi Indonesia* (official energy balance, NCV basis — consistent with IPCC 2006 requirements); **exception:** coal uses HEES Kalimantan thermal (26.2 GJ/ton) and fuel oil uses HEES fallback (42.582 GJ/kL) — see §7.5 footnote d | ESDM HEES (inferred GCV basis for LPG — ~13% overstatement vs NCV) |
| **IPCC EF (Scope 1)** | IPCC 2006 Table 2.3, manufacturing sector — **identical across both specs** | ← same |
| **Grid EF (Scope 2)** | Time-varying, 0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh — constructed from Neraca Energi PLN fuel consumption × IPCC EF ÷ total kWh generated, year by year | Static 0.000867 tCO₂/kWh — PLN RUPTL 2015 (overstates 2006–2010 Scope 2 by ~33–45%) |
| **Key difference** | LPG NCV 45.5 GJ/t (NCV-correct); Scope 2 tracks actual grid mix | LPG NCV 52.1 GJ/t (GCV — inflated); Scope 2 uses a single 2015-vintage factor |
| **Scope 1 variables** | `co2_scope1_s1` | `co2_scope1_s2` |
| **Scope 2 variables** | `co2_scope2_s1` | `co2_scope2_s2` |
| **Total variables** | `co2_total_s1`, `ln_co2_total_s1` | `co2_total_s2`, `ln_co2_total_s2` |

---

### 3 · Output Variables and Example

**Output dataset:** `output/si_energy_emissions.dta` — 314,576 firm-years, Spec 1 primary + Spec 2 robustness.

| Variable | Description | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| `co2_scope1_s1` | Scope 1: direct fuel combustion (Spec 1) | tCO₂e/year |
| `co2_scope2_s1` | Scope 2: purchased electricity × time-varying grid EF (Spec 1) | tCO₂e/year |
| `co2_total_s1` | Total Scope 1+2, Spec 1 — **primary emission estimate** | tCO₂e/year |
| `ln_co2_total_s1` | Log total emissions, Spec 1 — **primary DiD outcome for emission levels** | log tCO₂e |
| `co2_scope1_s2` | Scope 1: direct fuel combustion (Spec 2, HEES NCV) | tCO₂e/year |
| `co2_scope2_s2` | Scope 2: purchased electricity × static 0.000867 tCO₂/kWh | tCO₂e/year |
| `co2_total_s2` | Total Scope 1+2, Spec 2 — robustness check | tCO₂e/year |

**Worked example** — a firm in 2010 consuming 5,000 litres diesel + 10,000 kWh PLN electricity:

| Step | Spec 1 | Spec 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Diesel → tCO₂e | 5,000 L × 0.002654 = **13.27 tCO₂e** | 5,000 L × 0.002978 = **14.89 tCO₂e** |
| Electricity → tCO₂e | 10,000 kWh × 0.000599 (2010 grid EF) = **5.99 tCO₂e** | 10,000 kWh × 0.000867 = **8.67 tCO₂e** |
| `co2_total` | **19.26 tCO₂e** → `ln_co2_total_s1` = 2.96 | **23.56 tCO₂e** → `ln_co2_total_s2` = 3.16 |
| Spec 1 vs Spec 2 gap | — | +22% (driven by diesel NCV difference: Neraca 36.0 vs. HEES 40.4 GJ/kL; and 2010 grid EF: time-varying 0.000599 vs. static 0.000867) |

---

### 4 · Energy Intensity Measures (Appendix C)

Two firm-level energy intensity measures are constructed in `si_energy_intensity.dta`:

| Measure | Formula | Variable | Denominator | Primary use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Physical GJ intensity** | ln(total\_gj\_s1 / output\_real) | `ln_ei_gj_real` | WPI-deflated real output, 2000 Rp | **Primary DiD outcome for energy efficiency question** (genuine physical efficiency, strips price inflation) |
| **Monetary intensity** | ln(energy\_exp\_zero / output) | `ln_ei_monetary_zero` | Nominal output Rp000 | Secondary outcome (cost efficiency, Imbruno & Ketterer 2018) |

`total_gj_s1` aggregates all Scope 1 fuels (physical units × Spec 1 NCV) plus purchased electricity (kWh × 0.0036 GJ/kWh). Note: for *physical energy intensity* only, the 0.0036 GJ/kWh thermodynamic constant converts electricity to comparable GJ units — this is separate from the emission conversion in §7.7, which applies the grid EF directly to kWh without an intermediate GJ step.

Physical GJ intensity declined ~1.3 log points over 2000–2014 (genuine efficiency gain); monetary intensity rose ~0.1 log points over the same period (energy price effects, especially the 2005 industrial diesel desubsidization, outweighed physical efficiency gains in nominal cost terms).
:::

# Data Sources and Linkage

This document records all data cleaning decisions for Mba Deasy's research on whether newly internationalising Indonesian manufacturing firms become more energy-efficient. It covers: (1) where the data come from and how they link; (2) what the questionnaire collects and how it changes across years; (3) what the raw panel looks like before cleaning; (4) unit problems and structural gaps that require correction; (5) the harmonization pipeline that produces canonical variables; (6) the data cleaning decision — informed by eleven prior SI studies — including which observations to flag, which to drop, and why; (7) the emission conversion methodology, including emission factors, energy content coefficients, and sensitivity variants; and (8) the variable construction code that produces the final `si_energy_emissions.dta` dataset.

This document draws on two data products from the Indonesian Industrial Survey (Statistik Industri / IBS — the annual census of medium and large manufacturing establishments conducted by BPS, the national statistics agency):

| Source | File | Coverage | Energy vars | Panel covariates |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|-----------------|
| **Annual SI files** | `si2000.dta` – `si2014.dta` | 2000–2014, ~20–29K firms/year | ✓ Full `E*` fuel + electricity vars | ✓ Region, workers, output, intermediate inputs — kept during initial append |
| **Long panel** | `data8514_SI.dta` | 1985–2014, 579K obs | ✗ Absent | ✓ Full (output, wages, trade status, export indicator) + ✓ ISIC/KBLI 5-digit code (`disic5`) used as `isic5_raw` for all years |

**ISIC** (International Standard Industrial Classification) / **KBLI** (Klasifikasi Baku Lapangan Usaha Indonesia, the Indonesian national equivalent) codes identify each firm's 2- to 5-digit industry group and are used to disaggregate energy use by sector.

The two files share a common firm identifier `psid`. A `merge 1:1 psid year` is valid — `psid` is unique within each source × year — but the match is not perfect (82–95% by year; see §1.1).

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Industry codes (ISIC) come from `data8514_SI.dta` — not from the annual SI files.** The variable `isic5_raw` in the base panel is sourced from `disic5` in `data8514_SI.dta`, applied uniformly across all years 2000–2014 during the 1:1 merge in `01_append_si_energy.do`.

| Years | Source variable | File |
|-------|:---:|:---:|
| 2000–2014 (all) | `disic5` | `data8514_SI.dta` |

Because we restrict to matched firms only (`merge==3`), **100% of observations have an ISIC code** (326,382/326,382).
:::

# Questionnaire Structure

The SI questionnaire changed substantially across survey waves. This chapter maps every energy-related item by year to establish which variables can be used in a balanced panel, which have structural gaps (years where the item was simply not collected — not a data quality problem), and which require corrections. Understanding these questionnaire-level facts is necessary before interpreting any patterns in the raw data.

**Panel C — Structural features**

Three structural features cut across all fuel items. The **generator-only sub-column** records how much of each fuel was consumed specifically to run on-site electricity generators (as opposed to direct production use); it appears in every year as a `*e`-suffix variable. The **production/non-production split** separates fuel used in the production process from fuel used in non-production activities (offices, transport); this is available only from 2007 onward and is *not* encoded in the compiled data files (only totals are stored).

::: {.table-scroll}

| Feature | 2000 | 2001 | 2002 | 2003 | 2004 | 2005 | 2006 | 2007 | 2008 | 2009 | 2010 | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 | 2014 |
|---------|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|:----:|
| Coal unit (questionnaire label) | Kg | — | — | Kg | Ton^a^ | Ton^a^ | Kg | Kg | Kg | Kg | Kg | Kg | Kg | Kg | Kg |
| Prod. / non-prod. fuel use split (questionnaire only) | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Generator-only sub-column | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

:::

> ^a^ The questionnaire label for 2004–2005 reads "Ton," but expenditure-based diagnostic evidence shows respondents reported in Kg (see §4.1). **No conversion is applied.** The data is taken as-reported for all years.
> ^b^ LPG in 2000 has no physical-quantity column — expenditure value only.

---

### Key changes across survey waves

- **2000** — Full set of fuel items individually. Coal, gas/LPG have separate rows. No prod/non-prod split.
- **2001–02** — Simplified: kerosene, coal, coke, gas/LPG, fuel oil collapsed into *bahan bakar lainnya*.
- **2003** — Kerosene and coal restored as separate rows.
- **2004** — Kerosene absorbed into other fuels. Coal listed separately in **Ton**. IDO and Bunker C absorbed into *bahan bakar lainnya* (same as 2003).
- **2005** — Kerosene and coal (in **Ton**) restored.
- **2006** — SE06 (Sensus Ekonomi 2006, the decennial economic census) form: 14 items; charcoal, briket batubara, firewood explicit. Coal returns to Kg.
- **2007–11** — Stable 8-item core. Production vs. non-production fuel use reported as separate columns from 2007.
- **2010** — Exception: monetary values only for solid fuels and gas (physical quantities available for liquid fuels and electricity; PLN/non-PLN merged into a single purchased row).
- **2012–14** — Briket batubara re-added; gas non-PGN separated from gas PGN (from 2013).

## Electricity

The table below maps every electricity item in the IBS/SI questionnaire for 2000–2014. **PLN** (Perusahaan Listrik Negara) is the state electricity utility; PLN-purchased electricity is the dominant source for most firms. **Non-PLN** electricity refers to power purchased from private generators or industrial estates. **PGN** (Perusahaan Gas Negara) is the state gas distribution company; "Gas dari PGN" in the fuel tables refers to piped city gas supplied through the PGN network.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| ✓ | Collected as a **separate line item** in the questionnaire |
| — | **Absent** or not separately listed that year |

::: {.callout-warning}
**2010 exception:** The 2010 questionnaire uses a completely different variable naming convention.
Purchased electricity is `ELRPCH` (kWh) / `ELVPCH` (Rp000) instead of the standard `EPLKHU`/`EPLVCU`.
Self-generated: `ELRGEN`/`ELVGEN`; Sold: `ELRSLD`/`ELVSLD`.
PLN and non-PLN are **not separated** in 2010.
:::

### Key changes across survey waves

- **2000** — PLN electricity only (Q24 Part V); non-PLN not separately collected.
- **2001** — Non-PLN added as separate item (Q16 Part V); both kWh and Rp000 columns for each source.
- **2002** — Self-generated electricity section added; structure otherwise similar to 2001.
- **2003–05** — Stable PLN + non-PLN structure, moved to Q8 block.
- **2004** — Self-generated (Q9) and sold electricity (Q10) first appear explicitly.
- **2006** — SE06 Special Census form: generator capacity (Q17), purchased (Q18), self-generated (Q19). Sold not collected.
- **2007–09** — Core structure stable (PLN + non-PLN); self-generated not always listed as a separate question.
- **2010** — Variable naming overhaul: `ELRPCH`/`ELVPCH` replace `EPLKHU`/`EPLVCU`. PLN and non-PLN merged. Sold electricity (`ELRSLD`/`ELVSLD`) re-added.
- **2011** — Reverts to standard naming; self-generated (`ESGKHU`) explicitly listed.
- **2012** — Self-generated absent again; only PLN + non-PLN.
- **2013–14** — Self-generated restored (Q9). Sold electricity re-added in 2014 with `OELKHU`/`YELVCU`.

## Potential Issues and Items to Confirm

The items below flag ambiguities that arose from cross-referencing the questionnaire PDFs against the actual data. Each was confirmed through one of two routes: (a) questionnaire text alone, or (b) data analysis on `si_panel_2000_2014.dta`. The confirmation source is noted for each.

*"Confirmed by" legend: **Questionnaire** = questionnaire PDF/text files only · **do-file name** = confirmed via data analysis in that specific do-file · **variable name** = inferred from variable naming convention*

| # | Item | Status | Confirmed by | Finding |
|---|------|:------:|:------------:|---------|
| 1 | **Coal unit 2004–2005** (`eclkgu`) | Cleared — no correction ✓ | Questionnaire + `04_unit_consistency.do` + `13_coal_correction_check.do` | Questionnaire labels 2004–2005 as Ton; quantity distribution shows 98% median drop — initially consistent with a unit change. Pipeline applied ×1,000 correction. **Expenditure diagnostic overturns this:** pre-correction implied price (Rp000/unit) in 2004–2005 = 0.750, matching 2003 exactly (0.751). Post-correction price = 0.001 — 1/1,000 of adjacent years. Data was already in Kg. **No correction should be applied.** See §4.1 for the full diagnostic. |
| 2 | **Minyak Diesel/IDO absent from 2007+** | Confirmed ✓ | Questionnaire | Not listed as a separate item in the 2007+ form; absorbed into *bahan bakar lainnya*. |
| 3 | **2010 electricity variable renaming** | Confirmed ✓ | Questionnaire | 2010 form uses `ELRPCH`/`ELVPCH` in place of `EPLKHU`/`EPLVCU`; PLN and non-PLN merged into one row. Standard names resume in 2011. |
| 4 | **`efuvcu` is independently filled, not a computed sum** | Confirmed ✓ | Questionnaire + `06_efuvcu_check.do` | The questionnaire total row is filled by respondents independently. `06_efuvcu_check.do` on `si_panel_2000_2014.dta` confirms mean(`efuvcu`) exceeds sum of components by 5–39% in every year 2000–2014 (see Figure below). **Action: do not use `efuvcu` as an aggregate or for arithmetic checks.** |
| 5 | **Briket Batubara absent 2007–2011** | Confirmed ✓ | Questionnaire | Absorbed into *bahan bakar lainnya* 2007–2011; re-added as a separate row from 2012. |
| 6 | **Prod./non-prod. fuel split from 2007** | Confirmed ✓ | `02_variable_coverage.do` | Variable list from `02_variable_coverage.do` shows only total-use (`*u`) and generator sub-item (`*e`) suffixes — no production vs. non-production encoding exists in the compiled SI data. **Action: use `*u` variables as total fuel use; production split is unavailable.** |
| 7 | **Gas non-PGN unit** (`egom3u`) | Confirmed ✓ | Questionnaire + variable name | Variable name encodes `m3` = m³, consistent with 2012–2014 questionnaire text. No unit variation. |

Visual evidence for this excess is provided in [Appendix A](#sec-appendix-efuvcu) (Figure A1): the mean ratio `efuvcu` / component-sum exceeds 1.0 in every year 2000–2014, and firm-level scatters confirm the same excess at the observation level.

::: {.callout-important}
**Conclusion — no data corrections required; two analytical constraints identified:**

The coal unit issue (item 1) was initially flagged as requiring a ×1,000 correction but was subsequently cleared by the expenditure-based diagnostic — see §4.1. The data was already in Kg; no correction is applied in the final pipeline.

Two items impose **analytical constraints** that must be respected in variable construction and regression:

1. **`efuvcu` excluded:** Cannot be used as a fuel expenditure aggregate — use individual fuel variables and sum manually.
2. **Production/non-production fuel split unavailable:** `E*u` variables capture total use only.

All other items (2, 3, 5, 7) are informational — they explain structural absences and naming conventions with no action needed.
:::

# Data Panel Structure (2000–2014)

This chapter describes the compiled base panel — what observations it contains, which variables are present, and how missingness is distributed across years. The numbers here are the ground truth for sample size and variable coverage before any cleaning is applied. All figures in this chapter come from `si_panel_2000_2014.dta`, which is built by appending the 15 annual SI files, retaining energy-related variables, then merging 1:1 with `data8514_SI.dta` and keeping matched firms only (N=326,382).

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Source:** `output/si_panel_2000_2014.dta` — appended from annual SI files `si2000.dta`–`si2014.dta`, keeping `psid`, `year`, and all `E*`/`IF*` energy variables; then merged 1:1 (psid×year) with `data8514_SI.dta`, retaining matched firms only (N=326,382; ~82–95%/year). Do-files: `dofiles/01_append_si_energy.do` (build and merge base panel) · `dofiles/02_variable_coverage.do` (coverage tables).
:::

| Year | Firm-years | Year | Firm-years |
|------|---:|------|---:|

The spike in 2006–2007 reflects a BPS census expansion (SE06 census year with enlarged sampling frame).

## Variable Inventory

The base panel contains **72 variables**: `psid`, `year`, and 70 energy variables. Variables follow the `E*` naming convention and cover both monetary expenditure (`*vcu`, Rp000) and physical quantities (`*liu` = liters, `*kgu` = kg, `*m3u` = m³, `*khu` = kWh). Each fuel also has an elec-generator sub-item (`*e` suffix) recording consumption for on-site electricity generation only.

# Unit Consistency and Data Gaps

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Do-files:** `dofiles/04_unit_consistency.do` (distributions & gap detection) · `dofiles/05_graph_unit_expenditure.do` (figures)
**Source:** `output/si_panel_2000_2014.dta` · **Figures:** `output/figures/fig01_coal_unit_expenditure.png`, `output/figures/fig02_fuel_coverage.png`
**Tables:** `output/tables/unit_consistency.csv` (unit distributions by year), `output/tables/structural_gaps.csv` (missing-by-year counts)
:::

The physical quantity variables span two survey waves (2000–2005 and 2006–2014) that used different questionnaire formats. This section documents where the reported unit changes across years, and which absences reflect survey design rather than non-response.

## Coal (`eclkgu`): Initially Flagged, Subsequently Cleared {#sec-coal-diagnostic}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Summary:** The questionnaire labels 2004–2005 coal as "Ton," and the quantity distribution shows a 98% median drop — initially pointing to a unit mismatch. A ×1,000 correction was applied. A subsequent expenditure-based diagnostic overturned this conclusion: the raw 2004–2005 price per unit exactly matches 2003, while the post-correction price falls to 1/1,000 of adjacent years. **The data was already in Kg. No correction is applied in the final pipeline.** Do-files: `04_unit_consistency.do`, `05_graph_unit_expenditure.do`, `13_coal_correction_check.do`. **Tables:** `output/tables/coal_correction_check.csv` (Tables C0a/C0b — by-year median price pre- and post-correction).
:::

### Step 1 — Initial Evidence: Quantity Distribution

The questionnaire PDFs confirm that 2004–2005 asked respondents to report coal in **Ton**, while all other years used **Kg**. The raw distribution appeared consistent with this:

| Year | N (positive) | Median (raw) | Notes |
|------|----------:|-------------:|-------|
| 2000 | 118 | 290,035 | Kg (pre-wave) |
| 2001–2002 | — | — | Absent |
| 2003 | 104 | 97,700 | Kg |
| **2004** | **403** | **2,175** | Apparent Ton — ratio to 2003: **0.02** (98% drop) |
| **2005** | **534** | **5,800** | Apparent Ton — ratio to 2004: 2.67 |
| 2006 | 1,475 | 3,087 | Kg (post-wave) |
| 2007 | 1,448 | 20,734 | Kg |
| 2008 | 1,315 | 82,670 | Kg |
| 2009 | 1,298 | 144,000 | Kg |
| 2010 | 1,436 | 90,304 | Kg |
| 2011 | 1,546 | 100,658 | Kg |
| 2012 | 1,852 | 35,700 | Kg |
| 2013 | 2,282 | 24,973 | Kg |
| 2014 | 2,520 | 38,144 | Kg |

The 98% median drop in 2004 looked like a 1 Ton = 1,000 Kg mismatch. Figure 1 reinforces this: physical quantity drops sharply in 2004–2005, but expenditure does not.

![**Figure 1.** Coal physical unit vs. expenditure by year. Top panel: median raw `eclkgu` (Kg/Ton as reported). Bottom panel: mean `eclvcu` (Rp 000). Source: `si_panel_2000_2014.dta` · Do-file: `05_graph_unit_expenditure.do`.](../output/figures/fig01_coal_unit_expenditure.png){fig-align="center" width="75%"}

Based on this, a ×1,000 correction (`eclkgu × 1000` for 2004–2005) was applied in `06_harmonize_si_energy.do`. However, this produced anomalously large 2004–2005 aggregate emission totals in §9 (4.4 billion and 11.4 billion thousand tCO₂e respectively), prompting the diagnostic below.

### Step 2 — Diagnostic: Implied Unit Price Test

The key test compares the **implied unit price** (coal expenditure ÷ coal quantity) across years. If the data was genuinely in Ton, the raw 2004–2005 price would be in Rp000/Ton — approximately 1,000× higher than the Rp000/Kg price in adjacent years. If the data was already in Kg, the raw price should match adjacent years directly.

**Table C0a — Implied price (Rp000 per unit), raw data before any correction**

::: {.table-scroll}

| Year | N | Median implied price | Matches adjacent years? |
|------|--:|---------------------:|:-----------------------:|
| 2003 | 104 | **0.7511** | — baseline |
| **2004** | **403** | **0.7500** | **Yes — matches 2003 exactly** |
| **2005** | **534** | **0.7500** | **Yes — matches 2003 exactly** |
| 2006 | 1,475 | 1.7496 | — (coal price rose 2005–2006) |
| 2007 | 1,448 | 1.7500 | Consistent |
| 2008–2014 | — | 1.91–3.31 | Consistent (rising coal prices) |

:::

If the 2004–2005 values were genuinely in Ton, the implied price would be ~750 Rp000/Ton (not 0.75 Rp000/Ton). The raw price matching 2003 to four significant figures means respondents reported in Kg despite the questionnaire label.

**Table C0b — Implied price (Rp000 per kg), after applying ×1,000 correction**

_If the correction were correct, post-correction prices should be consistent across all years._

::: {.table-scroll}

| Year | N | Median price (post-correction) | Ratio vs. adjacent avg | Assessment |
|------|--:|-------------------------------:|:----------------------:|------------|
| 2003 | 104 | 0.7511 Rp000/kg | — | Baseline |
| **2004** | **403** | **0.0008 Rp000/kg** | **0.0006** | Over-corrected — 1/1,000 of adjacent |
| **2005** | **534** | **0.0008 Rp000/kg** | **0.0006** | Over-corrected — 1/1,000 of adjacent |
| 2006 | 1,475 | 1.7496 Rp000/kg | — | Adjacent |
| 2007–2014 | — | 1.75–3.31 Rp000/kg | — | Consistent |

:::

^†^ Adjacent average:

$$\frac{0.7511 + 1.7496}{2} = 1.250 \text{ Rp000/kg}$$

A ratio of 1.0 = correction correct; ratio of 0.001 = over-corrected by ×1,000. Observed: **0.0006**.

### Step 3 — Conclusion: No Correction Applied

::: {.callout-important}
**The data was already in Kg. No correction is applied.**

The quantity-distribution evidence (98% drop, questionnaire label "Ton") pointed toward a unit mismatch, but the expenditure-based price test overturns it decisively: the raw 2004–2005 price per unit matches 2003 to four significant figures, and the post-correction price is 1/1,000 of all adjacent years.

**Why respondents reported in Kg despite the Ton label** is a documented pattern in Indonesian survey data — respondents fill based on their internal bookkeeping unit, not the questionnaire label. The 2004–2005 coal reporters were a rapidly growing group (104 → 403 → 534 firms), many of them smaller operations likely recording daily purchases in kg.

:::

**Note on the 2006→2007 quantity jump (ratio = 6.72):** This algorithmic flag is a composition effect, not a unit change. The 2006 wave was the first year of the expanded questionnaire; N_pos nearly tripled (534 → 1,475), bringing in many smaller coal users with low per-firm consumption. By 2007 the sample stabilized and the median climbed back toward 2008–2011 levels. No questionnaire evidence supports a unit change at 2006–2007.

## Other Flagged Variables

The ratio flag (> 5 or < 0.2 between adjacent years) also fired on several other variables. The table below classifies each flag:

| Variable | Year boundary | Ratio | Most likely explanation |
|----------|:-------------:|------:|------------------------|
| `efoliu` (fuel oil, liters) | 2000→2001 | 0.01 | Survey wave break; 2000 only 547 obs, 2001 expanded to 1,789 with different composition |
| `epelie` (gen-elec petrol, liters) | 2000→2001 | 0.03 | Small sample (161 → 383); likely composition shift |
| `enpkhu` (non-PLN elec, kWh) | 2000→2001 | 0.13 | Sample expansion at wave transition; no questionnaire evidence of unit change |
| `esgkhu` (self-gen elec, kWh) | 2005→2006 | 0.12 | Wave transition 2005→2006; sample nearly doubled; composition shift |
| `eoilie` (gen-elec oil, liters) | 2007→2008 | 0.15 | Very small sample (38 obs); high noise expected |
| `ecbkgu` (coal briquettes, kg) | 2012→2013 | 0.18 | Variable introduced 2012; composition shift as more firms entered |
| `egom3u` (gas from others, m³) | 2012→2013 | 11.44 | Variable introduced 2012 with 203 obs; 2013 first full year (701 obs); likely composition shift |

All flags at the 2000→2001 and 2005→2006 boundaries align with the known survey wave break and sample frame expansion. **None of these are treated as unit-change corrections** — the underlying values are taken at face value pending further questionnaire review.

Dashed lines: variables with structural gaps or late introduction. **Mostly absent variables** are not usable in a balanced panel regression. For Mba Deasy's firm-level panel, the practically usable fuel variables are those with near-continuous coverage: `esoliu`/`esolie` (diesel), `epeliu`/`epelie` (petrol), `eluliu` (lubricants), `eplkhu` (PLN electricity), `esgkhu` (self-generated electricity), and `eclkgu` (coal, taken as-reported — no unit correction applied; see §4.1). Gas (`egam3u`) and LPG (`elpkgu`) are available only from 2006 onward.

# Harmonization

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Do-files:** `dofiles/06_harmonize_si_energy.do` · `dofiles/07_graphs_harmonized.do` · `dofiles/08_outlier_flags.do` · `dofiles/09_clean_apply.do` · **Input:** `output/si_panel_2000_2014.dta` (326,382 obs, matched panel) · **Output:** `output/si_energy_harmonized.dta` (326,382 obs) · `output/si_energy_flagged.dta` · `output/si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta` (314,576 obs) · `output/figures/fig03–fig07`
:::

This chapter documents the harmonization pipeline that transforms the raw SI panel into an analysis-ready dataset. It covers five steps in order: (1) confirm no coal unit correction is needed (§4.1 diagnostic established data already in Kg); (2) rename all cryptic SI variable codes to **canonical names** — stable, human-readable names that do not change across survey waves; (3) construct purchased electricity aggregates in two variants; (4) carry through economic covariates unchanged; and (5) verify coal values visually and contextually with diagnostic figures.

No observations are dropped and no variables are deleted — sparse and mostly-absent variables are retained under their new names so that every cleaning decision is fully reversible.

The naming convention follows the prior pipeline (Natanael, Jan–Feb 2026) for compatibility:

- `fuel_{type}_{unit}` for physical quantities
- `fuel_{type}_rp` for expenditures (Rp000)
- `_gen` suffix for generator sub-items
- `elec_{source}_{unit}` for electricity

## Coal Unit: No Correction Applied

The coal quantity variable (`eclkgu`, renamed `fuel_coal_kg`) is taken as-reported for all years. The questionnaire labels 2004–2005 as "Ton," but the expenditure-based diagnostic (§4.1) established that respondents reported in Kg. No conversion is applied.

**Verification (raw medians, as-reported):**

| Year | Median `fuel_coal_kg` (as-reported) | N positive | Source |
|------|------------------------------------:|----------:|--------|
| 2003 | 97,700 Kg | 104 | `06_harmonize_si_energy.log` |
| 2004 | 2,175 Kg | 403 | `06_harmonize_si_energy.log` |
| 2005 | 5,800 Kg | 534 | `06_harmonize_si_energy.log` |
| 2006 | 3,087 Kg | 1,475 | `06_harmonize_si_energy.log` |

The lower 2004–2005 medians reflect genuine composition effects: the rapid entry of new coal users (104 → 403 → 534 firms) brought in many smaller, lower-consumption establishments. This coal surge coincided with the 2004–2005 global oil price shock and Indonesia's fuel subsidy restructuring, which made coal a more cost-competitive industrial fuel — particularly for medium-sized manufacturers in Java and Sumatra.

## Purchased Electricity Aggregates

Because some years have structural gaps in one electricity source (e.g., non-PLN is absent in 2000), simply adding PLN + non-PLN would silently produce zeros where the true value is unknown. Two variants handle this differently — choose based on your estimation strategy:

**Strict variant** — the aggregate is set to missing (`.`) if *either* PLN or non-PLN component is missing. Use this when you want conservative treatment: an unknown component means the total is unknown.

```stata
gen elec_purchased_kwh_strict = elec_pln_kwh + elec_nonpln_kwh
```

**Zerofill variant** — structural missing is treated as 0 (i.e., the absent component is assumed to be zero for that firm-year). A flag variable (`_nfilled`) records how many components were zero-filled per observation, so you can subset or weight accordingly. Use this for balanced-panel regressions where a missing aggregate would drop too many observations.

```stata
egen elec_purchased_kwh_zero   = rowtotal(elec_pln_kwh elec_nonpln_kwh)
gen  elec_purchased_kwh_nfilled = missing(elec_pln_kwh) + missing(elec_nonpln_kwh)
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Own-generated electricity (`elec_owngene_kwh`) is excluded from both aggregates.** Including it would double-count with the Scope 1 fuel combustion used to run the generator. It is retained as a standalone variable for energy capacity or total-use analysis.
:::

## Emission-Input Variable Mapping

The table below identifies which harmonized variables enter the carbon-emission calculation and which are retained for diagnostic purposes only. This is the definitive reference for what feeds into `co2_*` output variables in `si_energy_emissions.dta`.

### Scope 1 — Direct Fuel Combustion

| Harmonized variable | Unit | Emission output variable | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fuel_diesel_ltr` | liters | `co2_diesel_s1`, `co2_diesel_s2` | Primary fuel; high coverage (223 k obs) |
| `fuel_petrol_ltr` | liters | `co2_petrol_s1`, `co2_petrol_s2` | |
| `fuel_kerosene_ltr` | liters | `co2_kerosene_s1`, `co2_kerosene_s2` | Absent 2001–2002 |
| `fuel_coal_kg` | kg | `co2_coal_s1`, `co2_coal_s2` | Absent 2001–2002; unit confirmed kg |
| `fuel_lpg_kg` | kg | `co2_lpg_s1`, `co2_lpg_s2` | Absent 2001–2005 |
| `fuel_citygas_m3` | m³ | `co2_gas_s1`, `co2_gas_s2` | Absent 2001–2005 |
| `fuel_coalbriq_kg` | kg | `co2_coalbriq_s1`, `co2_coalbriq_s2` | 2012–2014 only; 894 obs; low coverage — missing treated as not-reported |
| `fuel_othergas_m3` | m³ | `co2_othergas_s1`, `co2_othergas_s2` | 2012–2014 only; 1,352 obs; low coverage — missing treated as not-reported |

Spec 1 (BPS Neraca Energi NCV) and Spec 2 (ESDM HEES NCV) differ only in the NCV applied to each fuel; the physical quantity inputs are identical. **Spec 1 is the primary analysis; Spec 2 is the robustness check.**

### Scope 2 — Purchased Electricity

Two source variables are summed to form the emission input:

| Harmonized variable | Original SI name | Unit | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `elec_pln_kwh` | `eplkhu` | kWh | PLN state grid electricity |
| `elec_nonpln_kwh` | `enpkhu` | kWh | Non-PLN purchased electricity |

These are combined into a single derived aggregate:

```
elec_purchased_kwh_strict = elec_pln_kwh + elec_nonpln_kwh
```

> Set to missing if either component is missing (strict rule — avoids understating emissions from partial data).

`co2_scope2 = elec_purchased_kwh_strict × grid_EF`

where `grid_EF` is the electricity emission factor (kg CO₂/kWh). The primary specification (Spec 1) uses a **time-varying** grid EF from BPS Neraca Energi stored in `co2_scope2_s1`; Spec 2 uses the static PLN RUPTL 2015 factor (0.000867 tCO₂/kWh).

|---|---|---|---|
| `elec_owngene_kwh` | `esgkhu` | kWh | Own-generated electricity — fuel burned already counted in Scope 1; including here would double-count |
| `elec_pln_rp` | `eplvcu` | Rp000 | Expenditure — diagnostic only (unit-price checks) |
| `elec_nonpln_rp` | `enpvcu` | Rp000 | Expenditure — diagnostic only |
| `fuel_diesel_rp`, `fuel_petrol_rp`, … | `esovcu`, `epevcu`, … | Rp000 | Fuel expenditures — diagnostic only |
| `fuel_total_reported_rp` | `efuvcu` | Rp000 | Aggregate reported total — flagged unreliable (§2.3); never used for emissions |

## Key Decision: Quantity Variables as the Primary Input for Emission Conversion

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
**Decision:** All emission estimates are computed from **physical quantity variables** (liters, kg, m³, kWh) — not from fuel expenditure variables (Rp000). Expenditure variables are retained in the dataset for diagnostics and cross-checks but are not used in the emission conversion pipeline.
:::

The SI questionnaire collects both physical quantities and expenditure values for most fuel types (see §4 variable rename map). Either could, in principle, serve as the basis for emission conversion — quantities directly, or expenditures after dividing by a price to recover an implied quantity. We use physical quantities exclusively, for three reasons:

**1. Price variability across firms and regions.** Fuel prices in Indonesia vary substantially across provinces, firm size, procurement channels (subsidised vs. non-subsidised), and over time. <a href="#ref-rentschler2017">Rentschler & Kornejew (2017)</a> document significant within-year variation in firm-level energy prices across Indonesian manufacturing using the SE2013 cross-section: price dispersion is large even within narrowly defined industry–region cells. Converting expenditure to implied quantities using a single national price — or even a province × year average — would introduce systematic measurement error that varies with firm size, location, and procurement access.

**2. Granular price data are unavailable at the firm × fuel × year level.** The SI questionnaire does not record the price at which each firm purchased each fuel. Constructing implied quantity as (expenditure ÷ price) would require an external price series matched to each observation. No publicly available series provides Indonesian fuel prices at the firm × province × year resolution needed to do this without strong and untestable assumptions.

**3. Uniform-price assumption is implausible.** The only tractable alternative — dividing all firms' expenditures by a single (or province-level) average price — implicitly assumes every firm faces the same marginal fuel price. This is implausible in the Indonesian context, where large manufacturers often negotiate bulk-purchase discounts, where subsidised fuel allocation has historically favoured smaller firms, and where transport costs create substantial regional price wedges. Physical quantities, as self-reported by the firm, require no such assumption.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Implication:** Fuel expenditure variables (`fuel_*_rp`) should not be interpreted as emission proxies or used in place of quantity-based emission variables. Their appropriate use is as a cross-check (e.g., confirming that a quantity spike is matched by a proportional expenditure spike, as done in the §4.1 coal unit diagnostic) or as a cost-side outcome in a separate analysis.
:::

As supporting evidence of the price variation previously documented by Rentschler & Kornejew (2017) using the SE2013 cross-section, this study also estimates median energy and electricity unit prices by industry and province from the SI panel 2000–2014. The purpose is to verify whether the decision to use physical quantities — rather than expenditure-derived prices — to estimate energy efficiency is justified. If unit prices vary substantially across industries and provinces, then a monetary intensity measure would embed systematic price differences as apparent efficiency differences, which would be confounded with the quantity-based measure we aim for.

The figure below has a 2×2 structure: the top row covers **diesel** (by industry and by province), the bottom row covers **PLN electricity** (same layout). Each row is a horizontal boxplot (box = IQR, vertical line = median, whiskers = Tukey 1.5×IQR). For the province panels, boxplots are sorted by island group from **West to East** — Sumatera → Jawa → Bali+NT → Kalimantan → Sulawesi → Maluku → Papua — making inter-island price gradients directly visible alongside within-island variation.

Key patterns: IQR whiskers show that price dispersion exists not only *between* industries but also *within* the same industry, reflecting differences in procurement channel, fuel grade, and transaction scale. The province panels reveal that outer-island firms (Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Maluku+Papua) tend to face higher diesel prices than Jawa and Sumatera, consistent with higher transport costs and thinner distribution networks. PLN electricity tariffs show a similar geographic gradient, driven by PLN's regional cost structures and uneven subsidy pass-through. A monetary intensity measure would embed all of these price gradients as apparent differences in energy efficiency — when they reflect nothing more than location and market access. This confirms the rationale for using physical quantity-based emission estimates as the primary outcome variable.

![**Figure 5.6.** Energy unit price heterogeneity across industries and provinces, SI panel 2000–2014. Prices computed as expenditure (Rp000) ÷ physical quantity; trimmed at p1–p99. **Panel A (navy, top-left):** Median diesel unit price (Rp000/litre) by 2-digit ISIC manufacturing industry, sorted by median; box = IQR, vertical line = median, whiskers = Tukey 1.5×IQR. **Panel B (navy, top-right):** Median diesel price by province, sorted by island group **West → East** (Sumatera → Jawa → Bali+NT → Kalimantan → Sulawesi → Maluku → Papua), then price within group — the inter-island gradient is directly visible. **Panel C (teal, bottom-left):** Median PLN electricity price (Rp000/kWh) by industry. **Panel D (teal, bottom-right):** Median electricity price by province with the same West → East island-group sorting. Across both fuels, prices span roughly a **3–5× range** across industries and a **2–4× range** across island groups — confirming that a monetary intensity measure would embed systematic price gradients as apparent efficiency differences. Source: `si_energy_emissions.dta` · Script: `scripts/fig_unit_price.py`.](../output/figures/fig_unit_price_heterogeneity.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

# Data Quality Diagnostics

This chapter documents the quality of the harmonized energy variables through two complementary lenses: trend figures that reveal structural patterns and survey-gap artefacts, and a systematic three-dimension flagging strategy (D1 cross-sectional, D2 longitudinal, D3 intensity) that identifies observations with suspicious level, growth, or intensity characteristics. No observations are removed here — the cleaning decision is made in the next chapter.

## Data-Quality Flags

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Do-file:** `dofiles/08_outlier_flags.do` · **Input:** `output/si_energy_harmonized.dta` · **Output:** `output/si_energy_flagged.dta` · `output/tables/flag_summary_by_year.csv` · `output/tables/flag_summary_by_isic2.csv`
:::

This section documents the data-quality flagging strategy applied to `si_energy_harmonized.dta`. At this detection stage, the strategy follows a **flag-never-delete** principle: no observations are removed; instead, flag variables are attached so that robustness checks can be run on sub-samples defined by flag severity. The cleaning decision — which flags to act on and how — is made in §6.

### Why Not DEA or ML Smoothing?

A common suggestion for detecting irregular firm-level energy use is to apply Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) or ML-based outlier correction. Both approaches are inappropriate here:

- **DEA** benchmarks firms against the frontier of the most efficient producers and flags those furthest from it. Because the research question asks whether internationalizing firms *become more efficient*, pre-selecting on efficiency using DEA would remove the variation of interest — a circular exclusion that biases the treatment effect toward zero. <a href="#ref-simar2007">Simar & Wilson (2007)</a> formally demonstrate that when efficiency scores serve as dependent or conditioning variables in a second-stage model, the circularity induces inconsistent estimation; the same logic applies when DEA scores are used as a pre-filter before a treatment effects analysis. <a href="#ref-heckman1997">Heckman, Ichimura & Todd (1997)</a> establish the underlying general principle: conditioning on the outcome variable — rather than on pre-treatment covariates — invalidates causal identification.

- **ML smoothing** (e.g., smoothing splines, isolation forests trained on the outcome) imputes or down-weights unusual values based on distributional assumptions. This manufactures artificial smoothness in the data and makes inference on genuine efficiency changes unreliable. <a href="#ref-bound2001">Bound, Brown & Mathiowetz (2001)</a> document how imputing or smoothing measurement error in panel data biases within-firm estimators, attenuating the coefficient of interest; <a href="#ref-bollinger2006">Bollinger & Hirsch (2006)</a> show that survey-data imputation compresses the variance and attenuates estimated effects — precisely the problem that arises when genuine efficiency improvements are smoothed away as statistical outliers.

The correct approach is to flag on *data-plausibility* criteria that are orthogonal to the efficiency outcome: cross-sectional level extremes, year-on-year growth rates, and internal consistency checks.

### Three-Dimension Flagging Strategy

Eleven variables are flagged: the seven main series (`fuel_diesel_ltr`, `fuel_petrol_ltr`, `fuel_kerosene_ltr`, `fuel_coal_kg`, `fuel_lpg_kg`, `fuel_citygas_m3`, `elec_pln_kwh`) plus four additional emission inputs (`fuel_coalbriq_kg`, `fuel_othergas_m3`, `fuel_coke_kg`, `elec_nonpln_kwh`). Each passes through three diagnostic dimensions:

| Dim | Name | What is checked | Moderate flag | Severe flag |
|:---:|------|-----------------|:---:|:---:|
| **D1** | Cross-sectional level | Is this firm's energy consumption level unusually high or low **compared to other firms in the same industry (ISIC 2-digit) and year**? Flags when log value deviates from the ISIC × year cell median by more than *k* × IQR. Threshold basis: k = 3 is Tukey's standard "extreme outlier" fence; k = 5 is a conservative extension that retains genuine energy-intensive firms. | > 3 × IQR from cell median | > 5 × IQR from cell median |
| **D2** | Year-on-year growth | Does this firm's own energy consumption change by an implausible amount **from one year to the next**? Flags when the absolute log change between consecutive firm-years exceeds the threshold. Threshold basis: 10× (moderate) is already well above any documented genuine operational change; 50× (severe) is unambiguous — almost certainly a unit error (e.g., kWh vs MWh) or transcription error. | > 10× year-on-year change | > 50× year-on-year change |
| **D3** | Intensity per worker | Is this firm's **energy use per worker** unusually high or low compared to peers in the same industry and year? Same IQR check as D1 but applied to log(value / workers). Catches firms whose absolute level looks normal but whose intensity is extreme — e.g., a plant consuming a normal absolute amount of coal but employing very few workers. Same threshold basis as D1. | > 3 × IQR from cell median | > 5 × IQR from cell median |

**Cell-size tiering (D1, D3):** Cells with N ≥ 30 apply both moderate and severe thresholds. Cells with N 10–29 apply severe only. Cells with N < 10 fall back to year-level thresholds. This prevents small-cell noise from generating spurious moderate flags in sparse ISIC × year combinations.

**Structural gap suppression (D2):** Year-on-year changes crossing known survey-design gaps are not flagged. Specifically: `fuel_coal_kg` and `fuel_kerosene_ltr` (2001–2002 gap); `fuel_lpg_kg` and `fuel_citygas_m3` (2001–2005 gap). The first post-gap year is excluded from the D2 computation for the affected variable.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Literature basis for the three-dimension strategy.** Each dimension maps directly to a cleaning approach used in prior SI/IBS studies reviewed in Appendix B (§B.1):

- **D1 (cross-sectional level)** follows the **<a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a>** tradition of applying distributional bounds within industry × period cells — their mode × 500 rule on intensity variables is the same logic applied to a kernel density rather than an IQR. **<a href="#ref-rentschler2017">Rentschler & Kornejew (2017)</a>** apply an analogous provincial industry percentile trim (2.5th/97.5th) to energy price variables in the same SI questionnaire structure.

- **D2 (year-on-year growth)** is directly taken from **<a href="#ref-amiti2007">Amiti & Konings (2007, *American Economic Review*)</a>** — the SI benchmark for causal inference — who "exclude plants with unrealistically large spikes in the data, by dropping the 1st and 99th percentiles of the distribution of plant-level output growth and input growth." **<a href="#ref-narjoko2006">Narjoko (2006)</a>** applies an equivalent asymmetric growth threshold on value added (< −90% or > +300%) and employment (< −70% or > +200%), finding approximately 11% of observations removed per year from this step alone.

- **D3 (intensity per worker)** follows **<a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a>**, who apply the mode × 500 rule to *intensity* variables (energy per unit output) rather than raw levels — D3 adapts this to log(energy / workers) as the intensity metric, and **<a href="#ref-hartono2011">Hartono, Irawan & Achsani (2011)</a>** standardise physical energy quantities to a common intensity unit as their primary filter.

Together, D1 and D3 represent the **intensity-bounds family** (Armundito-Kaneko tradition) and D2 represents the **growth-trim family** (Amiti-Konings tradition). The two families cover the main approaches documented across eleven prior SI studies without requiring a balanced panel — which would eliminate most treatment events for the event study design.
:::

### Recommended Robustness Specifications

All robustness samples are available in `si_energy_flagged.dta` via the composite flag variables.

| Specification | Condition | N retained |
|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Full matched sample | 326,382 |
| **Conservative** | `flag_any_mod == 0` | 285,541 |
| **Stringent** | `flag_any_sev == 0` | 314,576 |
| **Multi-dim** | `flag_n_dims < 2` | 324,203 |

The **recommended baseline** is the full matched sample (flag-never-delete). For robustness tables in the paper, run the main specification on the Stringent sample (`flag_any_sev == 0`) and the Multi-dim sample (`flag_n_dims < 2`) and report whether emission estimates change materially.

## Cleaning Rule Applied

Based on the flag evidence above, the following rule is applied in `dofiles/09_clean_apply.do`:

| Filter | Rule | Obs dropped |
|--------|------|-------------|
| D1/D2/D3 severe | `flag_any_sev == 1` | 11,806 — extreme level, growth, or intensity outliers |
| **Cleaned total** | | **314,576 obs retained (96.38% of matched panel)** |

**Output:** `output/si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta`. This is the primary input to the emission conversion pipeline. The full flagged sample (`si_energy_flagged.dta`, N = 326,382) is retained for robustness.

Full justification — including comparison with eleven prior SI studies and the causal-inference rationale for this threshold — is in [Appendix B](#sec-appendix-cleaning).

**Input:** `output/si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta` (primary) · `output/si_energy_flagged.dta` (full sample, robustness) · **Output:** `output/si_energy_emissions.dta`

## Input Variable Coverage

Before applying emission factors it is necessary to know which physical quantity variables are sufficiently populated to serve as reliable inputs, and how missing values will be handled.

### Coverage summary

N-positive counts are documented in §5.4. The table below extends that summary by classifying each input variable by its usability for emission conversion across the 2000–2014 panel (326,382 firm-years).

| Variable | Scope | N positive | Coverage | Usable in balanced panel? |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| `elec_pln_kwh` | 2 | 308,513 | 87.5% | Yes — backbone of Scope 2 |
| `elec_nonpln_kwh` | 2 | 20,278 | 5.8% | Yes — minority supplement |
| `fuel_diesel_ltr` | 1 | 223,163 | 63.3% | Yes — most common fuel |
| `fuel_petrol_ltr` | 1 | 181,616 | 51.5% | Yes |
| `fuel_kerosene_ltr` | 1 | 59,963 | 17.0% | Partial — absent 2001–2002 |
| `fuel_lpg_kg` | 1 | 42,349 | 12.0% | Partial — absent 2001–2005 |
| `fuel_coal_kg` | 1 | 16,331 | 4.6% | Partial — absent 2001–2002; heavy industry only |
| `fuel_citygas_m3` | 1 | 14,350 | 4.1% | Partial — absent 2001–2005 |
| `fuel_othergas_m3` | 1 | 1,352 | 0.4% | **Yes** — 2012–2014 only; included for reporting firms ^†^ |
| `fuel_coalbriq_kg` | 1 | 894 | 0.3% | **Yes** — 2012–2014 only; included for reporting firms ^†^ |
| `fuel_coke_kg` | 1 | ~sparse | <0.1% | **Yes** — sparse; included for reporting firms ^†^ |
| `fuel_firewood_kg` | 1 | ~sparse | <0.1% | No — biogenic (biomass); CO₂ excluded from Scope 1 per IPCC 2006 ^‡^ |
| `fuel_charcoal_kg` | 1 | ~sparse | <0.1% | No — biogenic (biomass); CO₂ excluded from Scope 1 per IPCC 2006 ^‡^ |
| `fuel_lubricant_ltr` | — | — | — | No — non-combustion; no direct CO₂ emissions |

> ^†^ **Why include sparse and short-panel fuels?** Excluding `fuel_othergas_m3`, `fuel_coalbriq_kg`, and `fuel_coke_kg` from the emission sum would systematically understate emissions for the firms that do report them. Low coverage is a data limitation — it does not mean the emissions are absent. These fuels are treated identically to others: missing = not reported (not zero); the `co2_scope1_nfuels` counter (0–9) records how many fuels contributed to each firm-year's Scope 1 total.

> ^‡^ Per IPCC 2006 guidelines and GHG Protocol, CO₂ from biomass combustion (firewood, charcoal) is reported separately from fossil fuel Scope 1 and is not counted in the manufacturing sector total. This is a methodological convention, not a data limitation.

### Missingness treatment

**Missing physical quantity values are treated as missing (`.`), not zero.** A firm that does not report a fuel quantity may genuinely not use that fuel, or may have failed to report it — these two cases cannot be distinguished from the data alone. Setting missing to zero would systematically understate emissions for non-reporting firms and bias cross-firm comparisons.

The practical implication:

- `co2_scope1_s1` will be missing for any firm-year where **all** fuel quantity variables are missing.
- Firm-years that report some fuels but not others will have a **partial** Scope 1 figure — it covers only the reported fuels.
- The `_nfilled` flag pattern from §5.3 (used for electricity aggregates) is applied analogously: a companion variable `co2_scope1_nfuels` records how many of the 9 fuel types contributed to the Scope 1 sum (range 0–9), so analysts can filter on completeness.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
**Implication for panel analysis:** Scope 1 emissions are most comparable cross-sectionally within years where the same fuel variables are collected. For 2001–2005, gas and LPG are structurally absent — firms in those years will have lower Scope 1 totals than identical firms post-2005 purely due to survey design. Regressions spanning the full 2000–2014 panel should include fuel-type fixed effects or restrict to diesel + petrol + electricity as the consistently-measured components.
:::

### Lubricants

`fuel_lubricant_ltr` is retained in `si_energy_harmonized.dta` for reference but is **excluded from Scope 1 emission conversion**. Lubricants are a non-combustion petroleum product — they are consumed as mechanical input, not burned as fuel, and therefore generate no direct CO₂ emissions under IPCC GHG accounting.

## Literature Basis

With the coverage constraints established above, the conversion follows the standard approach in the Indonesian manufacturing literature. **Scope 1 (direct fuel combustion)** uses a two-step process:

1. **Physical units → GJ** using energy content coefficients (Net Calorific Values, NCV) specific to Indonesian fuel quality
2. **GJ → kg CO₂e** using <a href="#ref-ipcc2006">IPCC (2006)</a> Tier-1 default emission factors

**Scope 2 (purchased electricity)** uses a single-step approach: firm kWh are multiplied directly by a grid emission factor (tCO₂/kWh). No intermediate GJ conversion is applied to firm electricity consumption — the grid EF is already expressed in tCO₂/kWh because it is constructed by dividing total power-plant emissions (computed from generating fuel quantities × NCV × IPCC EF) by total kWh generated. This is documented separately in §7.7.

**Step 2 is identical across all prior studies** — IPCC 2006 Tier-1 defaults are the accepted standard for Indonesia because country-specific emission factors are incomplete. **What distinguishes this pipeline is Step 1:** the choice of NCV source. Prior studies (Zain et al. 2025; Rosita et al. 2020) use the ESDM HEES as their NCV source. This pipeline introduces **BPS Neraca Energi** NCV values as the primary specification (Spec 1) — the same source used by BPS for Indonesia's official national energy balance — and retains ESDM HEES as a robustness check (Spec 2). This choice affects LPG in particular, where the ESDM HEES value (52.145 GJ/ton) is on a GCV basis while IPCC 2006 emission factors require NCV; the BPS Neraca Energi value (45.544 GJ/ton) is on a consistent NCV basis (see §7.5).

This approach is used by **<a href="#ref-zain2025">Zain, Patunru & Hartono (2025)</a>** (Hybrid Energy IO framework) and is consistent with **<a href="#ref-rosita2020">Rosita et al. (2020)</a>**, who apply the same IPCC-based logic via a BOE/TCE intermediate step. **<a href="#ref-ramstetter2014">Ramstetter & Narjoko (2014)</a>** apply a closely related approach for cross-sectional energy efficiency analysis using the same BPS census data (1996 and 2006), using purchased electricity quantity as a proxy for total energy following Eskeland & Harrison (2003).

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Key references:** <a href="#ref-ipcc2006">IPCC (2006)</a> — Table 2.3, _Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories_, Vol. 2, Ch. 2 (manufacturing-specific emission factors, CO₂ + CH4 + N2O) · <a href="#ref-zain2025">Zain et al. (2025)</a> — Table 1 (ESDM HEES energy content factors) · <a href="#ref-rosita2020">Rosita et al. (2020)</a> — confirms same IPCC-based approach. Full synthesis in `literature/literature_synthesis.md`.
:::

### National Benchmark: Indonesian Manufacturing Emission Intensity Trends

Two BPS publications provide aggregate *Industri Pengolahan* (ISIC Section C) benchmarks that contextualise the firm-level emission estimates. The **2011–2015 Experimental Energy Flow Accounts** (<a href="#ref-bps2018naei">BPS 2018</a>, *Laporan Uji Coba Neraca Arus Energi Indonesia*, Catalog 6204002) overlaps directly with the final years of the SI panel; the **2015–2019 Neraca Emisi GRK** (<a href="#ref-bps_neraca_grk">BPS 2021</a>) extends the picture forward.

**Panel A — Manufacturing CO₂ Emissions (Gg = thousand tCO₂), 2011–2015**

| Indicator | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 | 2014 | 2015 | 2019 |
|-----------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Manufacturing CO₂ (thousand tCO₂) | 161,832 | 169,302 | 129,492 | 69,555 | 89,441 | 161,652 |
| Energy intensity (PJ/trillion IDR GVA)^a^ | 3.37 | 3.03 | 2.87 | 2.35 | 2.21 | — |
| Energy intensity (GJ/Rp billion GVA)^b^ | — | — | — | — | 706 | 987 |
| Energy consumption (PJ)^b^ | — | — | — | — | 4,273 | 5,302 |

> ^a^ Source: <a href="#ref-bps2018naei">BPS (2018)</a> *Laporan Uji Coba Neraca Arus Energi Indonesia 2011–2015* (Catalog 6204002, extracted). Unit: PJ per trillion IDR GVA at current prices. 1 PJ/trillion IDR ≈ 1,000 GJ/billion IDR (current prices); the difference vs. Panel B reflects GVA deflator and scope differences between publications.
>
> ^b^ Source: <a href="#ref-bps_neraca_grk">BPS (2021)</a> *Neraca Arus Energi dan Neraca Emisi GRK Indonesia 2015–2019* (extracted). Unit: GJ per Rp billion GVA; energy consumption in PJ.

**Key observations:**

- Manufacturing CO₂ emissions **peaked in 2012** (169,302 thousand tCO₂), fell sharply to a low in 2014 (69,555), then partially recovered in 2015 (89,441) and rose strongly through 2019 (161,652 — nearly matching the 2012 peak).
- Energy intensity in manufacturing **declined consistently 2011–2015** (3.37 → 2.21 PJ/trillion IDR) — the only major industry with a monotone improvement in that period. This suggests efficiency gains even as absolute emissions fluctuated.
- The sharp **2014 dip in CO₂** (−46% from 2013) is puzzling; it likely reflects a combination of lower output in energy-intensive subsectors and composition effects rather than a genuine efficiency shock.

**Interpretation for this study:** In 2015–2019, Indonesian manufacturing reversed its intensity gains and became *more* carbon-intensive — aggregate CO₂ rose 81% on only 24% more energy consumption, driven by rising coal share in the fuel mix (coal surpassed natural gas by 2018). If the analysis finds that newly internationalising firms show *declining* emission intensity over our 2000–2014 window, they are swimming against a macro tide that was already worsening — making any such finding more economically meaningful.

This aggregate trend also has a methodological implication: coal-intensive industries (ISIC 23 – non-metallic minerals, ISIC 27 – basic metals) drive the aggregate worsening and should be checked for composition effects in the analytical sample.
