## Conversion Workflow (Detail)

For **Scope 1 fuels**, the preferred approach is the **direct GJ pathway** (per <a href="#ref-zain2025">Zain et al. 2025</a>):

```
physical unit  ×  energy content (GJ/unit)  →  GJ  ×  EF (kg CO₂e/GJ)  ÷  1,000  →  tCO₂e
```

For **Scope 2 (purchased electricity)**, the pathway skips the GJ step entirely:

```
kWh  ×  grid_EF (tCO₂/kWh, year-specific)  →  tCO₂e
```

**Example — diesel (Solar):**

$$\underbrace{\text{fuel\_diesel\_ltr}}_{\text{litres}} \times \underbrace{0.040051}_{\text{GJ/litre (Spec 2 NCV)}} \times \underbrace{74.35}_{\text{kg CO}_2\text{e/GJ}} \div 1{,}000 = \mathbf{0.002978} \text{ tCO}_2\text{e/litre}$$

The composite per-unit factors in §7.6 are pre-computed from this formula and applied directly in Stata. The next two sections document each input separately: §7.5 provides the energy content values (Step 1 — physical unit → GJ); §7.6 provides the emission factors and the resulting composite conversion rate (Step 2 — GJ → tCO₂e).

## Energy Content Factors {#sec-ncv}

> **Role in the pipeline:** This is **Step 1** — converting the SI/IBS physical quantity (litres, kg, m³) into a common energy unit (GJ). These values answer the question *"how much energy is in one unit of this fuel?"* They are **not** emission factors — no carbon content information is used at this stage. Two sources are used: **Spec 1 (primary)** draws from BPS *Neraca Energi* — Indonesia's official national energy balance; **Spec 2 (robustness)** draws from ESDM HEES, following prior literature.

> **These values are physical constants and do not vary by year.** NCV values for individual fuels are stable properties of the fuel's chemical composition. For **Spec 1 (BPS Neraca Energi)**: values were verified as identical across the 2006–2010 and 2011–2015 editions ("Standar Faktor Konversi" table). The 2000–2004 edition does not contain a standalone conversion-factor table in the extracted text; the 2006–2010 values are therefore applied for years 2000–2005 — a standard assumption given that fuel chemistry does not change. For **Spec 2 (ESDM HEES)**: conversion factors (BOE/tonne basis) are identical across all editions 2007–2014; all editions cite the same source: *"Indonesia Energy Balance 1990–1994, Departemen of Mining and Energy"* — the table has not been revised since 1994. What *does* vary year-to-year in the Neraca Energi is the **grid emission factor** (Scope 2), which depends on PLN's fuel mix and is handled separately as a time-varying series (`co2_scope2_s1`, see §7.7).

| Fuel | SI/IBS variable | Unit | **Spec 1 — BPS Neraca Energi (primary)** | Spec 2 — ESDM HEES (robustness) |
|------|----------------|------|:--------------:|:--------------:|
| Diesel / Solar (HSD) | `fuel_diesel_ltr` | GJ/kL | **35.697** | 40.051 |
| Gasoline / Bensin | `fuel_petrol_ltr` | GJ/kL | **33.225** | 35.647 |
| Kerosene / Minyak Tanah | `fuel_kerosene_ltr` | GJ/kL | **34.559** | 36.258 |
| Fuel Oil / Bunker C | `fuel_fueloil_ltr` | GJ/kL | [**42.582** *(HEES fallback)*]{style="color:red"} | 42.582 |
| Coal / Batubara | `fuel_coal_kg` | GJ/tonne | **26.200** ^d^ | 25.691 |
| Coke / Kokas | `fuel_coke_kg` | GJ/tonne | **26.377** ^f^ | 27.000 |
| Coal Briquettes / Briket | `fuel_coalbriq_kg` | GJ/tonne | **29.308** ^f^ | **20.700** ^a^ |
| LPG | `fuel_lpg_kg` | GJ/tonne | **45.544** | 52.145 ^e^ |
| City gas / PGN (`egam3u`) | `fuel_citygas_m3` | GJ/m³ | **0.048** | 0.039 |
| Gas non-PGN (`egom3u`) | `fuel_othergas_m3` | GJ/m³ | **0.048** | 0.039 |
| Firewood / Kayu Bakar | `fuel_firewood_kg` | GJ/tonne | *Biogenic — excluded from Scope 1* | *Biogenic — excluded from Scope 1* |
| Charcoal / Arang | `fuel_charcoal_kg` | GJ/tonne | *Biogenic — excluded from Scope 1* ^a^ | *Biogenic — excluded from Scope 1* ^a^ |

Sources: **Spec 1** — BPS *Neraca Energi Indonesia*, editions 2006–2010 and 2011–2015 ("Standar Faktor Konversi" table), published by Badan Pusat Statistik. Basis: NCV, aligned with UN/IRES international standards (explicitly stated in Neraca Energi methodology). Liquid fuel values converted using Indonesian standard fuel densities per KESDM (diesel 0.840 kg/L, gasoline 0.740 kg/L, kerosene 0.800 kg/L). **Spec 2** — ESDM *Handbook of Energy and Economic Statistics of Indonesia* (HEES), editions 2007–2014 ("Conversion Factor" table), via <a href="#ref-zain2025">Zain, Patunru & Hartono (2025)</a> Table 1. HEES conversion factors are expressed as BOE/tonne (or BOE/kL) and are identical across all editions 2007–2014; all editions cite *"Indonesia Energy Balance 1990–1994, Departemen of Mining and Energy"* as source. **HEES does not explicitly label its conversion factors as GCV or NCV.** However, HEES uses "gross calorific value" (*nilai kalor kotor*) terminology when defining fuel categories, and the LPG value (52.145 GJ/tonne) is ~14.6% higher than the BPS Neraca Energi NCV (45.544 GJ/tonne) — a margin consistent with the known GCV–NCV gap for LPG (~12–14%). As IPCC 2006 emission factors require NCV inputs, Spec 1 (BPS Neraca Energi, explicit NCV) is the methodologically preferred specification. The Fuel Oil Spec 1 value (42.582 GJ/kL) is consistent with the Neraca Energi "Minyak Bakar" value of 41.500 GJ/ton when converted at heavy fuel oil density (~1.026 kg/L).

> ^a^ HEES does not publish a separate NCV for coal briquettes, so **Spec 2 uses the IPCC 2006 default** for brown coal briquettes: **20.700 GJ/tonne**. **Spec 1 uses the BPS Neraca Energi 2011–2015 value (29.308 GJ/tonne)**; see footnote ^f^ for edition details. Charcoal is biogenic (made from wood) — CO₂ from combustion is not counted in Scope 1 per IPCC 2006 and GHG Protocol (short-cycle carbon, reported separately).

> ^f^ BPS Neraca Energi 2011–2015 (Standard Conversion Factors table) lists **Kokas (Coke) = 26.377 GJ/tonne** and **Briket (Briquettes) = 29.308 GJ/tonne**. The 2016–2020 edition lists different values (20.195 and 30.209 respectively), reflecting a revision to BPS's conversion methodology after the sample period ends. Since SI/IBS data for coke and briquettes first appears in 2012–2014, the 2011–2015 Neraca edition is the appropriate reference for Spec 1. The 2016–2020 values should not be used for a panel ending in 2014.

> ^d^ **Why not Neraca Energi "Hard Coal" (29.3 GJ/tonne)?** That figure refers to high-rank coal (*batubara keras/antrasit*) — not the thermal coal used by Indonesian manufacturing firms, which is predominantly sub-bituminous from Kalimantan. Using 29.3 would overstate coal emissions by ~14%. **Why Kalimantan (26.2)?** HEES `table_101.md` gives Kalimantan thermal coal a BOE conversion factor of 4.2766, yielding:

$$4.2766 \text{ BOE/ton} \times 6.117 \text{ GJ/BOE} = 26.2 \text{ GJ/ton}$$

This is the same factor as "Imported Coal", confirming HEES treats this as the reference Indonesian thermal coal. Kalimantan (East + South + Central) supplies approximately 86–89% of national coal production (Arinaldo & Adiatma, [2019](#ref-arinaldo2019); data from Petromindo), making it the most likely supply source for the average SI firm. Note: SI data does not record coal origin — this is an assumption. The Kalimantan thermal NCV (26.2 GJ/ton, based on HEES regional tables) is used as the Spec 1 base; the sensitivity of this assumption is tested via the `alt_coal_kalimantan` variant (see §7 — Sensitivity Variants).

> ^e^ **LPG GCV/NCV flag:** ESDM HEES does not explicitly state whether its conversion factors are GCV or NCV basis. However, the LPG value (52.145 GJ/tonne) is ~14.6% higher than the BPS Neraca Energi NCV (45.544 GJ/tonne) and substantially above the IPCC 2006 NCV default (47.3 GJ/tonne) — a margin consistent with the known GCV–NCV gap for LPG (~12–14%). This inference is reinforced by HEES's use of "gross calorific value" terminology in its fuel-category definitions. Since IPCC 2006 emission factors require NCV inputs, using the HEES LPG value as-is would overstate LPG emissions by ~12.7%. Spec 1 (BPS Neraca Energi, explicit NCV basis per IRES) is therefore methodologically preferred for LPG.

### NCV Comparison: Spec 1 vs. Prior Work (Spec 2)

Key NCV values from the "Standard Conversion Factors" table in BPS Neraca Energi editions (2006–2010 and 2011–2015 editions used; the 2016–2020 edition is outside the sample period).

**Cross-edition consistency:** BPS publishes the Neraca Energi in multi-year editions (2000–2004, 2006–2010, 2011–2015, 2012–2016, 2016–2020). The NCV values for each fuel are physical properties of the fuel's chemical composition — they do **not** change year to year and are consistent across all editions consulted. We verified this by comparing the "Standard Conversion Factors" table across the 2006–2010 and 2011–2015 editions: all liquid fuel and gas NCV values are identical. **The single exception** is Coke (Kokas) and Coal Briquettes (Briket), which were revised between the 2011–2015 and 2016–2020 editions (see footnote ^g^). Since coke and briquettes appear in SI data only from 2012–2014, the **2011–2015 Neraca edition** is used for those two fuels. All other NCV values in the table below apply uniformly across the full 2000–2014 sample period.

Note: the values in this comparison table are expressed in **GJ/tonne** (mass basis) — the native unit in BPS Neraca Energi. The §7.5 main table expresses liquid fuel NCVs in **GJ/kL** (volume basis) after applying standard fuel densities. The two representations are equivalent, e.g. for diesel:

$$42.496 \text{ GJ/tonne} \times 0.840 \text{ kg/L} \times \frac{1 \text{ tonne}}{1{,}000 \text{ kg}} \times 1{,}000 \text{ L/kL} = \mathbf{35.697} \text{ GJ/kL}$$

No information is lost in conversion.

| Fuel | SI variable | Indonesia NCV | Prior work | Diff | Assessment |
|------|------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| Diesel / Gas Oil | `fuel_diesel_ltr` | 42.496 GJ/ton | 43.0 GJ/ton (IPCC) | −1.2% | Minor |
| Gasoline | `fuel_petrol_ltr` | 44.899 GJ/ton | 44.3 GJ/ton | +1.3% | Minor |
| Kerosene | `fuel_kerosene_ltr` | 43.199 GJ/ton | 43.8 GJ/ton | −1.4% | Minor |
| Fuel Oil | `fuel_fueloil_ltr` | 41.500 GJ/ton | 40.4 GJ/ton | +2.7% | Minor |
| LPG | `fuel_lpg_kg` | 45.544 GJ/ton | 52.145 GJ/ton (Zain) | **−12.7%** | **Investigate** |
| Hard Coal | `fuel_coal_kg` | 29.308 GJ/ton | 25.691 GJ/ton (prior) | +14.1% | See note |
| Lignite | — | 11.283 GJ/ton | 11.9 GJ/ton (IPCC) | −5.2% | Minor |
| Coke | `fuel_coke_kg` | 26.377 GJ/ton ^g^ | 27.0 GJ/ton (HEES) | −2.3% | Minor (low coverage) |
| Coal Briquettes | `fuel_coalbriq_kg` | 29.308 GJ/ton ^g^ | ~20.7 GJ/ton (IPCC default) | +41.6% | Substantial diff; low coverage |
| Natural Gas | — | 48.000 GJ/ton | 48.0 GJ/ton | ~0% | Consistent |

> ^g^ Neraca Energi 2011–2015 "Standard Conversion Factors" table (the most recent edition within the 2000–2014 sample period). The 2016–2020 edition revised these values to **Coke = 20.195 GJ/ton** and **Briquettes = 30.209 GJ/ton**, reflecting a post-sample methodology change and should not be applied to SI data ending in 2014.

**LPG:** Neraca Energi 45.54 vs. <a href="#ref-zain2025">Zain et al.</a> 52.145 GJ/ton (−12.7%). IPCC 2006 Tier 1 = 47.3 GJ/ton. HEES does not label this value as GCV or NCV, but the ~14.6% gap relative to Neraca Energi NCV is consistent with a GCV convention for LPG (typical GCV–NCV spread ~12–14%). Prior work using HEES likely applied this value without GCV→NCV correction. This difference is fully captured by the Spec 1 (Neraca Energi, explicit NCV) vs. Spec 2 (HEES, unlabelled — inferred GCV) comparison.

**Coal — why not the Neraca Energi "national" value (29.3 GJ/ton)?** The BPS Neraca Energi publishes a single "Hard Coal" (*batubara keras*) NCV of 29.3 GJ/ton. This figure refers to **high-rank coal** — closer to antrasit or bituminous tua with high carbon density. Indonesian manufacturing firms overwhelmingly use **thermal coal** (sub-bituminous to bituminous), which has substantially lower calorific value. Applying 29.3 GJ/ton to typical SI coal reporters would overstate their energy content — and therefore their CO₂ emissions — by approximately **+14%** relative to the HEES baseline (25.691). The Neraca Energi "Hard Coal" category is therefore not the appropriate reference for the SI panel.

**Why Kalimantan (26.2 GJ/ton)?** The ESDM HEES publishes region-specific BOE conversion factors for Indonesian coal by origin (`literature/03_energy_statistics_handbooks/_extracted/tables/table_101.md`, using 1 BOE = 6.117 GJ):

| Coal type | BOE/ton | GJ/ton | vs. prior (25.691) |
|-----------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Kalimantan thermal** | 4.2766 | **26.2** | **+2%** |
| Imported Coal | 4.2766 | 26.2 | +2% |
| Tanjung Enim (South Sumatra) | 3.7778 | 23.1 | −10% |
| Ombilin (West Sumatra) | 4.8452 | 29.6 | +15% |
| Anthracite | 4.9893 | 30.5 | +19% |
| Lignite | 3.0649 | 18.7 | −27% |

Two observations from this table support the Kalimantan choice: (1) **Kalimantan coal and Imported Coal share the identical BOE factor (4.2766)** — HEES itself treats Kalimantan thermal as the reference thermal coal for Indonesia; (2) Kalimantan (East + South + Central combined) accounts for approximately **86–89% of Indonesia's national coal production** in 2014–2017 ([Arinaldo & Adiatma, 2019](#ref-arinaldo2019), Fig. 7; underlying data: Petromindo, 2019), making it the statistically most likely supply source for the average SI manufacturing firm.

**Limitation:** The SI questionnaire does not record coal origin — we cannot verify from firm-level data which region each firm sources coal from. The Kalimantan value is an assumption based on national supply patterns. Since 26.2 is only +2% above the Spec 2 baseline (25.691), the choice between the two has negligible aggregate impact and is fully captured by the Spec 1 (primary) vs. Spec 2 (robustness) comparison.

Coke and coal briquettes together account for <0.1% of firm-years in the SI panel — negligible panel impact.

> **Cross-check:** <a href="#ref-rentschler2017">Rentschler & Kornejew (2017)</a> Table 5 reports diesel at 36.25 MJ/litre vs. Spec 1 (Neraca Energi) 35.697 MJ/litre (−1.5%) — close agreement. Spec 2 (HEES) at 40.051 MJ/litre is ~10% higher, likely reflecting GCV rather than NCV conventions. **Spec 1 (BPS Neraca Energi) values are preferred** as they are NCV-consistent and aligned with Indonesia's official energy balance.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Handoff to §7.6:** The energy content values in this table convert physical quantities to GJ — but GJ is still an energy unit, not a carbon unit. To complete the conversion to tCO₂e, each fuel's GJ figure must be multiplied by its carbon emission factor. That is what §7.6 does. The "tCO₂e / physical unit" column in §7.6 is simply the product of the NCV (this table) and the emission factor (§7.6) already combined into a single Stata-ready multiplier.
:::

## CO₂ Emission Factors (Scope 1 — Direct Combustion) {#sec-ef}

> **Role in the pipeline:** This is **Step 2** — converting GJ of energy into tonnes of CO₂-equivalent (tCO₂e). These values answer the question *"how much carbon is released when one GJ of this fuel is burned?"* They come from <a href="#ref-ipcc2006">IPCC (2006)</a> and are independent of Indonesian fuel quality. The IPCC emission factors (kg CO₂e/GJ) are **identical across both specifications** — Spec 1 and Spec 2 differ only in the NCV (Step 1), not in the carbon content (Step 2). The composite tCO₂e/unit columns below pre-multiply Step 1 × Step 2 for each specification into a single Stata-ready multiplier.

> **Why tCO₂e?** Emissions are reported in metric tonnes of CO₂-equivalent (tCO₂e) because this is the standard unit used by the IPCC, GHG Protocol, and Indonesian national GHG inventory. At the firm level, individual plants emit in the range of tens to tens of thousands of tCO₂e per year — kilograms would produce unwieldy numbers, while megatonnes (Mt) would suppress meaningful variation across firms. For sector-level aggregates we convert to million tonnes (Mt CO₂e) where noted.

Source: **<a href="#ref-ipcc2006">IPCC (2006)</a> Table 2.3** — Default emission factors for stationary combustion in Manufacturing Industries and Construction (kg greenhouse gas per TJ, Net Calorific Value basis). The **kg CO₂e/GJ** values in the table below are taken directly from IPCC 2006 Table 2.3 as published — they are not computed or estimated here. What is computed in this pipeline is the **composite tCO₂e/unit** column: this multiplies the IPCC EF by the fuel-specific NCV from §7.5 and divides by 1,000 (TJ→GJ unit correction), yielding a single Stata-ready multiplier per physical unit. The CO₂e aggregation uses CO₂ + CH4×21 + N2O×310 (SAR GWPs per IPCC 2006), which is already incorporated in the Table 2.3 figures.

| Fuel | SI/IBS variable | Unit | kg CO₂e/GJ | **Spec 1 tCO₂e/unit** *(BPS Neraca Energi NCV, primary)* | **Spec 2 tCO₂e/unit** *(ESDM HEES NCV, robustness)* | IPCC 2006 Table 2.3 category |
|------|----------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| Diesel / Solar | `fuel_diesel_ltr` | litre | 74.35 | **0.002654** | 0.002978 | Gas/Diesel oil |
| Gasoline / Bensin | `fuel_petrol_ltr` | litre | 69.55 | **0.002310** | 0.002479 | Motor gasoline |
| Kerosene | `fuel_kerosene_ltr` | litre | 72.15 | **0.002494** | 0.002616 | Other kerosene |
| Fuel Oil / Bunker C | `fuel_fueloil_ltr` | litre | 77.65 | **0.003306** | 0.003306 | Residual fuel oil |
| Coal (bituminous) | `fuel_coal_kg` | kg | 95.28 | **0.002496** ^†^ | 0.002448 ^†^ | Other bituminous coal |
| Coal (sub-bituminous) | `fuel_coal_kg` | kg | 96.78 | **0.002536** ^†^ | 0.002486 ^†^ | Sub-bituminous coal |
| Coke | `fuel_coke_kg` | kg | 107.68 | **0.002840** ^f^ | 0.002907 | Coke oven coke and lignite coke |
| Coal Briquettes | `fuel_coalbriq_kg` | kg | 98.18 | **0.002877** ^f^ | 0.002032 ^a^ | Brown coal briquettes |
| LPG | `fuel_lpg_kg` | kg | 63.15 | **0.002876** | 0.003293 | Liquefied petroleum gases |
| City gas / non-PGN | `fuel_citygas_m3`, `fuel_othergas_m3` | m³ | 56.15 | **0.002695** | 0.002190 | Natural gas |

> ^†^ Coal sub-type affects the emission factor. Indonesia primarily mines **sub-bituminous coal** (Kalimantan, South Sumatra). Both Spec 1 and Spec 2 use the IPCC 2006 Other Bituminous Coal EF (95.28 tCO₂e/TJ) — the difference across specs is entirely in the NCV assumption (Kalimantan 26.2 GJ/ton for Spec 1; HEES 25.691 GJ/ton for Spec 2). The sub-bituminous EF (96.78) is only 1.6% higher than the bituminous default; this marginal difference is within measurement uncertainty and is not separately tested.

## Scope 2 — Purchased Electricity

Electricity consumed from the grid generates indirect (Scope 2) emissions. The SI/IBS data reports purchased electricity in kWh (`elec_pln_kwh`, `elec_nonpln_kwh`).

**Scope 2 uses a single-step, direct conversion — no intermediate GJ step.** The firm's kWh are multiplied directly by a grid emission factor expressed in tCO₂/kWh:

```
co2_scope2 = elec_purchased_kwh_strict × grid_EF_t
```

The 3.6 MJ/kWh thermodynamic constant (1 kWh = 0.0036 GJ) does **not** appear as an intermediate step in this calculation. Instead, the NCV of the fuels burned by PLN power plants (coal, HSD, gas) is embedded *inside* the grid EF formula when constructing the year-specific factor from Neraca Energi data — the denominator of that formula is total electricity generated in kWh, so the result is already in tCO₂/kWh (see formula below). Electricity does not appear in the §7.5 NCV table; it is handled entirely in this section.

Unlike Scope 1 fuel NCV values — which are stable physical constants across Neraca Energi editions (see §7.5) — the **grid emission factor varies meaningfully by year** because Indonesia's power generation fuel mix shifted substantially over 2000–2014 (from oil/gas-dominant to coal-dominant post-Fast Track program). Spec 1 and Spec 2 therefore use different grid EF assumptions for Scope 2:

| | **Spec 1 (primary)** | **Spec 2 (robustness)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope 2 grid EF** | Time-varying, 0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh | Static 0.000867 tCO₂/kWh |
| **Source** | BPS Neraca Energi fuel consumption × IPCC 2006 EFs ÷ total electricity generated | PLN RUPTL 2015 |
| **Variable** | `co2_scope2_s1` (year-specific EF; **primary**); `co2_total_s1` = `co2_scope1_s1` + `co2_scope2_s1` | `co2_scope2_s2` (static EF 0.000867 applied uniformly); `co2_total_s2` |
| **Rationale** | Matches actual 2000–2014 grid mix; avoids overstating 2006–2010 Scope 2 by ~33–45% | Consistent with prior SI literature; RUPTL 2015 is the standard Indonesian grid EF |

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**`co2_scope2_s1` uses the time-varying EF — fully consistent with the Spec 1 methodology.** Spec 1 draws all inputs from BPS official sources: Neraca Energi NCV values for Scope 1 and the Neraca Energi-derived year-specific grid EF for Scope 2. `co2_scope2_s1` is therefore computed using the time-varying series (0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh), implemented in `10_carbon_convert.do`. The Spec 1 vs. Spec 2 comparison (`co2_total_s1` vs. `co2_total_s2`) reflects **both** the NCV difference (Scope 1) and the grid EF difference (Scope 2) — this is the full and intended specification contrast. To isolate the pure NCV effect alone, compare `co2_scope1_s1` vs. `co2_scope1_s2` directly.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
**Why Spec 1 does not use PLN RUPTL 2015.** The PLN RUPTL 2015 value (0.000867 tCO₂/kWh) reflects the grid fuel mix of 2015 — when coal already dominated power generation. Our data covers **2000–2014**, when the grid was substantially less coal-heavy (particularly 2000–2010). Applying a 2015-calibrated factor to pre-2015 data systematically overstates Scope 2 emissions for the earlier years by ~33–45%. Spec 1 therefore constructs a year-specific grid EF from BPS Neraca Energi — the same official source used for Scope 1 NCV values — ensuring methodological consistency within the specification.
:::

**Grid EF approaches by source and period:**

| Approach | Spec | Factor | Source | Notes |
|----------|:----:|:------:|--------|-------|
| **Time-varying (Neraca Energi)** | **Spec 1** | 0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh | BPS Neraca Energi | Year-specific; primary for Spec 1 |
| **Static (PLN RUPTL 2015)** | **Spec 2** | 0.000867 tCO₂/kWh | PLN RUPTL 2015 | Uniform 2000–2014; prior literature standard |
| <a href="#ref-rosita2020">Rosita et al. (2020)</a> | Alt | 3.249 tCO₂/TCE | IPCC-based | ~0.000904 tCO₂/kWh for 2010–2014; additional robustness variant |

### Time-Varying Grid Emission Factor — Computed from BPS Neraca Energi

The BPS *Neraca Energi Indonesia* series (editions covering 2000–2004, 2006–2010, 2011–2015, 2012–2016) provides two inputs needed to compute a year-specific grid EF entirely from official Indonesian statistics:

1. **Fuel consumption by power plants** (PLN): coal (tons), HSD (kilo-litre), fuel oil (kilo-litre), natural gas (MMSCF) — from the "Konsumsi Bahan Bakar Pembangkit Listrik" table in each edition.
2. **Total electricity generated** (GWh) — from the "Produksi Listrik PLN" table.
3. **Standard conversion factors** (NCV in TJ per 000 ton) — printed in every edition; identical across all years.

The grid EF is computed year by year as:

$$\text{Grid EF}_t = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{f} \left( Q_{f,t} \times \text{NCV}_f \times \text{EF}_f \right)}{E_t}$$

where $Q_{f,t}$ = quantity of fuel $f$ consumed by PLN power plants in year $t$; $\text{NCV}_f$ = net calorific value of fuel $f$ (GJ per physical unit); $\text{EF}_f$ = IPCC 2006 Tier-1 emission factor for fuel $f$ (tCO₂/TJ); and $E_t$ = total PLN electricity generated in year $t$ (kWh). The result is in tCO₂/kWh.

Parameters used (same IPCC Tier-1 defaults as throughout the pipeline):

| Fuel | NCV | Unit | IPCC EF (tCO₂/TJ) | Source |
|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| Coal | 25.691 | GJ/tonne | 95.28 | HEES; see §7.5 note on why Neraca "Hard Coal" 29.3 is not used |
| HSD (diesel) | 42.496 | GJ/tonne (at 0.840 kg/L) | 74.35 | BPS Neraca Energi |
| Fuel oil | 41.4996 | GJ/tonne (at 0.960 kg/L) | 77.65 | BPS Neraca Energi |
| Natural gas | 1.087 | TJ/MMSCF | 56.15 | BPS Neraca Energi |

**Computed grid EFs for years with direct Neraca Energi fuel data:**

| Year | Coal input (Mt) | Gas (MMSCF) | HSD (MKL) | Fuel Oil (MKL) | Elec generated (GWh) | **Grid EF (tCO₂/kWh)** | Source |
|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| 2006 | 19.08 | 157,894 | 7.59 | 2.39 | 133,108 | **0.000630** | Neraca Energi 2006–2010 |
| 2007 | 21.47 | 171,209 | 7.87 | 2.80 | 142,441 | **0.000650** | Neraca Energi 2006–2010 |
| 2008 | 21.00 | 181,661 | 8.13 | 3.16 | 149,548 | **0.000627** | Neraca Energi 2006–2010 |
| 2009 | 21.60 | 266,539 | 6.37 | 3.03 | 156,796 | **0.000609** | Neraca Energi 2006–2010 |
| 2010 | 23.96 | 283,275 | 6.89 | 2.43 | 169,786 | **0.000599** | Neraca Energi 2006–2010 |
| 2011 | — | — | — | — | — | *~0.000690* | Interpolated |
| 2012 | — | — | — | — | — | *~0.000782* | Interpolated |
| 2013 | 58.70 | 485,023 | 6.37 | 1.19 | 222,020 | **0.000873** | Neraca Energi 2011–2015 |
| 2014 | 65.08 | 568,265 | 6.37 | 1.11 | 234,549 | **0.000914** | Neraca Energi 2011–2015 |

> **Baseline comparison:** PLN RUPTL 2015 = 0.000867 tCO₂/kWh; <a href="#ref-rosita2020">Rosita (2020)</a> alt = 0.000904 tCO₂/kWh.

> **2011–2012 interpolation — data genuinely absent in available editions.** The BPS *Neraca Energi 2011–2015* edition's "Konsumsi Bahan Bakar Pembangkit Listrik PLN" table begins its time series in **2013**, not 2011 — fuel consumption data for 2011 and 2012 is simply not tabulated in this edition. The *Neraca Energi 2006–2010* edition ends in 2010. There is therefore a genuine two-year gap (2011–2012) in the available Neraca Energi power-plant fuel consumption data; no workaround exists within these official sources.
>
> **Method — linear interpolation.** Values for 2011 and 2012 are linearly interpolated between the last directly computed point (2010: 0.000599) and the next directly computed point (2013: 0.000873), with a 3-year span:
>
> $$\text{Grid EF}_{t} = 0.000599 + \frac{t - 2010}{2013 - 2010} \times (0.000873 - 0.000599)$$
>
> Applying this formula:
>
> $$\text{Grid EF}_{2011} = 0.000599 + \tfrac{1}{3}(0.000274) = \mathbf{0.000690} \text{ tCO}_2\text{/kWh}$$
> $$\text{Grid EF}_{2012} = 0.000599 + \tfrac{2}{3}(0.000274) = \mathbf{0.000782} \text{ tCO}_2\text{/kWh}$$
>
> Linear interpolation is a conservative choice here: the actual 2011–2012 trajectory was likely non-linear (accelerating upward as Fast Track coal plants came online, roughly tripling coal input from 19 Mt in 2010 to 59 Mt by 2013). The interpolated values therefore probably understate the 2011–2012 EF relative to the true path, meaning Scope 2 emissions in those years may be slightly understated. The uncertainty is immaterial for within-firm panel estimates (year fixed effects absorb any factor that is constant within a year, including the grid EF) but should be flagged in aggregate trend-based descriptive comparisons.

> **2000–2005 — backward extrapolation.** Fuel consumption data for 2000–2004 is tabulated in the *Neraca Energi 2000–2004* edition, but natural gas quantities in that edition are expressed in MSCF (thousand standard cubic feet) rather than MMSCF (million standard cubic feet) used in later editions — a unit inconsistency that prevents direct computation without further verification. Rather than risk a unit-error in the backward series, the implementation assigns the **2006 computed EF (0.000630 tCO₂/kWh) uniformly to 2000–2005** as a proxy. The rationale: Indonesia's power generation mix in 2000–2005 was oil-and-gas-dominant (coal capacity was minimal before the Fast Track program launched in 2006), so the 2006 EF — computed from an already oil/gas-heavy mix — provides a reasonable backward approximation. This is equivalent to:
>
> $$\text{Grid EF}_{t} = 0.000630 \quad \forall\ t \in \{2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005\}$$
>
> The direction of any bias is uncertain: if coal share was slightly lower in 2000–2005 than in 2006, the true EF was slightly lower (proxy overstates); if oil's higher EF dominated, the proxy may be conservative. The 2000–2005 period has relatively sparse energy data in the SI panel regardless, so this extrapolation has limited impact on aggregate estimates.

**Key finding — direction of bias with static PLN RUPTL 2015 EF:**

| Period | Computed EF | Static EF (0.000867) | Bias direction |
|--------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 2006–2010 | 0.000599–0.000650 | 0.000867 | **Overstates** Scope 2 by ~33–45% |
| 2013 | 0.000873 | 0.000867 | Approximately correct (+0.7%) |
| 2014 | 0.000914 | 0.000867 | **Understates** Scope 2 by ~5% |

The static EF substantially overstates Scope 2 emissions in the early panel years and slightly understates them in 2014. **Year fixed effects in a panel regression absorb any factor that varies only by time (including the grid EF)**, so ln(co2_scope2) = ln(elec_kwh) + constant_{year} under both static and time-varying EF assumptions — within-firm estimates are not affected. The bias matters for: (a) reported absolute emission totals and carbon intensity benchmarks; (b) trend analysis; and (c) cross-year aggregate descriptive statistics.

**The time-varying EF series above is the Spec 1 Scope 2 grid EF**, implemented in `10_carbon_convert.do` and stored as `co2_scope2_s1`. It is used for all aggregate emission totals, trend charts, and descriptive statistics. Spec 2 uses the static 0.000867 tCO₂/kWh factor (`co2_scope2_s2`) for comparability with prior literature.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Applying the PLN grid EF to both PLN and non-PLN purchased electricity.**

The SI/IBS questionnaire records two purchased-electricity variables: `elec_pln_kwh` (bought directly from PLN) and `elec_nonpln_kwh` (bought from non-PLN sources, primarily private generators or industrial estate operators). Both are assigned the same grid EF for Scope 2. The justification is as follows:

1. **Non-PLN purchased ≠ self-generated.** In the SI/IBS data, `elec_nonpln_kwh` captures electricity *purchased* from an external party — not electricity the firm generated itself. Self-generated electricity (`esgkhu`) is a separate variable and is **excluded from Scope 2** entirely (it is an on-site Scope 1 activity if fuelled by fossil fuels). The non-PLN *purchased* category therefore represents a third-party supply relationship, not on-site generation.

2. **Most non-PLN private power producers are IPPs feeding the national grid.** Under Indonesia's electricity regulatory framework, Independent Power Producers (IPPs) sell electricity to PLN under long-term Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). PLN's RUPTL (*Rencana Usaha Penyediaan Tenaga Listrik*) — its statutory electricity supply business plan — explicitly incorporates IPP capacity alongside PLN-owned capacity. Electricity recorded as "non-PLN purchased" in the SI therefore largely originates from the same national grid, routed through industrial estate operators or IPP billing rather than PLN billing directly. The underlying fuel mix — and hence the applicable grid emission factor — is therefore the same.

3. **Residual non-grid electricity is a small minority.** Some `elec_nonpln_kwh` may reflect captive off-grid power from industrial estate generators not connected to the national grid. However, `elec_nonpln_kwh` covers only **5.8% of firm-years** (vs. 87.5% for PLN), and the share is smaller still in energy terms. Applying the PLN-computed grid EF uniformly to both components introduces negligible bias at the aggregate level.

**Implementation:** The Spec 1 time-varying EF series (`co2_scope2_s1`) applies the PLN-computed EF uniformly to `elec_pln_kwh + elec_nonpln_kwh`. The computed grid EFs cover PLN-operated power plants only, as non-PLN IPP fuel consumption is not separately tabulated in the Neraca Energi series — but given points (1)–(3) above, this is the methodologically appropriate factor for the purchased-electricity aggregate.
:::

### Worked Example: Computing the 2006 Grid EF

The computation for 2006 illustrates the full chain from Neraca Energi fuel inputs to a tCO₂/kWh grid EF. Inputs from *Neraca Energi 2006–2010*, "Konsumsi Bahan Bakar Pembangkit Listrik PLN" table:

| Fuel | Quantity | Unit | NCV | GJ total | IPCC EF (tCO₂/TJ) | tCO₂ |
|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Coal | 19.08 Mt | 19,080,000 t | 25.691 GJ/t | 490,184,280 GJ | 95.28 | 46,720,751 tCO₂ |
| HSD | 7.59 MKL | 7,590,000 kL × 0.840 kg/L | 42.496 GJ/t | 270,974,669 GJ | 74.35 | 20,147,959 tCO₂ |
| Fuel oil | 2.39 MKL | 2,390,000 kL × 0.960 kg/L | 41.4996 GJ/t | 95,220,882 GJ | 77.65 | 7,395,926 tCO₂ |
| Natural gas | 157,894 MMSCF | — | 1.087 TJ/MMSCF | 171,630,718 GJ | 56.15 | 9,637,085 tCO₂ |
| **Total** | | | | **1,028,010,549 GJ** | | **83,901,721 tCO₂** |

PLN electricity generated in 2006: **133,108 GWh** = 133,108,000,000 kWh

$$\text{Grid EF}_{2006} = \frac{83{,}901{,}721 \text{ tCO}_2}{133{,}108{,}000{,}000 \text{ kWh}} = \mathbf{0.000630} \text{ tCO}_2/\text{kWh}$$

The same formula is applied for 2007–2010 and 2013–2014 where Neraca Energi fuel data are available. Years 2011–2012 are linearly interpolated between 2010 (0.000599) and 2013 (0.000873). Years 2000–2005 use the 2006 value (0.000630) as a proxy — the pre-Fast Track grid had a similar oil/gas-heavy mix.

### Stata Implementation — `co2_scope2_s1` (time-varying) and `co2_scope2_s2` (static)

**`10_carbon_convert.do`** implements Spec 1 Scope 2 using the **time-varying** BPS Neraca Energi grid EF and Spec 2 Scope 2 using the **static** PLN RUPTL 2015 factor. The two specs therefore differ in both Scope 1 (NCV convention) and Scope 2 (grid EF choice):

```stata
* ── 10_carbon_convert.do — Scope 2 ──────────────────────────────────────────
* Spec 1 (PRIMARY): time-varying grid EF from BPS Neraca Energi
gen double gridEF_s1 = .
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000630 if inrange(year, 2000, 2006)  // pre-Fast Track proxy
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000650 if year == 2007
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000627 if year == 2008
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000609 if year == 2009
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000599 if year == 2010
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000690 if year == 2011   // interpolated
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000782 if year == 2012   // interpolated
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000873 if year == 2013
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000914 if year == 2014
gen double co2_scope2_s1 = elec_purchased_kwh_strict * gridEF_s1
drop gridEF_s1   // temp; EF values documented in §7.7.1

* Spec 2 (robustness): static PLN RUPTL 2015
gen double co2_scope2_s2 = elec_purchased_kwh_strict * 0.000867
```

**`co2_total_s1` is the primary outcome variable** for all descriptive statistics, trend charts, and DiD regression. For DiD with firm and year fixed effects, the choice between static and time-varying Scope 2 EF is irrelevant — year FE absorb any EF constant within year — but `co2_total_s1` is the methodologically consistent specification for absolute emission levels and cross-year trends.

**Note on why EFs are hard-coded.** The grid EF is a scalar constant within each year — there is no firm-level variation. The values are fully documented in §7.7.1 and traceable to the Neraca Energi source tables.

### Grid EF Summary: Spec 1 (Time-Varying) vs. Spec 2 (Static)

| Source | Factor | Notes |
|--------|:------:|-------|
| Prior work baseline | 0.000867 tCO₂/kWh | PLN RUPTL 2015 — single snapshot applied 2000–2014 |
| <a href="#ref-rosita2020">Rosita et al. (2020)</a> | ~0.000904 tCO₂/kWh | IPCC-based, estimated for 2010–2014 period |
| **Computed from Neraca Energi (2006–2010)** | **0.000599–0.000650 tCO₂/kWh** | **BPS Neraca Energi fuel input + IPCC EFs; oil/gas-heavy mix (see §7.7)** |
| **Computed from Neraca Energi (2013–2014)** | **0.000873–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh** | **BPS Neraca Energi; post-Fast Track coal dominance** |

Indonesian grid shifted from oil/gas-heavy (2000) to coal-dominant (2010s onward), driven by the 2006 Fast Track coal power program (capacity additions 2010–2013). The computed time-varying EFs confirm: (a) the static 2015 PLN factor **overstates** early-panel Scope 2 by ~33–45%; (b) it is approximately correct for 2013; (c) it **understates** 2014 by ~5%. The full time-varying series is implemented as `co2_scope2_s1` in `10_carbon_convert.do` (primary Spec 1 Scope 2 variable; see §7.7 for methodology and computed values).

## Sensitivity Variants

Five sensitivity variants are implemented in `11_sensitivity_variants.do` and appended as additional columns to `si_energy_emissions.dta`. Each variant replaces one assumption and recomputes the total, isolating the marginal effect.

| Variant | Priority | Output variable | What it tests |
|---------|:--------:|-----------------|---------------|
| `alt_lpg_neraca` | High | `co2_total_alt_lpg` | LPG NCV GCV→NCV (52.145→45.544 GJ/ton); confirms Spec 1 already uses Neraca NCV |
| `alt_coal_kalimantan` | Medium | `co2_total_alt_kali` | Coal NCV: HEES 25.691→Kalimantan 26.2 GJ/ton (Spec 2 base); tests dominant supply-region NCV |
| `alt_elec_rosita` | Medium | `co2_total_alt_rosita` | Grid EF: static 0.000867→0.000904 tCO₂/kWh (Rosita et al. 2020) |
| `alt_gas_towngas` | Low | `co2_total_alt_towngas` | Gas EF: natural gas→gas works gas (56.15→44.45 kg CO₂/GJ) |
| `alt_coal_exclude2004` | Low | `co2_total_alt_exc2004` | Exclude coal 2004–2005 (unit-label ambiguity: "Ton" vs. "Kg") |

---

### `alt_elec_rosita` — Alternative Scope 2 Grid EF (Rosita et al. 2020)

**Baseline (Spec 2):** Scope 2 emissions use the static PLN RUPTL 2015 grid emission factor: **0.000867 tCO₂/kWh** applied uniformly across all years.

$$\text{co2\_scope2} = \text{elec\_purchased\_kwh} \times 0.000867$$

**Baseline (Spec 1):** Time-varying EF from BPS Neraca Energi, ranging 0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh by year (see §7.7).

**Alternative:** <a href="#ref-rosita2020">Rosita et al. (2020)</a> estimate an average Indonesian grid EF of **0.000904 tCO₂/kWh** for the 2010–2014 period, based on PLN generation data and IPCC 2006 factors. This is applied as a constant across the full 2000–2014 panel:

$$\text{co2\_scope2\_alt} = \text{elec\_purchased\_kwh} \times 0.000904$$

**Net change:** +4.3% on Scope 2 relative to the PLN RUPTL 2015 static factor; 2010–2014 Scope 2 approximately equal to the Spec 1 time-varying EF for those years.

**Rationale:** Tests whether the specific choice of aggregate grid EF constant affects results. Rosita et al. use a similar methodology to Spec 1 but compute a single cross-period average, making it a useful intermediate benchmark between the static RUPTL 2015 value and the Spec 1 year-specific series.

---

### `alt_gas_towngas` — Natural Gas vs. Manufactured Gas Emission Factor

**Baseline (Spec 1 and Spec 2):** Gas emissions are computed using the IPCC 2006 Natural Gas emission factor: **56.15 kg CO₂e/GJ** (Table 2.3, net calorific value basis). PGN (Perusahaan Gas Negara) distributes pipeline gas in Indonesia.

$$\text{co2\_gas} = \text{fuel\_gas\_gj} \times 56.15 \div 1000$$

**Alternative:** IPCC 2006 Table 2.3 also lists a factor for **Gas Works Gas (manufactured/town gas)**: **44.45 kg CO₂e/GJ**. This tests the lower-bound scenario where firms reporting gas consumption are drawing from manufactured gas rather than natural pipeline gas.

$$\text{co2\_gas\_alt} = \text{fuel\_gas\_gj} \times 44.45 \div 1000$$

**Net change:** −20.9% on gas-derived CO₂e per unit consumed. Aggregate impact is low because gas reporters account for <5% of firm-years in the SI panel.

**Rationale:** The SI questionnaire does not distinguish gas type. While PGN supplies natural gas in major industrial corridors (Java, Sumatra), some older manufacturing areas may have had access to manufactured gas networks. This variant documents the upper bound of misclassification risk.

---

### `alt_coal_exclude2004` — Exclude 2004–2005 Coal Cohort

**Baseline (Spec 1 and Spec 2):** Coal consumption for 2004–2005 is **included as reported**. The coal unit diagnostic (§4.1) cleared these years — values are in Kg and are plausible after the expenditure cross-check. The large jump in coal reporters in 2004 is treated as genuine firm entry into coal use.

$$\text{co2\_coal}_{2004,2005} = \text{fuel\_coal\_kg}_{2004,2005} \times \text{composite factor}$$

**Alternative:** The 2004–2005 coal cohort is **excluded entirely** — `co2_coal` is set to missing for all firm-years with coal > 0 in 2004 or 2005. Total emissions for those observations are then computed only from other fuels.

$$\text{co2\_coal\_alt}_{2004,2005} = 0 \quad (\text{treated as missing/excluded})$$

**Net change:** Reduces aggregate Scope 1 emissions in 2004–2005 by the coal contribution for that cohort; has no effect on years outside 2004–2005.

**Rationale:** Even though the expenditure diagnostic supports retaining 2004–2005 coal as-reported, the rapid entry of coal reporters in those years (likely linked to the Fast Track coal power program) may represent a structural break in how firms report coal. This variant tests whether including this cohort drives any of the 2004–2005 emission trend patterns. If results are robust to this exclusion, confidence in the baseline increases.

---

# Carbon Emission Variable Construction

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Do-files:** `dofiles/10_carbon_convert.do` (Specification 1 — IPCC 2006 + BPS Neraca Energi, **primary**; and Specification 2 — IPCC 2006 + ESDM HEES, robustness — both generated in a single pass) · `dofiles/11_sensitivity_variants.do` (sensitivity variants only; appends to output of `10_carbon_convert.do`)
**Input:** `output/si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta` (primary) · `output/si_energy_flagged.dta` (full sample, robustness)
**Output:** `output/si_energy_emissions.dta`
:::

This chapter documents the implementation of the emission conversion pipeline. Two primary specifications are defined, both using IPCC 2006 Tier-1 emission factors (kg CO₂e/GJ) but differing in the energy content (NCV) values used to convert physical units to GJ:

| Specification | Scope 1 NCV source | Scope 1 EF source | Scope 2 grid EF | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Spec 1 — Primary** | BPS *Neraca Energi* (Neraca Emisi GRK, extracted) | IPCC 2006 Table 2.3 | **Time-varying**, 0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh (BPS Neraca Energi + IPCC 2006; see §7.7) | Primary analysis |
| **Spec 2 — Prior literature** | ESDM HEES (via <a href="#ref-zain2025">Zain et al. 2025</a>) | IPCC 2006 Table 2.3 | **Static** 0.000867 tCO₂/kWh (PLN RUPTL 2015) | Robustness check |

The two specifications differ in both Scope 1 NCV values and the Scope 2 grid emission factor. Both use identical IPCC 2006 Tier-1 emission factors (kg CO₂e/GJ) — so the only differences are: (a) which NCV is used to convert physical fuel quantities to GJ, and (b) whether the electricity grid EF is time-varying or static. **Spec 1 Scope 2** uses the time-varying grid EF in `co2_scope2_s1` (0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh; see §7.7). **Spec 2 Scope 2** uses the static PLN RUPTL 2015 EF in `co2_scope2_s2` (0.000867 tCO₂/kWh).

---

## Specification 1: IPCC 2006 + BPS Neraca Energi (Indonesia Official NCV)

Spec 1 replaces the ESDM HEES energy content values with NCV values extracted from the BPS *Neraca Energi* (Energy Balance) and *Neraca Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca* publications. These values represent the calorific content used in Indonesia's official national energy balance and GHG inventory, and are the NCV values implicit in BPS sector-level energy reporting.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Why a single (time-invariant) NCV table?** The BPS *Neraca Energi* is published in multi-year editions (2000–2004, 2006–2010, 2011–2015, 2012–2016). For most fuel types, the per-fuel NCV constants are stable across editions — they are standardised physical properties, not measured annually. This is verified by cross-checking the NCV tables in the extracted markdown files (`literature/04_energy_balance_ghg/_extracted/neraca-energi-indonesia-2011-2015.md` and `neraca-energi-indonesia-2016-2020.md`). *Exception:* Kokas (coke) and Briket (coal briquettes) NCV values differ between the 2011–2015 edition (26.377 and 29.308 GJ/ton) and the 2016–2020 edition (20.195 and 30.209 GJ/ton). Since SI coke and briquettes data appear only in 2012–2014, **the 2011–2015 edition values are used** (see footnote ^f^ in §7.5). A time-varying NCV does not apply to the remaining fuel types. The one component that **is** time-varying is the **Scope 2 grid emission factor**, implemented directly as `co2_scope2_s1` in `10_carbon_convert.do` using the BPS Neraca Energi EF series (0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh; see §7.7). Spec 2 uses the static PLN RUPTL 2015 EF (0.000867 tCO₂/kWh) in `co2_scope2_s2`.
:::


### Unit Conversion Note

The *Neraca Energi* reports NCV in **GJ per tonne** for all fuel types. The SI/IBS data reports liquid fuels in **litres**. The conversion to GJ/litre requires a density assumption. The values below use Indonesian standard fuel densities consistent with KESDM quality standards:

| Fuel | Neraca NCV (GJ/tonne) | Density (kg/litre) | **NCV (GJ/litre)** | Source |
|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| Diesel / HSD | 42.496 | 0.840 | 0.035697 | BPS Neraca Energi; density per KESDM |
| Gasoline / Premium | 44.899 | 0.740 | 0.033225 | BPS Neraca Energi; density per KESDM |
| Kerosene | 43.199 | 0.800 | 0.034559 | BPS Neraca Energi; density per KESDM |
| Coal (Kalimantan thermal) | 26.200 | — | 0.026200 GJ/kg | HEES regional table; preferred over Neraca "Hard Coal" (29.3 GJ/ton = high-rank, not representative of SI firms) ^‡^ |
| LPG | 45.544 | — | 0.045544 GJ/kg | BPS Neraca Energi; SI data in kg — no density needed |
| City gas | 48.000 | — | 0.048000 GJ/m³ | BPS Neraca Energi |
| Coke / Kokas | 26.377 | — | 0.026377 GJ/kg | BPS Neraca Energi 2011–2015 (Kokas); see footnote ^f^ |
| Coal Briquettes / Briket | 29.308 | — | 0.029308 GJ/kg | BPS Neraca Energi 2011–2015 (Briket); see footnote ^f^ |

> ^‡^ **Why not Neraca Energi "Hard Coal" (29.3)?** It refers to high-rank coal (*batubara keras*), not the thermal coal used by SI firms — applying it would overstate coal emissions by ~14%. **Why Kalimantan (26.2)?** HEES `table_101.md` gives Kalimantan thermal coal = 4.2766 BOE/ton × 6.117 = 26.2 GJ/ton, the same factor as "Imported Coal" — HEES treats this as the Indonesian thermal coal reference. Kalimantan supplies ~86–89% of national production ([Arinaldo & Adiatma, 2019](#ref-arinaldo2019), Fig. 7), making it the most representative assumption. Limitation: SI data does not record coal origin. See §7.9 for the full regional comparison table.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
**LPG GCV/NCV flag:** Spec 1 (BPS Neraca) reports LPG at 45.544 GJ/tonne vs. Spec 2 (ESDM HEES) at 52.145 GJ/tonne — a 12.7% difference. The IPCC 2006 Tier-1 default for LPG is 47.3 GJ/tonne (NCV basis). The Spec 2 value appears to use **GCV** rather than NCV; the Spec 1 (Neraca) value is consistent with NCV. Since IPCC emission factors are defined on an NCV basis, Spec 1 is methodologically more consistent for LPG. This is the largest unresolved liquid fuel issue and raises LPG emissions under Spec 2 by ~15% relative to the IPCC-consistent Spec 1.
:::

### Composite Per-Unit Conversion Factors (Spec 1) {#sec-spec1-factors}

> The full side-by-side comparison of Spec 1 and Spec 2 composite factors is in **§7.6**. The table below is a Stata-ready quick reference for Spec 1 only — the values implemented in `10_carbon_convert.do`.

| Fuel | SI/IBS variable | Unit | NCV (GJ/unit) | EF (kg CO₂e/GJ) | **tCO₂e/unit** |
|------|----------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Diesel / Solar | `fuel_diesel_ltr` | litre | 0.035697 | 74.35 | **0.002654** |
| Gasoline / Bensin | `fuel_petrol_ltr` | litre | 0.033225 | 69.55 | **0.002310** |
| Kerosene | `fuel_kerosene_ltr` | litre | 0.034559 | 72.15 | **0.002494** |
| Coal (Kalimantan thermal) | `fuel_coal_kg` | kg | 0.026200 | 95.28 | **0.002496** |
| LPG | `fuel_lpg_kg` | kg | 0.045544 | 63.15 | **0.002876** |
| City gas | `fuel_citygas_m3` | m³ | 0.048000 | 56.15 | **0.002695** |
| Other gas / non-PGN | `fuel_othergas_m3` | m³ | 0.048000 | 56.15 | **0.002695** |
| Coal briquettes | `fuel_coalbriq_kg` | kg | 0.029308 | 98.18 | **0.002877** ^f^ |
| Coke | `fuel_coke_kg` | kg | 0.026377 | 107.68 | **0.002840** ^f^ |
| Electricity | `elec_purchased_kwh_strict` | kWh | — | — | **0.000599–0.000914** (time-varying, year-specific; see §7.7) |

### Stata Code — Specification 1

```stata
* ============================================================
*  10_carbon_convert.do  (Spec 1 block — key variables only)
*  Spec 1: IPCC 2006 EF + BPS Neraca Energi NCV  [PRIMARY]
*  Note: 10_carbon_convert.do generates BOTH Spec 1 (_s1) and
*        Spec 2 (_s2) in a single pass. Shown here: Spec 1 only.
* ============================================================

use "output/si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta", clear

* --- Scope 1: Direct fuel combustion (Neraca NCV) ---
gen co2_diesel_s1    = fuel_diesel_ltr   * 0.002654
gen co2_petrol_s1    = fuel_petrol_ltr   * 0.002310
gen co2_kerosene_s1  = fuel_kerosene_ltr * 0.002494
gen co2_coal_s1      = fuel_coal_kg      * 0.002496   // Kalimantan thermal NCV
gen co2_lpg_s1       = fuel_lpg_kg       * 0.002876
gen co2_gas_s1       = fuel_citygas_m3   * 0.002695
gen co2_othergas_s1  = fuel_othergas_m3  * 0.002695   // same NCV as city gas (Neraca)
gen co2_coalbriq_s1  = fuel_coalbriq_kg  * 0.002877   // Neraca 2011-2015 (29.308 GJ/ton × 98.18)
gen co2_coke_s1      = fuel_coke_kg      * 0.002840   // Neraca 2011-2015 (26.377 GJ/ton × 107.68)

label var co2_diesel_s1   "Diesel emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca)"
label var co2_petrol_s1   "Petrol emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca)"
label var co2_kerosene_s1 "Kerosene emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca)"
label var co2_coal_s1     "Coal emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca)"
label var co2_lpg_s1      "LPG emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca)"
label var co2_gas_s1      "City gas emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca)"
label var co2_othergas_s1 "Other gas emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca)"
label var co2_coalbriq_s1 "Coal briquette emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca 2011-2015, 29.308 GJ/ton)"
label var co2_coke_s1     "Coke emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca 2011-2015, 26.377 GJ/ton)"

egen co2_scope1_s1 = rowtotal(co2_diesel_s1 co2_petrol_s1 co2_kerosene_s1 ///
                               co2_coal_s1 co2_lpg_s1 co2_gas_s1           ///
                               co2_othergas_s1 co2_coalbriq_s1 co2_coke_s1), missing
label var co2_scope1_s1 "Scope 1 total, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca, 9 fuels)"

* Scope 2 — Spec 1: time-varying BPS Neraca Energi grid EF (0.000599–0.000914 tCO2/kWh)
* See §7.7 for full year-by-year values; 2011–2012 are interpolated.
gen double gridEF_s1 = .
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000630 if inrange(year, 2000, 2006)   // 2006 = computed anchor; 2000–2005 = backward proxy using the 2006 value
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000650 if year == 2007
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000627 if year == 2008
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000609 if year == 2009
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000599 if year == 2010
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000690 if year == 2011   // interpolated
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000782 if year == 2012   // interpolated
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000873 if year == 2013
replace gridEF_s1 = 0.000914 if year == 2014
gen double co2_scope2_s1 = elec_purchased_kwh_strict * gridEF_s1
label var co2_scope2_s1 "Scope 2 electricity emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: time-varying Neraca EF 0.000599–0.000914)"
drop gridEF_s1   // temp variable; used only to compute co2_scope2_s1

* Scope 2 — Spec 2: static PLN RUPTL 2015 EF
gen double co2_scope2_s2 = elec_purchased_kwh_strict * 0.000867
label var co2_scope2_s2 "Scope 2 electricity emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: static PLN RUPTL 2015 EF 0.000867)"

gen double co2_total_s1 = co2_scope1_s1 + co2_scope2_s1
label var co2_total_s1 "Total Scope 1+2 emissions, tCO2e (Spec 1: IPCC+Neraca) — PRIMARY outcome"

gen double co2_intensity_worker_s1  = co2_total_s1 / ltlnou
gen double co2_intensity_output_s1  = co2_total_s1 / (vtlvcu / 1000)   // per M Rp (nominal; vtlvcu in Rp000)
gen double ln_co2_total_s1           = ln(co2_total_s1)
gen double ln_co2_scope1_s1          = ln(co2_scope1_s1)
gen double ln_co2_intensity_worker_s1 = ln(co2_intensity_worker_s1)
label var ln_co2_total_s1            "Log total emissions, Spec 1 (primary specification)"
label var ln_co2_scope1_s1           "Log Scope 1 (combustion only), Spec 1"
label var ln_co2_intensity_worker_s1 "Log emission intensity per worker, Spec 1"

* co2_scope2_s1 already uses the time-varying Neraca EF. Use co2_total_s1 for
* descriptive trend charts and level comparisons. Use ln_co2_total_s1 for DiD
* regression (year FE absorb grid EF variation across years).
save "output/si_energy_emissions.dta", replace
```

## Specification 2: IPCC 2006 + ESDM HEES (Baseline)

This is the standard approach in the Indonesian manufacturing literature, following <a href="#ref-zain2025">Zain, Patunru & Hartono (2025)</a> and consistent with <a href="#ref-rosita2020">Rosita et al. (2020)</a>. Energy content values come from the ESDM *Handbook of Energy and Economic Statistics* (HEES), expressed in GJ per kilolitre (liquid fuels) or GJ per tonne (solid fuels and gas). Full factor derivation is in §7.5–7.6.

### Composite Per-Unit Conversion Factors (Spec 2)

Pre-multiplied from: NCV (GJ/unit) × EF (kg CO₂e/GJ) ÷ 1,000

| Fuel | SI/IBS variable | Unit | NCV (GJ/unit) | EF (kg CO₂e/GJ) | **tCO₂e/unit** |
|------|----------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Diesel / Solar | `fuel_diesel_ltr` | litre | 0.040051 | 74.35 | **0.002978** |
| Gasoline / Bensin | `fuel_petrol_ltr` | litre | 0.035647 | 69.55 | **0.002479** |
| Kerosene | `fuel_kerosene_ltr` | litre | 0.036258 | 72.15 | **0.002616** |
| Coal | `fuel_coal_kg` | kg | 0.025691 | 95.28 | **0.002448** |
| LPG | `fuel_lpg_kg` | kg | 0.052145 | 63.15 | **0.003293** |
| City gas | `fuel_citygas_m3` | m³ | 0.039000 | 56.15 | **0.002190** |
| Electricity | `elec_pln_kwh` + `elec_nonpln_kwh` | kWh | — | — | **0.000867** ^†^ |

> ^†^ Grid emission factor applied directly on kWh (PLN RUPTL 2015). Not a fuel NCV.

### Stata Code — Specification 2

```stata
* ============================================================
*  10_carbon_convert.do
*  Spec 2: IPCC 2006 EF + ESDM HEES NCV (Baseline)
*  Input:  si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta
*  Output: si_energy_emissions.dta (appends emission variables)
* ============================================================

use "output/si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta", clear

* --- Scope 1: Direct fuel combustion ---
gen co2_diesel_s2    = fuel_diesel_ltr   * 0.002978   // tCO2e
gen co2_petrol_s2    = fuel_petrol_ltr   * 0.002479
gen co2_kerosene_s2  = fuel_kerosene_ltr * 0.002616
gen co2_coal_s2      = fuel_coal_kg      * 0.002448
gen co2_lpg_s2       = fuel_lpg_kg       * 0.003293
gen co2_gas_s2       = fuel_citygas_m3   * 0.002190

label var co2_diesel_s2   "Diesel emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"
label var co2_petrol_s2   "Petrol emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"
label var co2_kerosene_s2 "Kerosene emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"
label var co2_coal_s2     "Coal emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"
label var co2_lpg_s2      "LPG emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"
label var co2_gas_s2      "City gas emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"

* Spec 2 also includes sparse fuels (othergas, coalbriq, coke)
gen co2_othergas_s2  = fuel_othergas_m3  * 0.002190   // same as city gas, HEES
gen co2_coalbriq_s2  = fuel_coalbriq_kg  * 0.002032   // IPCC 2006 brown coal briquette
gen co2_coke_s2      = fuel_coke_kg      * 0.002907   // HEES coke oven coke
label var co2_othergas_s2  "Other gas emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"
label var co2_coalbriq_s2  "Coal briquette emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"
label var co2_coke_s2      "Coke emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"

* Scope 1 total — 9 fuels (missing if ALL fuels missing; partial sum otherwise)
egen co2_scope1_s2 = rowtotal(co2_diesel_s2 co2_petrol_s2 co2_kerosene_s2 ///
                               co2_coal_s2 co2_lpg_s2 co2_gas_s2           ///
                               co2_othergas_s2 co2_coalbriq_s2 co2_coke_s2), missing
label var co2_scope1_s2 "Scope 1 total, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES, 9 fuels)"

* Number of fuels contributing to Scope 1 (for partial-coverage flag; 0–9)
gen co2_scope1_nfuels = (!missing(co2_diesel_s2))    ///
                      + (!missing(co2_petrol_s2))     ///
                      + (!missing(co2_kerosene_s2))   ///
                      + (!missing(co2_coal_s2))       ///
                      + (!missing(co2_lpg_s2))        ///
                      + (!missing(co2_gas_s2))        ///
                      + (!missing(co2_othergas_s2))   ///
                      + (!missing(co2_coalbriq_s2))   ///
                      + (!missing(co2_coke_s2))
label var co2_scope1_nfuels "N fuels contributing to Scope 1 (0–9)"

* --- Scope 2: Spec 2 uses the static PLN RUPTL 2015 EF (0.000867 tCO2/kWh) ---
* Spec 1 (co2_scope2_s1) uses the time-varying Neraca Energi EF; Spec 2 uses
* the static EF for comparability with prior literature.
gen double co2_scope2_s2 = elec_purchased_kwh_strict * 0.000867
label var co2_scope2_s2 "Scope 2 electricity emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: static PLN RUPTL 2015 EF 0.000867)"

* --- Total ---
gen double co2_total_s2 = co2_scope1_s2 + co2_scope2_s2
label var co2_total_s2 "Total Scope 1+2 emissions, tCO2e (Spec 2: IPCC+HEES)"

* --- Intensity measures ---
gen double co2_intensity_worker_s2 = co2_total_s2 / ltlnou   // ltlnou = total workers
label var co2_intensity_worker_s2 "Emission intensity per worker, tCO2e (Spec 2)"
* Note: co2_intensity_output_s2 is not created (only Spec 1 has output intensity)

* --- Log outcomes for DiD ---
gen double ln_co2_total_s2           = ln(co2_total_s2)
gen double ln_co2_scope1_s2          = ln(co2_scope1_s2)
gen double ln_co2_intensity_worker_s2 = ln(co2_intensity_worker_s2)
label var ln_co2_total_s2            "Log total emissions, Spec 2 (robustness check)"
label var ln_co2_scope1_s2           "Log Scope 1 emissions, Spec 2"
label var ln_co2_intensity_worker_s2 "Log emission intensity per worker, Spec 2"

save "output/si_energy_emissions.dta", replace
```

## Comparison of the Two Specifications

### Per-Fuel Percentage Difference (Spec 1 vs. Spec 2)

| Energy Source | Spec 1 tCO₂e/unit | Spec 2 tCO₂e/unit | Spec 1 vs. Spec 2 | Panel share ^*^ |
|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| ***Scope 1 — Direct Fuel Combustion*** | | | | |
| Diesel | 0.002654 | 0.002978 | **−10.9%** | High (63% of firm-years) |
| Gasoline | 0.002310 | 0.002479 | **−6.8%** | Medium (52%) |
| Kerosene | 0.002494 | 0.002616 | **−4.7%** | Low (17%) |
| Coal | 0.002496 | 0.002448 | **+2.0%** | Sparse (5%) |
| LPG | 0.002876 | 0.003293 | **−12.7%** | Low (12%) |
| City gas | 0.002695 | 0.002190 | **+23.1%** | Sparse (4%) |
| ***Scope 2 — Purchased Electricity*** | | | | |
| Electricity (PLN + non-PLN) ^†^ | 0.000599–0.000914 (time-varying) | 0.000867 (static) | Varies by year (−31% to +5%) | High (88%) |

> ^*^ N-positive share from §3.2 coverage table.
> ^†^ Electricity is **Scope 2** (indirect emissions from purchased grid power). The value shown is a **grid emission factor** (tCO₂/kWh) applied directly to kWh — it is not a fuel NCV × EF product. `co2_scope2_s1` uses the **time-varying** BPS Neraca Energi EF (0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh; see §7.7); `co2_scope2_s2` uses the **static** PLN RUPTL 2015 EF (0.000867 tCO₂/kWh). They are therefore **different** across the two specifications.

**Net direction:** For a typical firm consuming primarily diesel and purchased electricity (the two dominant energy inputs), Spec 1 produces **Scope 1 estimates approximately 8–11% lower** than Spec 2. This is driven entirely by the GCV/NCV convention difference in ESDM HEES liquid fuel values. Scope 2 estimates **differ** between Spec 1 and Spec 2: Spec 1 uses the time-varying Neraca EF (0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh) while Spec 2 uses the static 0.000867. The `co2_total_s1` vs. `co2_total_s2` comparison therefore reflects **both** the Scope 1 NCV convention and the Scope 2 EF choice. To isolate the Scope 1 NCV effect alone, compare `co2_scope1_s1` vs. `co2_scope1_s2` directly.

### Implications for Panel Regressions

Because the two specifications apply a constant scalar transformation per fuel type, the **choice of NCV source does not materially affect within-firm panel estimates** — firm fixed effects difference out the level difference. The log transformation of emissions further reduces the impact: a 10% level difference in emissions translates to a difference of log(1.10) ≈ 0.095 in the dependent variable mean, but not in within-firm comparisons.

The specifications differ meaningfully for:

1. **Cross-sectional level comparisons** — absolute emission totals and carbon intensity benchmarks against other countries or datasets will differ by 8–11% for liquid-fuel-intensive firms.
2. **Firms with unusual fuel mixes** — firms heavily reliant on LPG will show a larger gap (−12.7%); coal-intensive firms will show near-zero difference (+2%).
3. **Trend analysis** — if fuel mix shifts systematically over time (e.g., if firms switch from diesel to LPG post-treatment), the two specs can produce slightly different trend slopes even within firm.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Recommendation:** Report Spec 1 (IPCC + BPS Neraca Energi) as the primary specification — it uses Indonesia's official energy statistics and is NCV-consistent with the IPCC 2006 emission factors. Report Spec 2 (IPCC + ESDM HEES) in a robustness table for prior-literature comparability. If the emission estimates from `ln_co2_total_s1` and `ln_co2_total_s2` are similar in magnitude, this confirms that results are not sensitive to the GCV/NCV convention choice.
:::

## Recommended Specification for Main Analysis

| Criterion | Spec 1 (IPCC + Neraca) | Spec 2 (IPCC + HEES) |
|-----------|:---:|:---:|
| Consistent with prior SI literature | Partial | Yes |
| Uses Indonesian official NCV values | Neraca Energi (BPS) | HEES (KESDM) |
| NCV convention confirmed as NCV (not GCV) | Confirmed NCV | Uncertain for LPG |
| Methodological consistency (NCV basis aligns with IPCC EFs) | Yes | Partial |
| Impact on within-firm panel estimates | Negligible difference | Baseline |

**Use by context — three distinct use cases:**

| Use case | Variable to use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **DiD / event-study regression (year FE)** | `ln_co2_total_s1` | Year FE absorb grid EF variation entirely — static vs. time-varying Scope 2 EF is irrelevant for the treatment coefficient. `ln_co2_total_s1` is the primary outcome. |
| **Descriptive statistics, trend charts, carbon intensity levels** | `co2_total_s1` | Uses time-varying Scope 2 grid EF (`co2_scope2_s1`, 0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh) — avoids ~33–45% overstatement of early-period Scope 2 from a static 2015 EF. Primary variable; used in `12_descriptive_stats.do`. |
| **Robustness check on NCV convention + grid EF** | `ln_co2_total_s2` | Compares Spec 1 (Neraca Energi NCV + time-varying Scope 2 EF) vs. Spec 2 (HEES NCV + static 0.000867 Scope 2 EF). This comparison reflects **both** the Scope 1 NCV convention difference and the Scope 2 EF choice. To isolate the pure Scope 1 NCV effect alone, compare `co2_scope1_s1` vs. `co2_scope1_s2` directly. |

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Spec 1 vs. Spec 2 Scope 2 design.** `co2_scope2_s1` uses the **time-varying** BPS Neraca Energi grid EF (0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh); `co2_scope2_s2` uses the **static** PLN RUPTL 2015 EF (0.000867 tCO₂/kWh). The `co2_total_s1` vs. `co2_total_s2` comparison therefore reflects **both** the Scope 1 NCV convention (Neraca vs. HEES) and the Scope 2 EF choice (time-varying vs. static). To isolate the pure Scope 1 NCV effect alone, compare `co2_scope1_s1` vs. `co2_scope1_s2` directly.
:::

**Level-comparisons** (e.g., carbon intensity benchmarks in the descriptive section): use `co2_total_s1` (Spec 1 Scope 1 + time-varying Scope 2 EF) for year-over-year comparisons and external benchmarks.

# Descriptive Statistics — Emission Estimates

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Do-file:** `dofiles/12_descriptive_stats.do` · **Input:** `output/si_energy_emissions.dta` (cleaned sample, N = 314,576) · **Tables:** `output/tables/desc_*.csv` · **Figures:** `output/figures/figD1–figD5`
:::

This chapter provides a descriptive overview of the emission estimates produced in §7–8. It is organised in twelve parts, proceeding from aggregate totals to decompositions to cross-sections:

(1) **Total CO₂e by year — Spec 1 vs. Spec 2** — the aggregate trend, two specifications side-by-side.
(2) **Scope 1 vs. Scope 2 decomposition by year** — distinguishes direct fuel combustion from purchased-electricity emissions, and shows how much of the post-2010 emission growth reflects the grid getting dirtier (mechanical) vs. genuine fuel use growth.
(3) **Per-fuel Scope 1 time series** — disaggregates direct emissions by fuel type; makes the coal-switching story after the 2003–2005 oil price shock visible.
(4) **Distribution by ISIC 2-digit** — pooled cross-section; includes Scope 2 share by sector to show which industries are electricity-dominant vs. fuel-dominant.
(5) **Top-sector time series** — emission trends for the top 5 ISIC sectors; motivates sector heterogeneity in downstream DiD analysis.
(6) **Distribution by province** — pooled total and median by province.
(7) **Top ISIC × province emission cells** — the 20 industry-region combinations driving aggregate manufacturing emissions.
(8) **Carbon intensity time series** — median tCO₂e per unit of output by year; the most directly relevant descriptive for Mba Deasy's research question on energy efficiency.
(9) **FDI vs. domestic firms** — exploratory comparison of emission levels and carbon intensity between FDI firms (foreign ownership ≥ 10%) and domestic firms.
(10) **Per-fuel emission totals — Spec 1 vs. Spec 2** — pooled fuel-by-fuel comparison of the two specifications.
(11) **Correlations with value added and employment** — confirms expected size-emissions relationship.
(12) **Sense checks against external benchmarks** — external validation against BPS Neraca GRK, ISIC intensity ordering, and provincial patterns.

**Sample note:** All figures and tables in this chapter use `si_energy_emissions.dta`, which is produced from the **cleaned sample** (`si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta`, N = 314,576 — 96.38% of matched panel). The full flagged matched sample (326,382 obs) contains an additional 11,806 firm-years with severe-flag anomalies that are excluded from the primary emission estimates. Qualitative patterns are robust across samples.

**On the sense checks (§9.7).** The descriptive tables in §9.1–9.6 are internally consistent by construction — they are computed directly from `si_energy_emissions.dta`. What they cannot confirm on their own is whether the *level* of the estimates is plausible and whether the *cross-sectional ordering* by industry and province is consistent with what we know about Indonesia's industrial geography and energy system. §9.7 addresses this with three external checks: (1) comparing our aggregate CO₂e totals against the BPS *Neraca Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca* official manufacturing sector figures for the nearest available years (2015–2019); (2) verifying that the ISIC 2-digit energy intensity ranking follows the thermodynamic ordering expected for each sector; and (3) checking that provincial emission intensity patterns match Indonesia's known industrial geography. These checks do not prove the pipeline is correct — the IBS and the BPS Neraca GRK differ in coverage scope, emission boundary, and methodology — but they provide a meaningful sanity filter: a large unexplained discrepancy in any of the three checks would constitute evidence of a pipeline error warranting investigation.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Variable choice for descriptive statistics.** `12_descriptive_stats.do` uses `co2_total_s1` as the primary aggregate for trend charts and totals. `co2_scope2_s1` already incorporates the time-varying BPS Neraca Energi grid EF (0.000599–0.000914 tCO₂/kWh), so `co2_total_s1` is the correct choice for year-to-year trend comparisons and level benchmarks. For DiD regression, `ln_co2_total_s1` remains the primary outcome (year FE absorb grid EF variation).
:::

## Aggregate CO₂e by Year: Spec 1 vs. Spec 2

**Source:** `output/tables/desc_aggregate_by_year.csv` · **Figure:** `output/figures/figD1_total_co2_by_year.png`

The table below reports total manufacturing CO₂e (in thousands of tCO₂e) summed across all firm-years with non-missing `co2_total`, the median and mean per-firm emission level, and the number of firm-years contributing to each year's total. **Note on N:** The "N firm-years" column counts observations with non-missing `co2_total_s1` (i.e., firms that reported at least one energy input), produced by `collapse (count) n_firms = co2_total_s1 if !missing(co2_total_s1)` in `12_descriptive_stats.do`. This differs slightly from the total cleaned sample N by year (which includes all 314,576 obs regardless of energy reporting status).

Two specifications are shown side-by-side:

- **Spec 1 (Indonesia official NCV, primary):** IPCC 2006 Table 2.3 emission factors × BPS *Neraca Energi* NCV values. Produces ~8–11% lower Scope 1 totals for liquid-fuel-dominant firms (GCV/NCV convention difference in HEES liquid fuel values).
- **Spec 2 (prior literature, robustness):** Same IPCC emission factors × ESDM HEES energy content (NCV). Follows <a href="#ref-zain2025">Zain et al. (2025)</a>.

| 2001 | 19,708 | 27,350 | 34,502 | 69.3 | 1,388 |
| 2002 | 18,885 | 23,239 | 29,116 | 52.9 | 1,231 |
| 2003 | 18,213 | 32,097 | 39,193 | 65.3 | 1,762 |
| 2004 | 18,156 | 45,839 | 56,173 | 79.5 | 2,525 |
| 2005 | 18,818 | 60,034 | 72,889 | 82.2 | 3,190 |
| 2006 | 26,630 | 28,721 | 35,423 | 33.1 | 1,079 |
| 2007 | 25,267 | 30,316 | 35,681 | 43.4 | 1,200 |
| 2008 | 23,490 | 37,196 | 44,076 | 48.0 | 1,583 |
| 2009 | 22,382 | 35,289 | 42,431 | 48.6 | 1,577 |
| 2010 | 21,329 | 21,884 | 26,252 | 37.7 | 1,026 |
| 2011 | 21,325 | 32,856 | 36,247 | 42.7 | 1,541 |
| 2012 | 21,480 | 36,303 | 38,208 | 48.8 | 1,690 |
| 2013 | 19,496 | 45,085 | 45,350 | 54.3 | 2,313 |
| 2014 | 19,036 | 49,836 | 49,008 | 65.5 | 2,618 |

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Reading this table:** "Total CO₂e" = Scope 1 + Scope 2, summed across firms with at least one non-missing energy input. Firms with all inputs missing have `co2_total_s2` missing (8,591 obs — see §8.4). **The 2001–2002 totals are lower than adjacent years** because coal and kerosene were structurally absent in those survey waves. **The 2004–2005 increase** reflects genuine coal switching by manufacturers (fuel price deregulation + 2004–2005 oil price shock); values are now reliable following the coal unit diagnostic (§4 — no correction was needed, data were already in Kg). **The 2006 N jump** reflects the SE06 census expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**2010 data limitation — the dip is a measurement artefact, not a genuine emission reduction.**

The 2010 IBS questionnaire collected monetary values only for solid fuels and gas; physical quantities were not recorded for these fuel types (see §2.3). Specifically:

- **Fuels with no physical quantity in 2010:** coal (`eclkgu`), LPG (`elpkgu`), city gas (`egam3u`) → `co2_coal`, `co2_lpg`, `co2_citygas` are structurally missing for all 2010 observations.
- **Fuels with physical quantity available in 2010:** diesel, petrol, kerosene → these contribute to Scope 1 as normal.
- **Electricity (Scope 2):** kWh collected in 2010, but PLN and non-PLN are not separated (merged into a single total — see §2.4 footnote †). Scope 2 is available but uses the aggregated kWh.

The 2010 Scope 1 figure (13.41 Mt in §9.2) therefore represents **liquid fuels only**. Coal — the dominant Scope 1 contributor in all other years (see §9.3) — is absent. The drop from ~35 Mt (2009) to ~13 Mt (2010) is entirely attributable to this structural data gap. **Users should treat 2010 Scope 1 as a lower bound** and avoid interpreting year-on-year changes involving 2010 as evidence of genuine efficiency improvement or emission reduction.
:::

## Scope 1 vs. Scope 2 Decomposition by Year

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Source:** `output/tables/desc_scope_decomp_by_year.csv` · **Figure:** `output/figures/figD1b_scope_decomp_by_year.png`
:::

The §9.1 aggregate trend conflates direct fuel combustion (Scope 1) and purchased-electricity emissions (Scope 2). This section decomposes the total to distinguish the two channels — important because their drivers are different:

- **Scope 1** (direct fuel combustion) reflects *firm-level* fuel use decisions: switching fuels, improving combustion efficiency, or changing output scale. This is the channel directly relevant to Mba Deasy's internationalisation–efficiency hypothesis.
- **Scope 2** (purchased electricity) reflects *firm-level* electricity consumption *multiplied by the grid emission factor*, which changed substantially over 2000–2014 as Indonesia's power mix shifted from oil/gas to coal (Fast Track programme, ~2006–2011). A firm can see rising Scope 2 emissions simply because the grid got dirtier — without any change in its own energy behaviour.

The table below reports annual totals (million tCO₂e, Spec 1) for Scope 1, Scope 2, and their sum.

| Year | Scope 1 (M tCO₂e) | Scope 2 (M tCO₂e) | Total (M tCO₂e) | Scope 2 share (%) |
|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 2000 | 52.17 | 28.17 | 80.34 | 35.1% |
| 2001 | 12.22 | 15.13 | 27.35 | 55.3% |
| 2002 | 11.00 | 12.24 | 23.24 | 52.6% |
| 2003 | 17.50 | 14.60 | 32.10 | 45.5% |
| 2004 | 23.78 | 22.06 | 45.84 | 48.1% |
| 2005 | 31.77 | 28.27 | 60.03 | 47.1% |
| 2006 | 12.48 | 16.24 | 28.72 | 56.6% |
| 2007 | 15.94 | 14.37 | 30.32 | 47.4% |
| 2008 | 20.86 | 16.34 | 37.20 | 43.9% |
| 2009 | 19.82 | 15.47 | 35.29 | 43.8% |
| 2010 | 13.41 | 8.47 | 21.88 | 38.7% |
| 2011 | 21.93 | 10.93 | 32.86 | 33.2% |
| 2012 | 23.50 | 12.80 | 36.30 | 35.3% |
| 2013 | 24.59 | 20.50 | 45.09 | 45.5% |

## Per-Fuel Scope 1 Time Series

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Source:** `output/tables/desc_perfuel_s1_by_year.csv` · **Figure:** `output/figures/figD1c_perfuel_s1_by_year.png`
:::

This section disaggregates Scope 1 by fuel type to make the structural drivers of the direct-emission trend visible. The pooled per-fuel totals (§9.10) obscure important dynamics: coal was structurally absent in 2001–2002, spiked after the 2003–2005 oil price shock as manufacturers switched fuels, and has grown steadily since. Diesel is the dominant continuous fuel throughout.

**Key patterns to expect:**

- **Coal** — near zero 2001–2002 (structural gap), then rising from 2003 onward as the oil price shock and BLT fuel subsidy reform pushed manufacturers toward solid fuel.
- **Diesel** — dominant throughout; relatively stable trend, reflecting its role as the baseline fuel for industrial boilers and transportation.
- **City gas and LPG** — absent before 2006 (not collected in SI questionnaires); appear from 2006 as PGN network expanded.
- **Petrol and kerosene** — minor fuels; kerosene absent 2001–2002 (same structural gap as coal).
- **2010 dip** — affects all fuels because physical quantities were not collected in the monetary-only wave.

![**Figure D1c.** Per-fuel Scope 1 emissions by year (Spec 1, 000 tCO₂e). Coal (grey) and diesel (orange) dominate throughout. Coal spikes in 2000 then collapses in 2001–2002 (structural survey gap), resumes strongly post-2003 (oil price shock + fuel subsidy reform). City gas and LPG enter from 2006 only. The 2010 dip affects all fuels (monetary-only wave). Source: `si_energy_emissions.dta` · Do-file: `12_descriptive_stats.do`.](../output/figures/figD1c_perfuel_s1_by_year.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## Carbon Intensity Time Series

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Source:** `output/tables/desc_carbon_intensity_by_year.csv` · **Figure:** `output/figures/figD6b_carbon_intensity_by_year.png`
:::

The §9.1–§9.7 figures track *absolute* emission levels. For Mba Deasy's research question — whether newly-internationalising firms *improve energy efficiency* — the more relevant distributional context is **carbon intensity**: CO₂e per unit of output. A firm that emits more in absolute terms while growing faster may still be improving its carbon efficiency.

**Definition:** Carbon intensity = `co2_total_s1` / (`vtlvcu` / 1,000) — tCO₂e per million Rp of gross output (nominal). The median and interquartile range (P25–P75) are reported by year across all firms with both non-missing `co2_total_s1` and positive `vtlvcu`.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
**Nominal vs. real output.** `vtlvcu` is gross output in nominal Rp (not deflated). Inflation over 2000–2014 means that nominal output grows even without real output growth, mechanically reducing nominal carbon intensity over time. Interpret the *level* trend cautiously; within-firm changes (which a deflator would also address via year FE in a panel) are more reliable. For the DiD regression, year fixed effects absorb inflation-driven trends.
:::

| Year | N firms | Median CI (tCO₂e/M Rp) | P25 | P75 |
|------|---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 2000 | 20,361 | 0.177 | 0.061 | 0.474 |
| 2001 | 19,708 | 0.091 | 0.030 | 0.247 |
| 2002 | 18,885 | 0.067 | 0.023 | 0.175 |
| 2003 | 18,211 | 0.081 | 0.029 | 0.207 |
| 2004 | 18,156 | 0.090 | 0.033 | 0.227 |
| 2005 | 18,818 | 0.084 | 0.029 | 0.213 |
| 2006 | 26,630 | 0.040 | 0.014 | 0.106 |
| 2007 | 25,267 | 0.039 | 0.014 | 0.101 |
| 2008 | 23,490 | 0.039 | 0.014 | 0.101 |
| 2009 | 22,382 | 0.034 | 0.012 | 0.089 |
| 2010 | 21,329 | 0.021 | 0.007 | 0.057 |
| 2011 | 21,325 | 0.022 | 0.007 | 0.057 |
| 2012 | 21,480 | 0.019 | 0.007 | 0.051 |
| 2013 | 19,496 | 0.019 | 0.006 | 0.050 |
| 2014 | 19,036 | 0.018 | 0.006 | 0.051 |

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Interpreting the 2005→2006 drop.** Median CI drops sharply from 0.084 (2005) to 0.040 (2006) — a 52% decline. This is *not* a genuine efficiency improvement: it reflects the SE06 census expansion, which added ~8,000 smaller firms with relatively low emission intensity to the sample. The within-firm trend (controlling for firm FE) will be the appropriate estimand for Mba Deasy's analysis.
:::

![**Figure D6b.** Median carbon intensity (tCO₂e per million Rp gross output) by year, cleaned sample. Shaded band = IQR (P25–P75). The sharp 2005→2006 drop (~52%) reflects SE06 census expansion, not genuine efficiency improvement. The downward trend post-2006 is partly mechanical (nominal Rp inflation in denominator).
