## FDI vs. Domestic Firms — Exploratory

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Source:** `output/tables/desc_fdi_summary.csv`, `output/tables/desc_fdi_by_year.csv` · **Figures:** `output/figures/figD7a_fdi_share_by_year.png`, `figD7b_fdi_vs_domestic_co2.png`, `figD7c_fdi_vs_domestic_ci.png`
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
**Exploratory section — not part of the primary pipeline.** The `dasing` (foreign ownership share) variable is merged from `data8514_SI.dta` in `12_descriptive_stats.do` solely for this descriptive comparison. It is not currently in `si_energy_emissions.dta`. The FDI classification and regression design belong to Mba Deasy's upstream analysis; this section provides orientation on the firm-type distribution in the emission dataset.
:::

**FDI definition:** A firm-year is classified as **FDI** if `dasing ≥ 10` — the IMF 10% threshold for foreign direct investment (sufficient equity stake to imply control or significant influence). Domestic firms have `dasing < 10` (or `dasing = 0`). Firms with missing `dasing` are excluded from this comparison.

### FDI Share Over Time

![**Figure D7a.** Share of FDI firms (foreign ownership ≥ 10%) by year. FDI share ranges 6–10%, with a modest upward trend from ~7.7% (2000) to 9.6% (2014). The 2006 dip reflects the SE06 census expansion diluting the FDI share with newly-enumerated domestic firms. Source: `si_energy_emissions.dta` + `data8514_SI.dta` · Do-file: `12_descriptive_stats.do`.](../output/figures/figD7a_fdi_share_by_year.png){fig-align="center" width="75%"}

### Emission Levels: FDI vs. Domestic

| | FDI firms (dasing ≥ 10%) | Domestic firms (dasing < 10%) |
|---|---:|---:|
| N firm-years | 24,635 | 289,941 |
| Median total CO₂e (tCO₂e) | **588.4** | 44.7 |
| Median Scope 1 CO₂e (tCO₂e) | 94.6 | 14.3 |
| Median Scope 2 CO₂e (tCO₂e) | 251.7 | 11.3 |
| Scope 2 share of pooled total (%) | **52.0%** | 41.7% |
| Median carbon intensity (tCO₂e/M Rp) | **0.035** | 0.043 |

*Source: `desc_fdi_summary.csv` · `dasing` merged from `data8514_SI.dta`; 0 obs with missing `dasing`.*

**Key findings:**

- **FDI firms are larger emitters in absolute terms** — median total CO₂e is ~13× higher (588 vs. 45 tCO₂e). This primarily reflects firm size, not lower efficiency: FDI firms in the SI panel are typically larger enterprises.
- **FDI firms have lower carbon intensity** — 0.035 vs. 0.043 tCO₂e per million Rp output (−19%). Consistent with the "technology transfer" hypothesis: foreign-owned plants use more efficient equipment and processes.
- **FDI firms are more electricity-intensive** — Scope 2 share 52% vs. 42% for domestic. FDI plants may use more automated, electricity-driven processes; their Scope 2 emissions are therefore more exposed to the grid EF time-trend.
- **FDI share is low and slightly increasing** — ~7–10% of firm-years across the panel (see table below), rising modestly from 7.7% in 2000 to 9.6% in 2014.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Note on causal inference.** The raw FDI–CI gap (−19%) is cross-sectional and confounded by firm size, sector, and selection into FDI. It is descriptive context only. The DiD / event-study design in Mba Deasy's analysis — which exploits within-firm variation in internationalisation status across time — is the appropriate framework for causal claims.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| **Total** | — | **715,459** | **730,666** | **−2.1%** |

^‡‡^ The aggregate Spec 1 vs. Spec 2 difference for electricity is 0% because the time-varying Spec 1 EF (low in 2000–2010, high in 2013–2014) averages to approximately the static Spec 2 value (0.000867) over the full 15-year pool. Year-by-year differences are substantial — Spec 1 is 33–45% lower in 2000–2010 and ~5% higher in 2014 (see §7.7 bias table).

**Key findings:** Electricity (Scope 2, 365 million tCO₂e pooled; 365,125 thousand tCO₂e) and diesel (166 million tCO₂e Spec 1) are the two largest emission sources. Coal (139 million tCO₂e Spec 1) is a plausible and comparable third — consistent with the documented coal switching trend after 2003. LPG shows the largest NCV-driven Spec 1–Spec 2 gap (−12.7%), confirming the GCV/NCV issue documented in §7.5. City gas shows +23.1% because Spec 1 uses BPS Neraca Energi's higher NCV for natural gas.

:::

The tables and figures below characterise the cross-sectional relationship between emission levels and two firm-size proxies: **value added** (`vtlvcu`, thousand Rp nominal) and **total workers** (`ltlnou`). All correlations are in log-log space.

### Pooled correlation matrix

Source: `output/tables/desc_correlation_pooled.csv` · N ≈ 322,000 firm-years with non-missing ln_co2, ln_va, and ln_ltlnou.

| | ln CO₂ (S1) | ln CO₂ (S2) | ln value added | ln workers |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **ln CO₂ (Spec 1)** | **1.000** | 0.9999 | 0.718 | 0.649 |
| **ln CO₂ (Spec 2)** | 0.9999 | **1.000** | 0.718 | 0.648 |
| **ln value added (vtlvcu)** | 0.718 | 0.718 | **1.000** | 0.752 |
| **ln workers (ltlnou)** | 0.648 | 0.649 | 0.752 | **1.000** |

**Interpretation:** A high positive correlation between ln CO₂ and ln value added (or ln workers) is expected — larger firms consume more energy and emit more. The correlation between Spec 1 and Spec 2 will approach 1.0 because the two specifications apply a constant per-fuel scalar; the log transformation of a constant multiple shifts the mean but leaves the correlation unchanged.

**Note for downstream analysis:** The raw cross-sectional correlation between emissions and output reflects firm size, not efficiency. Panel fixed effects difference out firm-level variation, isolating within-firm changes. The correlations below are presented as descriptive context only.

## Sense Checks: External Validation

The three checks below test whether the emission estimates produced by this pipeline are internally consistent and plausible relative to external benchmarks. They are not formal tests — the IBS panel and the BPS Neraca Emisi GRK differ in coverage scope, emission boundary, and methodology. The goal is to flag large discrepancies that would indicate a pipeline error, and to confirm that the cross-sectional ordering by industry and province matches domain expectations.

---

### Check 1 — Aggregate CO₂e vs. BPS *Neraca Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca* (2015–2019)

**External reference:** BPS *Neraca Arus Energi dan Neraca Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca Indonesia* (editions 2015–2019 and 2019–2023) report total manufacturing sector CO₂e using Physical Supply and Use Table (PSUT) methodology — the official Indonesian national GHG inventory basis for manufacturing.

| Year | BPS Neraca GRK — Total manufacturing (thousand tCO₂e) |
|------|:---:|
| 2015 | 89,441 |
| 2016 | 96,602 |
| 2017 | 81,488 |
| 2018 | 123,791 |
| 2019 | 161,652 |

*Source: BPS Neraca Arus Energi dan Neraca Emisi GRK 2015–2019, Table 3.1.*

The IBS panel ends in 2014 so a year-exact comparison is not possible. We instead compare our terminal years against the nearest BPS figure:

| Year | IBS total (000 tCO₂e, Spec 1) | Nearest BPS reference | IBS / BPS ratio |
|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 2012 | 36,303 | — | — |
| 2013 | 45,085 | — | — |
| 2014 | 49,836 | BPS 2015 = 89,441 | **56%** |

**Assessment — directional plausibility confirmed.** Our 2014 IBS total (49.8 Mt CO₂e) is approximately 56% of the BPS official 2015 manufacturing figure (89.4 Mt CO₂e). This ratio is consistent with three structural reasons why IBS should fall below the official total:

1. **Coverage gap — IBS excludes small establishments.** The SI surveys establishments with ≥20 workers (medium + large plants). Small enterprises (< 20 workers) are excluded and contribute to the BPS Neraca GRK aggregate, which covers all registered manufacturing establishments.
2. **Emission boundary — BPS includes transformation losses.** The BPS Neraca GRK accounts for energy transformed within manufacturing (petroleum refining, coke ovens) — a supply-side flow not captured in IBS final energy consumption.
3. **One-year gap.** BPS 2015 vs. IBS 2014: the rising trend in our data (45.1 Mt in 2013 → 49.8 Mt in 2014) is directionally consistent with BPS's upward trajectory through 2016.

**Rising trend confirmation.** The BPS series shows manufacturing CO₂e rising from 89.4 Mt (2015) to 161.7 Mt (2019), driven by coal substitution and the Fast Track industrial expansion. Our 2011–2014 series shows the same pre-cursor acceleration: 32.9 → 36.3 → 45.1 → 49.8 Mt — the IBS series is picking up the same structural trend beginning from the prior period.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Macro energy intensity reference.** BPS Neraca Emisi GRK 2015–2019 (Table 2.5) reports manufacturing energy intensity at **706 GJ per billion IDR of gross value added** in 2015, rising to **987 GJ/billion IDR** in 2019. CO₂e emission intensity was approximately **39–65 tCO₂e per billion IDR** over 2015–2019. These macro ratios cannot be directly compared to our firm-level medians (which are right-skewed and not GVA-weighted), but they confirm that energy-intensive manufacturing in Indonesia generates tens to hundreds of tCO₂e per billion Rp of output — consistent with our median per-firm range of 50–75 tCO₂e in 2011–2014.
:::

---

### Check 2 — ISIC 2-Digit Energy Intensity Ordering

The median tCO₂e per firm-year by ISIC 2-digit industry should follow an expected ordering based on process thermodynamics: sectors requiring high-temperature heat or electrolytic reduction (metals, chemicals, cement, paper) should sit well above sectors with primarily mechanical or assembly processes (apparel, furniture, printing).

**Assessment (§9.2 data, median tCO₂e, pooled 2000–2014):**

| ISIC2 | Industry | Median tCO₂e | Expected rank | Verdict |
|---:|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 27 | Basic metals | 551 | 1 | ✓ |
| 24 | Chemicals & chemical products | 354 | 2 | ✓ |
| 34 | Motor vehicles & trailers | 340 | 3–4 | ✓ (paint curing, stamping) |
| 25 | Rubber & plastics | 238 | 3–5 | ✓ |
| 21 | Paper & paper products | 229 | 3–5 | ✓ |
| 35 | Other transport equipment | 215 | 4–6 | ✓ |
| 29 | Machinery & equipment | 174 | 5–7 | ✓ |
| 28 | Fabricated metals | 143 | 5–7 | ✓ |
| 22 | Printing & publishing | 133 | 6–8 | ✓ (high electricity) |
| 20 | Wood products | 117 | 6–8 | ✓ |
| 17 | Textiles | 79 | 7–9 | ✓ |
| 15 | Food & beverages | 65 | 8–10 | ✓ |
| 36 | Furniture & other | 34 | 10–11 | ✓ |
| 18 | Wearing apparel | 30 | 11–12 | ✓ |
| 26 | Non-metallic minerals | 22 | Expected high | ⚠ (see note) |

**All sectors in expected rank order except ISIC 26 (non-metallic minerals).** The anomalously low median (22 tCO₂e) for ISIC 26 is explained by composition: this code bundles large **cement plants** (Semen Gresik, Indocement, Tonasa — each emitting hundreds of thousands of tCO₂e per year) with a large number of small **ceramic tile, glass, and lime workshops** with very low energy use. The bimodal distribution is visible in the mean/median gap: median = 22, mean = 4,566 tCO₂e. In the ISIC × province table (§9.4), ISIC 26 × Sulawesi Selatan (328 firm-years, ~9,984 thousand tCO₂e pooled) is entirely the Tonasa cement complex — averaging ~660,000 tCO₂e per year per firm. The low median therefore represents the ceramics/glass majority, not the cement minority, which is correctly identified in the mean.

**Motor vehicles (ISIC 34) ranking third** is slightly surprising given that automotive assembly is often considered relatively clean. In Indonesia, ISIC 34 includes stamping plants, paint shops (high-temperature curing ovens), and engine parts manufacturers alongside final assembly — consistent with a median above paper and rubber.

---

### Check 3 — Provincial Emission Intensity

Provincial median tCO₂e per firm-year should reflect industrial composition: resource-processing provinces (pulp, palm oil, petrochemicals, cement) should show high medians; Java garment/furniture provinces should show low medians; DKI Jakarta (finance, light assembly) should show a high Scope 2 share relative to Scope 1.

**Assessment (§9.3 data, median tCO₂e and Scope 1/2 split, pooled 2000–2014):**

| Province | Median tCO₂e | Scope 1 (000 t) | Scope 2 (000 t) | Scope 2 share | Industrial profile | Verdict |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|:---:|
| Riau | 555 | 23,500 | 6,488 | 22% | Palm oil mills, APRIL/APP pulp | ✓ |
| Kepulauan Riau | 404 | 7,707 | 8,646 | 53% | Batam EPZ: electronics, shipbuilding | ✓ |
| Banten | 287 | 39,093 | 43,309 | 53% | Krakatau Steel, petrochemicals | ✓ |
| Lampung | 208 | 8,041 | 2,753 | 26% | Sugar mills (PTPN), palm oil | ✓ |
| Sumatera Utara | 137 | 11,428 | 12,534 | 52% | Palm oil, rubber, paper | ✓ |
| DKI Jakarta | 95 | 14,174 | 32,414 | **70%** | Light industry, printing, food | ✓ |
| Jawa Barat | 99 | 99,588 | 135,287 | 58% | Textiles, chemicals, metals | ✓ |
| Jawa Timur | 41 | 46,692 | 68,827 | 60% | Food/beverages, ceramics | ✓ |
| Jawa Tengah | 21 | 28,394 | 29,949 | 51% | Garments, furniture, small food | ✓ |

**All provincial patterns consistent with known industrial geography.** Three specific checks:

1. **Riau — highest median (555 tCO₂e), Scope 1 dominant (78% of total).** Riau hosts APRIL's Kerinci mill and multiple Sinar Mas (APP) pulp operations — among Southeast Asia's largest kraft pulp plants. Pulp and paper requires continuous high-temperature steam (kraft cooking, chemical recovery boilers), producing predominantly direct fuel emissions (coal, biomass). High Scope 1 share with low Scope 2 share is exactly what coal/biomass-fired boiler operations produce. ✓

2. **DKI Jakarta — Scope 2 dominant (70%), lowest direct fuel share.** Jakarta's manufacturing base is predominantly light assembly, printing, garment design, and food processing — activities that consume purchased electricity but burn little direct fuel on-site. The 70% Scope 2 share is the highest in the dataset and exactly consistent with this profile. ✓

3. **Jawa Tengah — lowest median (21 tCO₂e).** Central Java's manufacturing is concentrated in garments (Semarang, Solo), furniture (Jepara), and small food processing — all labor-intensive, low-energy-use sectors. This is reflected in the ISIC decomposition: Central Java has high N for ISIC 18 (apparel) and ISIC 36 (furniture), both among the lowest-emission sectors. ✓

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Sulawesi Selatan — notable by intensity despite smaller sample.** Sulawesi Selatan has 4,654 firm-years and total CO₂e of 21,741 thousand tCO₂e — a mean of ~4,672 tCO₂e per firm-year, far above any Java province. The dominant contributor is the Tonasa cement complex (ISIC 26 × Sulawesi Selatan = ~9,984 thousand tCO₂e from 328 firm-years). This validates that the high-intensity ISIC 26 outliers flagged in Check 2 above are real industrial sites captured in the IBS, not data artefacts.
:::

# Appendix B — Data Cleaning Decision {#sec-appendix-cleaning .unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Do-files:** `dofiles/08_outlier_flags.do` (flag generation) · `dofiles/09_clean_apply.do` (apply cleaning rule) · **Input:** `output/si_energy_flagged.dta` · **Output:** `output/si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta`
:::

This annex documents the evidence and rationale behind the cleaning rule summarised in §6.3 of the main document. §B.1 surveys eleven prior published studies that used the same SI/IBS panel — reviewing exactly how each cleaned the data, what retention rates they achieved, and what the literature consensus is. §B.2–B.3 explain why those consensus approaches require refinement for a causal inference design, derive the cleaning rule used here, and document the resulting dataset. The annex closes with three diagnostic figures that verify the rule removes anomalies without distorting the main distribution.

## How Prior Studies Clean Indonesian SI Data

Eleven papers with documented data cleaning procedures are reviewed below. Four additional papers that use SI/IBS data but do not specify their cleaning approach (<a href="#ref-rosita2020">Rosita et al. 2020</a>; <a href="#ref-margono2006">Margono & Sharma 2006</a>; <a href="#ref-aswicahyono2010">Aswicahyono, Hill & Narjoko 2010</a>; <a href="#ref-narjoko2014">Narjoko 2014</a>) are cited elsewhere in the document but excluded from this comparison. The table spans top economics journals (AER, JIE, JDE, World Development, JPE) and specialist outlets (BIES, IRJFE, IZA JLD, Energy Economics, IDEC DP).

| Paper | Journal | SI/IBS coverage | N (after cleaning) | Cleaning approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a> | IDEC DP | 1990–2010 | 19,926 (4.4% of raw) | Five-stage: zero removal → structural year drop → mode×500 → CV filter → balanced panel |
| <a href="#ref-amiti2007">Amiti & Konings (2007)</a> | AER | 1991–2001 | ~167,000 (est. ~98%) | Growth-rate trim: drop 1st/99th pct of output and input growth |
| <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> | JIE | 1988–1996 | 108,100 (domestic firms) | Variable-by-variable; impute 1–2-yr gaps; drop frequent non-responders; unbalanced |
| <a href="#ref-blalock2004">Blalock & Gertler (2004)</a> | JDE | 1990–1996 | 73,635 (wholly domestic) | Exclude 1990 exporters (pre-existing); foreign-owned firms dropped; unbalanced |
| <a href="#ref-blalock2007">Blalock & Veloso (2007)</a> | World Dev | 1988–1996 | Not reported | Outer islands excluded; Maddala survival correction; balanced panel as robustness |
| <a href="#ref-harrison2010">Harrison & Scorse (2010)</a> | AER | 1990–1996 | ~5,920–6,165 (balanced) | Treatment defined "always-foreign/always-exporting"; balanced sub-panel for long-diff |
| <a href="#ref-alatas2008">Alatas & Cameron (2008)</a> | JPE | 1990–1996 | 1,224–1,519 (Jabotabek CTFL) | Geographic + sector restriction; balanced sub-panel for DiD; irregular obs dropped |
| <a href="#ref-delcarpio2015">Del Carpio et al. (2015)</a> | IZA JLD | 1993–2006 | 290,118 (40,169 firms) | Continuity filter (year-to-year appearance required); zero-worker obs dropped; provinces with multiple minimum wages dropped |
| <a href="#ref-hartono2011">Hartono, Irawan & Achsani (2011)</a> | IRJFE | 2002–2006 | 68,715 (13,743 firms × 5 yrs) | Balanced panel (firms present all 5 years); energy unit standardisation |
| <a href="#ref-rentschler2017">Rentschler & Kornejew (2017)</a> | Energy Econ | 2013 cross-section | 36,759 (from 41,402) | Exclude seasonal firms + missing cost/sales; 2.5th/97.5th pct price outlier trim |
| <a href="#ref-narjoko2007">Narjoko & Hill (2007)</a> | AEJ | 1993–2000 | ~10,050 (1996–2000) | Unbalanced panel via PSID-matching; Heckman two-step for exit selection; ISIC 353–354 excluded; full protocol in <a href="#ref-narjoko2006">Narjoko (2006 PhD)</a> |

### <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a> — The Standard Reference

<a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a>, IDEC Discussion Paper DP2-14-9, provide the most complete publicly documented procedure for cleaning SI data across 1990–2010. Their five-stage procedure is the most detailed reference available:

| Stage | Procedure | Observations retained |
|-------|-----------|----------------------|
| Remove zero/missing monetary values | Drop zero capital, wages, output | 253,610 (55.8%) |
| Remove missing energy variables | Drop years where coal/kerosene absent | 222,062 (49%) |
| **Outlier removal** | **Mode × 500 rule on intensity variables** | 91,311 (20%) |
| CV smoothing | Drop sub-sectors with CV > 1.0 | Further reduction |
| Panel balancing | Keep firms present in all years | **19,926 (4.4%)** |

**The mode × 500 rule:** For each ISIC sub-sector and time period, fit a kernel density (Epanechnikov) to the intensity variable (e.g., energy per unit output). The right-side outlier boundary is defined as `mode × 500`. The left-side boundary applies the same rule to the reciprocal variable. Three candidate multipliers (500×, 1000×, 1500×) and three central tendency measures (mean, median, mode) were tested; mode × 500 was selected as the strictest threshold that still retained sufficient sub-sectors for analysis.

**Years dropped entirely:** 1996 and 1997 (capital recorded as all-zero); 2001 and 2002 (coal and kerosene consumption missing — directly relevant to CO₂ estimation); 2007 (77% of observations lost after zero removal).

### <a href="#ref-amiti2007">Amiti & Konings (2007)</a> — AER Benchmark

<a href="#ref-amiti2007">Amiti & Konings (2007)</a>, *American Economic Review* 97(5), use the same SI data for 1991–2001 (~15,000 firms per year, 170,741 observations total). Their cleaning documentation is more concise:

> *"We excluded plants with unrealistically large spikes in the data, by dropping the 1st and 99th percentiles of the distribution of plant-level output growth and input growth."* — Footnote 23

This is a **growth-rate trim** (not a levels trim): extreme year-on-year changes are removed, not extreme absolute values. Capital stock for 1996 was interpolated as the average of 1995 and 1997 due to missing data. Year 2001 is treated cautiously because BPS introduced new firm codes, making some firm matching unreliable.

### <a href="#ref-hartono2011">Hartono, Irawan & Achsani (2011)</a> — Balanced Panel Approach

<a href="#ref-hartono2011">Hartono et al. (2011)</a>, *International Research Journal of Finance and Economics* 62, construct a **balanced firm-level panel** from the SI/IBS for 2002–2006: 13,743 firms observed in all five years, yielding 68,715 observations. Their cleaning approach is implicit rather than documented:

- **Panel balancing** is the primary filter: firms not present in every year of the panel are dropped. This is the same logic as <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko</a> but applied to a shorter window and without explicit reporting of how many firms were dropped at each step.
- **Energy unit standardisation**: physical energy quantities (multiple units — TJ, litres, kg, m³) are converted to a common energy unit for the intensity variable. No detailed unit-conversion procedure is described.
- **No outlier rule stated**: the paper notes it uses robust regression with `rreg` (iteratively reweighted least squares) to down-weight influential observations rather than dropping them.

This is the most methodologically relevant precedent for Mba Deasy's research: same data (SI/IBS, medium-large firms), same period overlap (2002–2006 sits within 2000–2014), and it explicitly uses panel FE — making the Griliches-Hausman measurement-error concern directly applicable.

### <a href="#ref-rentschler2017">Rentschler & Kornejew (2017)</a> — Cross-Sectional Energy Price Study

<a href="#ref-rentschler2017">Rentschler & Kornejew (2017)</a>, *Energy Economics* 67, use a 2013 cross-section from the **SE2013 (Sensus Ekonomi)** — not the annual SI/IBS panel — covering micro, small, medium, and large manufacturing firms. Despite the different source, their cleaning procedure is informative because the underlying questionnaire structure is similar:

- **Starting N:** 41,402 firms
- **Exclusions:** 3,543 seasonal firms; 1,100 firms with missing total costs or total sales
- **Final N:** 36,759 (88.8% retention)
- **Outlier treatment:** 2.5th/97.5th percentile trim of the provincial energy price distributions. This is applied to the independent variable (price), not the outcome — a different approach from level or growth-rate outcome trims.

**Relevance:** Cross-sectional cleaning is inherently simpler than panel cleaning because there is no longitudinal consistency requirement. <a href="#ref-rentschler2017">Rentschler & Kornejew</a>'s high retention rate (88.8%) is partly a consequence of working with a single cross-section. Their price-distribution trim is not directly applicable to a panel energy-quantity outcome.

### <a href="#ref-narjoko2007">Narjoko & Hill (2007)</a> — Unbalanced Panel with Heckman Selection

<a href="#ref-narjoko2007">Narjoko & Hill (2007)</a>, *Asian Economic Journal* 21(4), construct a panel of Indonesian manufacturing plants for 1993–2000 using the SI/IBS data to study firm-level adjustment during the 1997–98 Asian financial crisis. Their data construction is notable for two reasons relevant to this project:

**Panel approach — unbalanced, PSID-matched.** The panel retains plants for the years they appear, rather than requiring a balanced presence. This contrasts with the <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito-Kaneko</a> balanced approach and is more conservative in the sense that it preserves exit events. The panel yields ~10,050 plants pooled over 1996–2000, with roughly 75% observed continuously. Matching is done on the **PSID variable** (plant code), not an enterprise-level ID — a detail shared with our project.

**Data quality:** Full documentation of cleaning procedures is deferred to <a href="#ref-narjoko2006">Narjoko (2006)</a>, unpublished PhD thesis, but the paper records: (a) the panel "has been cleaned and adjusted for some possible mistakes in data entry, for changes in ISIC, and for variable definitions"; (b) ISIC 353 and 354 (oil and gas refining) are excluded because data quality in those sectors was "still weak" during the 1990s; (c) 1997 data is treated as ambiguous given the mid-year crisis onset and is excluded from the main performance regression.

**Heckman correction for exit.** Because ~33% of plants active before the crisis disappeared during 1997–2000 (exit or temporary closure), the regression sample is a non-random subsample of survivors. The paper applies a Heckman (1976) two-step estimator: a probit on plant survival generates an inverse Mills ratio (IMR), which is included in the performance OLS as a correction. This is methodologically relevant for event studies: if treatment (internationalisation) correlates with survival, OLS estimates of treatment effects are biased without such correction.

**Relevance for this project:** The unbalanced-panel approach and PSID-based matching are directly analogous to ours. The Heckman concern about selective survival is applicable to the internationalisation event study: firms that begin exporting are more likely to survive, which means a simple pre/post comparison of energy intensity within survivors would be upward-biased (surviving firms that did not export are a selected group, not a valid counterfactual).

#### Full Cleaning Protocol — <a href="#ref-narjoko2006">Narjoko (2006)</a> PhD Thesis, Section 5.3

The complete cleaning procedure is documented in <a href="#ref-narjoko2006">Narjoko</a>'s PhD thesis (*Indonesian Manufacturing and the Economic Crisis of 1997/98*, Australian National University, 2006), which provides the most comprehensive publicly available cleaning protocol for the SI panel after <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a>. The thesis describes the approach as "rather ad hoc" but applies three systematic steps. The overall effect is striking: **on average, 43% of raw SI observations are removed**, leaving 57% of the original panel.

**Table 5.1 — Cleaned vs. raw panel, 1993–2000:**

| Year | Cleaned N | Raw N | Drop rate | VA coverage | Emp coverage |
|------|----------:|------:|----------:|------------:|-------------:|
| 1993 | 10,984 | 18,163 | −39.5% | 68% | 61% |
| 1994 | 10,893 | 19,016 | −42.7% | 70% | 60% |
| 1995 | 11,578 | 21,551 | −46.3% | 69% | 57% |
| 1996 | 12,152 | 22,997 | −47.2% | 72% | 58% |
| 1997 | 11,908 | 22,386 | −46.8% | 86% | 60% |
| 1998 | 11,551 | 21,423 | −46.1% | 69% | 60% |
| 1999 | 13,343 | 22,070 | −39.5% | 67% | 62% |
| 2000 | 13,621 | 22,174 | −38.6% | 70% | 63% |
| **Avg** | **12,004** | **21,223** | **−43.3%** | **71%** | **60%** |

Despite removing 43% of observations, the cleaned panel covers 71% of manufacturing value added and 60% of employment — the dropped observations are disproportionately smaller or intermittent plants.

**Step 1 — ISIC code harmonisation (§5.3.1)**

BPS switched from ISIC Revision 2 to Revision 3 starting from 1998. The thesis harmonises all codes back to Revision 2 using the following rules:

- *1998 data:* BPS provided both Revision 2 and Revision 3 codes simultaneously; no adjustment needed.
- *1999–2000, plants previously observed in 1998:* Replace with the 1998 ISIC code directly.
- *1999–2000, plants new to the panel:* Apply the BPS (2000) concordance table. One-to-one matches are retained; non-one-to-one matches are retained only if the highest common digit is at the 3-digit level or finer — observations with ambiguity at the 2-digit level or above are removed.
- *Cross-year consistency:* Plants showing an inconsistent 2-digit ISIC code in any year of the panel are removed entirely. Plants with inconsistent 3-to-5-digit codes are retained (interpreted as multi-product firms shifting product mix over time, which is plausible).

Approximately 9% of 1999 and 2000 observations have incomplete 5-digit ISIC entries, creating residual ambiguity even after harmonisation.

**Step 2 — Variable definition consistency check (§5.3.2)**

Variable definitions are generally consistent across years, with one identified structural break: `LPMNOU` (male paid production workers) and `LPWNOU` (female paid production workers) are defined as **paid** workers for 1993–1996 but were **redefined as unpaid workers** for 1997–2000. This is a definitional shift built into the questionnaire design, not a data entry error, and requires adjustment for any analysis spanning these two sub-periods. The thesis flags this as a concrete example of how SI variable definitions change across years without clear announcement.

**Step 3a — Growth-rate outlier removal (§5.3.3), following <a href="#ref-hall1995">Hall & Mairesse (1995)</a>**

The primary cleaning variable is `VTLVCU` (total value added) paired with `LTLNOU` (total labour), identified as "consistent and contain minimum errors" — the two SI variables regarded as most reliable across years. Annual growth thresholds are applied:

- Value added growth < −90% or > +300% → observation removed
- Employment growth < −70% or > +200% → observation removed

The asymmetric upper/lower thresholds reflect the expectation that employment declines more gradually than value added during crises (labour hoarding), while sudden large employment jumps are implausible given hiring lags. **Effect: approximately 11% of observations are removed per year** from this step alone.

**Step 3b — Missing observation handling**

Four rules govern plants with missing data in some years:

1. Plants with **two or more temporary missing observations** across the panel are removed entirely.
2. Plants with **exactly one temporary missing observation** are retained; the missing year's values are replaced with the previous year's values (carry-forward imputation).
3. **Single-entry plants** — establishments appearing in only one year of the panel — are removed. These are treated as likely PSID data-entry errors rather than genuine one-year firms.
4. Exception: plants missing `VTLVCU` and `OUTPUT` in 1996 or 1997 but consistent on other variables are retained with those values replaced by the prior year.

The carry-forward imputation for one-year gaps is consistent with <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a>, the only other SI study in this review to impute rather than delete for short gaps.

**Step 3c — Variable-specific corrections**

Three independent variables are further corrected (focused on 1995–1996 values, with consistency checked over the full panel):

1. *`DYRSTR` (year of starting operation):* Approximately 50% of raw panel observations show year-to-year inconsistency in this variable — BPS officials attributed this to "lack of knowledge on the part of people responsible for responding to the questionnaire." Adjustments use a modal-entry rule grouped into three deviation categories (±2 years, ±10 years, >±10 years). Group 3 deviations (>±10 years) and clearly erroneous entries (coded as 0 or 1) are replaced by either the last non-missing value or the cross-year modal value.
2. *`DASING` (foreign ownership share):* Approximately 300 inconsistent entries (~45% of total panel observations). Rules target 1995–1996 entries; domestic, government, and regional-government ownership shares are adjusted correspondingly so all shares sum to 100%.
3. *`PRPREX` (percentage of output exported):* Inconsistent entries adjusted using a modal-value approach. Single-year extreme values (a plant showing 100% export orientation in one year while showing 0% in all adjacent years) are flagged and corrected.

**Data quality observations from the thesis**

Four conclusions from the thesis's examination of SI data quality are broadly applicable to any SI panel analysis:

1. *PSID reliability (1993–2000):* "Data examination suggests the extent of mistakes [in PSID] is low. Moreover it shows that the entry for PSID is highly consistent, at least for the period covered in this study." This validates PSID-based panel construction for the 1993–2000 sub-period; the same confidence should not be assumed for all later years without independent verification.
2. *SI under-enumeration in the 1970s–1980s:* "SI data were known to be more under-enumerated in the 1970s and 1980s, so that the first appearance [in the panel] is not necessarily the birth year of a plant." Plants entering the panel after 1988 may be pre-existing firms being enumerated for the first time.
3. *Value added and employment most reliable:* `VTLVCU` and `LTLNOU` are the variables identified as "consistent and contain minimum errors" — used as the primary anchors for outlier detection. Capital and asset variables are not used as cleaning anchors.
4. *The 43% removal rate is not a benchmark:* <a href="#ref-narjoko2006">Narjoko (2006)</a> removes 43%; <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a> remove 96%; <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> remove around 10%. The appropriate removal rate depends heavily on the analysis: balanced-panel productivity decomposition requires the most aggressive cleaning; causal fixed-effects estimation can tolerate more noise.

### Top-Journal SI Studies: Blalock, Gertler, Harrison, Alatas

The following six papers were published in top economics journals (AER, JIE, JDE, World Development, JPE, IZA JLD) and all use the same SI/IBS panel data. Their data cleaning choices are both more detailed and more relevant to causal inference than much of the Indonesian energy literature.

#### <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> — *Journal of International Economics*: FDI and Supply-Chain Technology Transfer

The most detailed cleaning documentation among the top-journal papers. <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> use 108,100 establishment-year observations from the SI for 1988–1996 to study productivity gains from downstream FDI. Their cleaning approach has three notable features:

1. **Variable-by-variable cleaning with selective imputation.** "We cleaned each variable independently and only removed establishments from the analysis for which the needed variables could not be constructed." For variables with non-reporting in just one or two years, values are **imputed** to preserve panel continuity — the only SI study in this review to do so. Establishments with "especially frequent non-responses to fundamental questions such as number of employees" are dropped.
2. **Sample varies by regression.** "Establishments with missing wage data could be used for the output regression but not for the profits regression." The production-function sample (108,100 obs) differs from the welfare/profits sample (91,616 obs). This variable-specific approach is appropriate for energy analysis: observations missing energy data can still contribute to production-function regressions if other inputs are present.
3. **Robustness on completely raw data.** "Analysis on completely raw data yields very similar results to what we report here, although standard errors are slightly higher." This directly supports the approach of flagging rather than removing observations.

**Energy variable construction:** Energy is defined as "the sum of deflated electrical and fuel expenditures" — a deflated monetary aggregate. This is the standard approach in the SI production-function literature, combining electricity and fuel expenditures into a single variable deflated by the IHPB wholesale price index. Coefficient on log(energy) in the translog = 0.123 (t = 17.98).

**Panel dates:** Starts at 1988 because "1988 is the first year data on fixed assets are available." Ends at 1996 to avoid "measurement error in price and other uncertainties introduced by the 1997–1998 Asian financial crisis." These two constraints define the canonical window for pre-crisis SI analyses.

#### <a href="#ref-blalock2004">Blalock & Gertler (2004)</a> — *Journal of Development Economics*: Learning by Exporting

Uses 73,635 establishment-year observations, 1990–1996, to test learning-by-exporting. Key data decisions:

- **1990 as the hard start for export analysis.** "The analysis here starts from 1990, the first year data on exporting activity are available." Export orientation is simply absent from the SI before 1990.
- **1990 exporters excluded.** Firms exporting in 1990 (unless founded that year) are excluded to obtain clean first-export events. This is a meaningful restriction: any analysis using export status as a treatment variable must decide how to handle pre-existing exporters.
- **Electricity as Levinsohn-Petrin proxy.** Electricity is used as the proxy for idiosyncratic productivity shocks because it "is widely reported in the data and cannot be stored from period to period." This is a direct endorsement of SI electricity data quality for the 1990-1996 period, and implies zero electricity observations reflect measurement issues rather than true zero consumption (handled via indicator interactions rather than deletion).
- **Fixed-effect justification for misreporting.** "Because the fixed-effect analysis used here admits only within-factory variation on a logarithmic scale, errors of under- or over-reporting will not bias the results provided that each factory consistently misreports over time." This is the methodological rationale for using panel FE with known SI data quality issues.
- **Capital/asset variables flagged as problematic.** "Questions that require some accounting expertise, such as the replacement and book value of fixed assets, were especially problematic." Fixed assets are the least reliable variable in the SI — consistent with energy project experience.

#### <a href="#ref-blalock2007">Blalock & Veloso (2007)</a> — *World Development*: Imports and Supply Chain Learning

Uses the SI for 1988–1996 with 14 provinces on Java, Sumatra, and Bali. Key decisions:

- **Outer island provinces excluded.** Kalimantan, Sulawesi, and eastern Indonesia are dropped because "what little industrial activity that occurs in those areas is largely related to natural resource extraction." For energy analysis, outer-island firms likely show systematically different fuel profiles (heavy diesel use, own-generation), which justifies treating them separately.
- **Survival correction via Maddala logit.** A first-stage logit models the probability of firm survival; the predicted probability is added as a control in the second stage. Results are "close to that obtained without the corrections" — consistent with <a href="#ref-narjoko2007">Narjoko & Hill</a>'s finding that survival correction matters methodologically but rarely overturns results.
- **Same energy variable.** Energy = sum of deflated electrical and fuel expenditures. Coefficient on log(energy) ≈ 0.110 (t = 15.54).

#### <a href="#ref-harrison2010">Harrison & Scorse (2010)</a> — *American Economic Review*: Anti-Sweatshop Activism

Uses SI 1990–1996 for a difference-in-differences study of anti-sweatshop campaigns. Key data decisions:

- **Treatment defined as "always-foreign / always-exporting."** Foreign ownership and export status are defined at the start of the period (1990) and required to hold throughout. This is a strong restriction (no treatment-status switching) designed to avoid endogenous selection, but it limits the sample to persisters.
- **No explicit outlier removal.** The paper does not describe dropping extreme values. Fixed-effects estimation is used without prior cleaning of outlier observations — consistent with the Blalock-Gertler "raw data yields similar results" finding.
- **Balanced sub-panel for long difference.** While the full sample is unbalanced (averaging 4.5 observations per establishment over 10 years), the main wage regressions use a balanced sub-sample of establishments present in both 1990 and 1996.
- **Education data available only for 1995–1997.** The educational composition of the workforce is included as a control only in specifications using those years, flagging a structural absence of education data in most SI years.

#### <a href="#ref-alatas2008">Alatas & Cameron (2008)</a> — *Journal of Political Economy*: Minimum Wages, Jabotabek

Uses SI 1990–1996, restricted to the Greater Jakarta area (Jabotabek) and the clothing/textiles/footwear/leather (CTFL) sectors only. Key data decisions:

- **Balanced sub-panel for matching DiD.** The matched DiD estimator requires establishments present in both the initial year and the 1996 base year. Closed firms are not assigned zero employment because the estimator uses log-transformed values. About 43% of 1991 establishments had closed by 1996 — high attrition rates over 5–7 years are normal in the SI.
- **"A small number of irregular observations" dropped.** No further specification. This is the minimum cleaning disclosure standard in the SI literature.
- **1990 geographic limitation.** The 1990 SI "does not allow identification of the firms' location beyond province," so sub-district location must be inferred from later years for surviving firms. This is a concrete example of geographic data limitations in early SI waves.
- **Coverage = formal sector only.** The 20+ employee threshold means the SI systematically misses the informal sector — where minimum wage effects appear strongest. For energy analysis, this means the panel captures medium-to-large formal plants exclusively.

#### <a href="#ref-delcarpio2015">Del Carpio, Nguyen, Pabon & Wang (2015)</a> — *IZA Journal of Labor & Development*: Minimum Wages, 1993–2006

The only paper in this review to span the full 2000s period of the SI panel (1993–2006), with 290,118 observations and 40,169 firms — the largest sample in the table. Key data decisions:

- **Continuity filter.** Only firms "continuously observed from year to year" are included. This removes firms that appear, disappear, and reappear in the SI — a common data quality problem in the SI where reporting lapses create apparent gaps. The continuity requirement is intermediate between a fully balanced panel and a fully unbalanced one.
- **Zero-worker observations dropped.** Firms with zero production or non-production workers are excluded. This removes observations that likely reflect data error or temporary closure rather than genuine zero-worker firms.
- **Provinces with multiple minimum wages excluded.** Provinces where district-level or sector-specific minimum wages differ from the provincial rate are dropped because they create ambiguity in the minimum wage variable.
- **Missing regressors in 2001, 2002, 2003, and 2005.** "Additional regressors have missing values in 2001, 2002, 2003, and 2005." This independently confirms that those survey years have structural data quality issues — consistent with the gaps identified in §2 of this document (2001–2002 absent coal/kerosene; 2007 structural data loss). The pattern of missing regressors in these years is not isolated to energy variables.
- **Education data available for 4 years only.** Worker educational composition is available only for 1995, 1996, 1997, and 2006 — a hard constraint on any education-controlled SI analysis.

### Common Patterns

Nine conclusions emerge from the eleven papers with documented cleaning procedures:

1. **Year dropping and structural constraints are standard.** Entire years are routinely excluded: 1997–1998 (Asian financial crisis — universal); 1996 and 2001–2002 (<a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito-Kaneko</a>: capital zeros and missing energy). Additionally, three hard structural constraints define what the SI panel can support: (a) export data available from **1990** only; (b) capital/fixed-asset data available from **1988** only; (c) specific regressors (<a href="#ref-delcarpio2015">Del Carpio et al.</a>: regressors missing in 2001, 2002, 2003, 2005) and energy variables (§2 of this document: coal/kerosene absent 2001–2002) confirm these years have broad data quality problems, not isolated to any one variable.

2. **Intensity-based bounds are the dominant method, but top-journal papers skip them.** Only <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a> and <a href="#ref-rentschler2017">Rentschler & Kornejew (2017)</a> apply explicit outlier bounds (mode × 500, and 2.5th/97.5th percentile respectively). <a href="#ref-amiti2007">Amiti & Konings</a> use growth-rate trimming (1st/99th percentile of output and input growth). All other papers — including all five Blalock/Gertler/Harrison/Alatas papers — do not document any outlier trimming. <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> explicitly verified that "analysis on completely raw data yields very similar results."

3. **Imputation is used by at least one leading paper.** <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> impute for 1–2 year gaps in variables, contrary to the claim that no prior SI study imputes. This is a reasonable approach to preserve panel continuity when non-reporting in a single year is likely clerical rather than structural.

4. **Fixed effects are the standard defense against misreporting.** Multiple papers (<a href="#ref-blalock2004">Blalock & Gertler 2004</a> and <a href="#ref-blalock2008">2008</a>; <a href="#ref-blalock2007">Blalock & Veloso 2007</a>) explicitly state that fixed-effects estimation is unbiased under consistent misreporting: "errors of under- or over-reporting will not bias the results provided that each factory consistently misreports over time." This is the theoretical basis for using panel FE with known SI data quality issues — and for the flag-and-estimate approach adopted here.

5. **Electricity is the most reliably reported energy variable.** <a href="#ref-blalock2004">Blalock & Gertler (2004)</a> chose electricity as the Levinsohn-Petrin proxy specifically because it "is widely reported in the data and cannot be stored from period to period." This provides external validation that `elec_pln_kwh` and related electricity variables are among the higher-quality observations in the SI energy block.

6. **Balanced panel is standard for decomposition studies; unbalanced is standard for causal inference.** Productivity decomposition and energy intensity papers use balanced panels (<a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko</a>, <a href="#ref-hartono2011">Hartono et al.</a>, <a href="#ref-margono2006">Margono & Sharma</a>). All five top-journal causal papers (Blalock × 3, <a href="#ref-harrison2010">Harrison & Scorse</a>, <a href="#ref-alatas2008">Alatas & Cameron</a>) use unbalanced panels — retaining establishments for the years they appear — or explicitly use balanced panels only as a robustness check.

7. **Selective survival is documented and can be corrected.** <a href="#ref-narjoko2007">Narjoko & Hill (2007)</a> use Heckman two-step; <a href="#ref-blalock2007">Blalock & Veloso (2007)</a> use Maddala logit to correct for selective exit. Both find results robust after correction. High attrition is normal: <a href="#ref-alatas2008">Alatas & Cameron</a> document 43% closure over 5–7 years.

8. **Sector and geographic restrictions create implicit clean samples.** Several papers impose hard restrictions that implicitly remove low-quality observations: ISIC 353–354 oil/gas refining (<a href="#ref-narjoko2007">Narjoko & Hill</a>, <a href="#ref-aswicahyono2010">Aswicahyono et al.</a>); Greater Jakarta only (<a href="#ref-alatas2008">Alatas & Cameron</a>); outer islands excluded (<a href="#ref-blalock2007">Blalock & Veloso</a>); CTFL sectors only (<a href="#ref-alatas2008">Alatas & Cameron</a>, <a href="#ref-harrison2010">Harrison & Scorse</a>). Energy analysis spanning all sectors and all regions of Indonesia is rarer and faces more data heterogeneity.

9. **Cleaning documentation is sparse, even in top journals.** <a href="#ref-alatas2008">Alatas & Cameron (2008)</a> (JPE) drop "a small number of irregular observations" without specifying criteria. <a href="#ref-harrison2010">Harrison & Scorse (2010)</a> (AER) describe no outlier procedure at all. <a href="#ref-narjoko2014">Narjoko (2014)</a> (BIES) only says "controlled for outliers." Only <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a> and <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> provide full cleaning protocols. The absence of documentation in top journals does not mean cleaning was not done — it reflects that cleaning choices are rarely considered a contribution worth reporting in high-impact outlets.

## Why Standard Approaches Need Refinement for Causal Inference

The prior literature was primarily concerned with descriptive analysis, productivity decompositions, and structural change. Mba Deasy's research question — whether newly internationalizing firms become more energy-efficient — is a **causal inference problem** using panel fixed effects and event study designs. This changes what data quality means in three specific ways.

**Panel FE amplifies measurement error (<a href="#ref-griliches1986">Griliches & Hausman 1986</a>).** In a fixed-effects regression, demeaning removes the between-firm signal and identifies from within-firm variation. The attenuation factor for the causal estimate is:

$$\lambda = \frac{\text{Var(true within-unit change)}}{\text{Var(true within-unit change)} + \text{Var(measurement error)}}$$

For energy variables where a firm's true annual consumption is relatively stable but the data show 50× spikes (§5.8 D2), the noise variance is large relative to the true signal — and $\lambda$ approaches zero. Any panel fixed-effects estimate can be severely attenuated toward zero even when the true effect is economically large. This argues for *removing* the most extreme spikes — but also *only* those spikes, not moderate deviations.

**Dropping entire years removes firms that switch status.** The <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito-Kaneko</a> balanced panel approach (retain only firms present in all years) reduces the sample to 4.4% of raw observations. This almost certainly discards firms with status changes (entry into exporting or importing) that are the key analytical variation. Year dropping is appropriate for productivity decompositions that require a balanced panel; it is inappropriate when observing transitions is central to the research question.

**DEA and ML correction are circular** (see §5.8). Methods that pre-select on energy efficiency remove the outcome variation the study seeks to measure.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Validation from the closest precedents.** The §6.1 review shows that papers with the most similar design to this project — <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> (JIE), <a href="#ref-harrison2010">Harrison & Scorse (2010)</a> (AER), <a href="#ref-alatas2008">Alatas & Cameron (2008)</a> (JPE) — do not apply aggressive cleaning. <a href="#ref-blalock2008">Blalock & Gertler (2008)</a> explicitly verified: *"analysis on completely raw data yields very similar results to what we report here."* This is direct evidence that flag-and-estimate is the right approach for SI causal inference, not just a compromise. It is what the top-journal causal SI literature does.
:::

**Selective survival is an estimation-stage problem, not a cleaning problem.** Common Pattern 7 in §6.1 shows that <a href="#ref-narjoko2007">Narjoko & Hill (2007)</a> and <a href="#ref-blalock2007">Blalock & Veloso (2007)</a> both documented and corrected for selective plant exit via Heckman two-step and Maddala logit respectively. For Mba Deasy's study — where internationalisation correlates with firm survival — this bias operates at the estimation stage. Data cleaning cannot address this; it requires an inverse Mills ratio or survival-probability control in the main regression. This is flagged here as a requirement for the analysis design, separate from the cleaning decision.

The appropriate design is therefore: **remove only unambiguous anomalies, keep the full sample as baseline, add a survival-correction term in estimation, and report robustness across cleaning thresholds.**

## Our Cleaning Choice and Rationale

We adopt a two-layer approach:

**Layer 1 — Full flagged sample (`si_energy_flagged.dta`, §5.8):** All 326,382 firm-years are retained with 72 flag variables attached. This is the baseline dataset for robustness checks.

**Layer 2 — Cleaned sample (`si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta`):** A derived dataset that drops severe outliers while retaining as much analysis variation as possible. The cleaning rule applies one filter:

| Filter | Rule | Observations dropped |
|--------|------|---------------------|
| D1/D2/D3 severe | Drop `flag_any_sev == 1` | ~11,806 obs |
| **Cleaned total** | | **~314,576 obs (96.38% of matched panel)** |

This is the **Stringent** robustness sample, promoted to the primary cleaned dataset. The choice of `flag_any_sev == 1` as the cleaning threshold reflects two decisions:

- The severe thresholds (k = 5 interquartile range, |Δlog| > log(50) ≈ 50× year-on-year change) are conservative — they are very unlikely to flag genuine firm behavior.
- The moderate threshold (k = 3) flags 12.5% of the sample, which is high enough to include genuine variation in energy-intensive industries and should not be deleted. Dropping moderate flags would remove firms that are legitimately energy-intensive relative to their sector, introducing a systematic downward bias in emission estimates for high-intensity industries.

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
**Recommended validation for the analysis stage.** The 11,806 dropped observations should be checked for systematic over-representation of *new exporters or importers* (i.e., firms in their first year of internationalisation). If treatment-event firm-years are disproportionately dropped, the cleaning rule introduces sample selection that would bias the DiD estimate. Specifically: tabulate `exporter == 1 & L.exporter == 0` (first-year exporter dummy) among `flag_any_sev == 1` obs and compare the rate to the retained sample. If the share is similar, the cleaning is non-selective and results are credible. This check is not implemented in the current pipeline and should be performed before the main regression is run.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Single-entry plants.** <a href="#ref-narjoko2006">Narjoko (2006)</a> removes plants appearing in only one year of the panel as likely PSID data-entry errors rather than genuine one-year firms. Our flagging strategy does not have an explicit singleton rule: D2 (longitudinal growth) cannot be computed for a firm with only one observation, so singletons pass through unless they trigger D1 or D3 cross-sectional flags. At the analysis stage, panel FE regressions automatically drop singletons because they contribute zero within-firm variation. For descriptive statistics and the emission conversion pipeline, singletons are retained. If PSID reliability in the 2000–2014 period is uncertain for a given year, researchers may wish to exclude singletons from descriptive comparisons.
:::

### Comparison with the literature benchmark

| Approach | Observations retained | % of raw | Years dropped |
|----------|----------------------|----------|---------------|
| <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito & Kaneko (2014)</a> | 19,926 | 4.4% | 1996,97,01,02,07 |
| <a href="#ref-amiti2007">Amiti & Konings (2007)</a> growth trim | ~167,000 (est.) | ~98% | None |
| **Our cleaned sample** | **314,576** | **96.38%** | None (gaps flagged only) |
| Our full flagged sample (baseline) | 326,382 | 100% | None |

Our approach is substantially more conservative than <a href="#ref-armundito2014">Armundito-Kaneko</a> (retaining ~16× more observations) while applying tighter per-observation thresholds than the 1st/99th growth trim. The higher retention rate preserves the full range of firm transitions that are the analytical interest of the downstream study.

## Evidence: Why Cleaning Matters for This Study

The flag counts from §5.8 quantify the scale of each problem:

**D2 — Longitudinal growth outliers:** The severe tier (|Δlog| > log(50) ≈ 50× change) identifies 11,379 firm-year pairs with any severe D2 flag. Most of these (6,172) are for `elec_pln_kwh`. A firm reporting 50× more or less electricity than the prior year without a corresponding change in output or workers almost certainly reflects a unit error (kWh vs. MWh) or a transcription error, not a genuine operational change. Under the Griliches-Hausman logic, these observations increase the noise variance in the within-firm series, attenuating the FE coefficient.

**D3 — Intensity outliers for coal and city gas:** Coal D3 severe count is 298 (vs. 30 at D1). The discrepancy between D1 and D3 is informative: these firms are not outliers in absolute coal consumption, but they are extreme outliers in coal per worker. This pattern is consistent with a small number of firms operating highly capital-intensive coal-fired processes with very few employees — plausible, but these observations disproportionately influence any energy-intensity regression.

`si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta` is produced by `09_clean_apply.do`, which applies the cleaning rule above to `si_energy_flagged.dta`. The cleaned dataset:

- Retains **~314,576 firm-years** (96.38% of the matched panel)
- Drops ~11,806 observations flagged as severe (`flag_any_sev == 1`) across D1, D2, or D3 dimensions
- Retains all 138 canonical energy variables from `si_energy_harmonized.dta`
- Retains all 72 flag variables (so dropped observations can be identified)
- Adds a variable `cleaned` = 1 for all retained observations (= 0 for the dropped 11,806, which are present in `si_energy_flagged.dta` but absent here)

**For the emission conversion pipeline (§7):** `si_energy_harmonized_cleaned.dta` is the primary input. `si_energy_flagged.dta` is retained as the full sample for robustness specifications.

# Appendix C — Energy Intensity Measures {#sec-annex-energy-intensity .unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Do-file:** `dofiles/16_energy_intensity.do` · **Input:** `output/si_energy_emissions.dta` · **Output:** `output/si_energy_intensity.dta`

**Reference:** Imbruno & Ketterer (2018), *Journal of Development Economics*
:::

This chapter constructs two firm-level energy intensity measures from the cleaned emission panel and compares their trends across 2000–2014. The comparison informs which outcome variable Mba Deasy should use in the DiD/event-study analysis of newly internationalising firms.

## Conceptual Framework

Energy intensity is defined as the ratio of energy use to output. Two operationalisations are available in this dataset:

**Measure A — Monetary intensity** (following Imbruno & Ketterer 2018):

$$\varepsilon^{monetary}_{it} = \frac{\text{fuel expenditure}_{it} + \text{electricity expenditure}_{it}}{\text{output}_{it}}$$

where both numerator and denominator are in nominal Rupiah (Rp000). This is a dimensionless cost share — the fraction of output value absorbed by energy costs.

**Measure B — Physical (GJ-based) intensity:**

$$\varepsilon^{GJ}_{it} = \frac{\text{Total GJ}_{it}}{\text{output}^{real}_{it}}, \quad \text{output}^{real}_{it} = \frac{\text{output}_{it}}{WPI_{it}/100}$$

where the numerator is total primary energy in Gigajoules — computed from physical fuel quantities (litres, kg, m³) using Spec 1 NCV values from BPS Neraca Energi (§7.5) plus purchased electricity converted at 0.0036 GJ/kWh. The denominator is **real output** deflated by the **3-digit ISIC** Wholesale Price Index (WPI, base 2000=100, from `wpio_extended.dta`); 2013–2014 values are extended from the BPS IHPB manufacturing sub-sector price index (base 2010=100) via chain-linking — see §[WPI Construction](#sec-wpi-construction) below. Deflation applies only to Measure B because Measure A's numerator and denominator are both in nominal Rp — applying the same deflator to both sides cancels exactly. CO₂ intensity uses the same WPI deflation logic as GJ intensity (`ei_co2_real = co2_total_s1 / output_real`) and is available as an alternative outcome variable.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Note on deflation.** Measure A requires no deflation: both numerator (energy expenditure) and denominator (output) are in nominal Rupiah, so any deflator cancels exactly. Measure B requires deflation of the denominator only: the numerator (GJ) is a physical unit with no price dimension, while the denominator (nominal output) conflates real production growth with price inflation. Without deflation, a firm that raises its output price while keeping physical energy use constant would *appear* more energy-efficient. In a panel DiD with firm + year FE, year FE absorbs aggregate price trends so regression coefficients are not biased, but descriptive figures and summary statistics benefit from the WPI correction. This approach is consistent with Imbruno & Ketterer (2018, fn. 32).
:::

## Variable Construction

**Measure A — Monetary intensity** is constructed with two electricity aggregations as a robustness check:

| Spec | Electricity variable | Treatment of missing |
|------|---------------------|---------------------|
| **Main** (`ei_monetary_zero`) | `elec_purchased_rp_zero` | Structural missing → 0 (firm has no non-PLN supply) |
| **Robustness** (`ei_monetary_strict`) | `elec_purchased_rp_strict` | Missing if either PLN or non-PLN component missing |

Fuel is always `fuel_total_reported_rp` (original SI variable `efuvcu`) — the survey-reported total fuel expenditure row. A diagnostic (`dofiles/06_efuvcu_check.do`) confirms that `efuvcu` is **independently filled by the respondent**, not computed as a sum of the individual fuel-type rows: it consistently exceeds the arithmetic sum of named components by 5–39% across all survey years 2000–2014 (ratio range: 1.046 in 2008 to 1.394 in 2000). This excess reflects fuel expenditure on items without a dedicated survey column in a given year. Consequently, `fuel_total_reported_rp` is the **more comprehensive** fuel expenditure measure for monetary intensity — the component sum is a lower bound. Using it is consistent with Imbruno & Ketterer (2018), who use the survey's total fuel expenditure variable directly.

**Measure B — Physical (GJ) intensity** is constructed in two steps. First, total GJ is computed from physical fuel quantities (litres, kg, m³) multiplied by Spec 1 NCV coefficients, plus purchased electricity at 0.0036 GJ/kWh (`elec_purchased_kwh_zero`). Second, output is deflated to 2000 real Rp000 using the **3-digit ISIC** WPI (`wpio_extended.dta`, base 2000=100); 2013–2014 values extended from IHPB (see §[WPI Construction](#sec-wpi-construction)). The resulting `ei_gj_real = total_gj_s1 / output_real` is the primary intensity measure. CO₂ intensity uses the same deflation: `ei_co2_real = co2_total_s1 / output_real` (physical numerator, WPI-deflated denominator — identical logic to GJ).

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Boundary difference between Measure A and Measure B.**
The monetary numerator (`fuel_total_reported_rp`) is the respondent-filled total fuel expenditure row in the SI questionnaire. Because it is independently filled by the respondent — not computed as a sum of the individual fuel lines — it may include expenditure on lubricants and biomass fuels (firewood, charcoal) where these were incurred. The physical (GJ) and CO₂ numerators, by contrast, apply a strictly defined Scope 1 boundary that excludes three fuel categories:

| Fuel | Excluded from GJ & CO₂? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Lubricant** | Yes | Non-combustion input (mechanical use); no calorific conversion applies |
| **Firewood** | Yes | Biogenic carbon — IPCC 2006 Scope 1 convention; quantity data available 2006 only |
| **Charcoal** | Yes | Biogenic carbon — same as firewood; quantity data available 2006 only |

The restriction of firewood and charcoal quantity data to the 2006 survey round means that including them in the GJ measure would produce an artificial spike in 2006 with zero coverage in all other years — making inclusion more misleading than informative. Both reasons (methodological and data availability) support the current boundary.

This asymmetry is **intentional and standard**: Measure A captures energy *cost efficiency* (what share of revenue goes to energy), while Measure B captures *physical energy efficiency* (how much energy is consumed per unit of real output). The two measures answer slightly different questions, and their divergence — documented in §[Time-Series Comparison](#time-series-comparison) — is itself informative about the role of energy price changes in the sample period.

For potential future use, three reference GJ variables are stored in `si_energy_intensity.dta` (labeled "NOT in total_gj_s1"): `gj_firewood_ref` (IPCC 2006: 15.6 GJ/tonne), `gj_charcoal_ref` (IPCC 2006: 29.5 GJ/tonne), and `gj_lubricant_ref` (IPCC 2006 potential heat content: 40.2 GJ/tonne × 0.88 kg/ltr = 0.035 GJ/ltr — theoretical only, not actual energy use).
:::

## Coverage

| Measure | Positive obs | Missing | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ei_monetary_zero` | 309,633 | 0 | 98.4% |
| `ei_monetary_strict` | 309,633 | 1 | 98.4% |
| `ei_gj_s1` (nominal) | 306,515 | 0 | 97.4% |
| `ei_gj_real` (WPI-deflated) | 305,321 | 9,253 | 97.1% |
| `ei_co2_real` (WPI-deflated) | 305,321 | 9,253 | 97.1% |

The 4,941 observations (1.6%) with zero monetary energy expenditure produce `ln(0) = .` and are excluded from log-scale analysis but retained in the dataset. No observation has energy costs exceeding output (ratio > 1), confirming data plausibility.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Note on N:** `si_energy_intensity.dta` contains **314,574** firm-years — 2 fewer than the 314,576 in `si_energy_emissions.dta`. The 2 observations have missing `output` (non-manufacturing ISIC or miscoded industry) and are dropped in `16_energy_intensity.do` (Section 2) when constructing WPI-deflated intensity measures. All other variables from `si_energy_emissions.dta` are unaffected.
:::


The single missing observation in `ei_monetary_strict` (but not in `ei_monetary_zero`) arises from the different aggregation rules: the strict spec uses standard addition — if either PLN or non-PLN electricity expenditure is missing, the sum is missing; the zero spec uses `rowtotal()` which treats structural missing as 0, so the result is always 0 or positive. The 1 observation in question has one missing electricity component: under the zero rule it contributes 0 (moving it from the "zero" bucket into a valid zero), while under the strict rule it becomes missing. This is the intended behavior of the robustness spec — it flags genuine ambiguity rather than imputing a value.

The 8,397 non-positive observations in `ei_gj_real` comprise: (a) approximately 8,168 zero-GJ manufacturing firms — the same zero-GJ firms as in `ei_gj_s1`, where `total_gj_s1 = 0` gives `ei_gj_real = 0`; and (b) 229 observations with non-manufacturing or unresolvable ISIC codes unmatched by the WPI, for which `output_real = .`. The 229 unmatched cases are: 227 obs with `isic5_raw = 93091` (KBLI "Jasa Penunjang Industri", present in SI raw data, 2010–2014) and 2 obs with `isic5_raw = 10200` (coal mining, likely miscoded in source data). An additional 993 observations with 4-digit `isic5_raw` codes (e.g. 1511 instead of 15110, common in early survey years 2000–2004) are corrected in `16_energy_intensity.do` by using `int(isic5_raw/10)` rather than `int(isic5_raw/100)` to derive the 3-digit code. Both groups produce `ln_ei_gj_real = .` and are excluded from log-scale analysis.

The two electricity specifications (`_zero` vs `_strict`) yield a correlation of **1.000** — effectively identical across 309,633 observations — confirming robustness of the main specification.

### WPI Deflator Construction {#sec-wpi-construction}

The WPI deflator (`wpio_extended.dta`) is constructed in two stages:

**Stage 1 — Base series 1983–2012.** The file `wpio.dta` provides WPI indices at the 4-digit ISIC level (base 2000=100) for 131 manufacturing codes across 1983–2012, originally derived from BPS IHPB publications following Imbruno & Ketterer (2018).

**Stage 2 — Extension to 2013–2014.** The 2013–2014 indices are chain-linked from the 2010 base using BPS IHPB annual averages (base 2010=100) from the *Indeks Harga Perdagangan Besar Indonesia* publications for 2013 and 2014. The chain-link formula is:

$$WPI^{isic4}_{t} = WPI^{isic4}_{2010} \times \frac{IHPB^{sub}_{t}}{100}, \quad t \in \{2013, 2014\}$$

where $IHPB^{sub}_{t}$ is the annual average of the corresponding BPS manufacturing sub-sector index and $WPI^{isic4}_{2010}$ is the existing 2010 value (base 2000=100).

**Stage 3 — Application to firm data.** Although `wpio_extended.dta` stores indices at the 4-digit ISIC level, the WPI is applied to firm-level observations at the **3-digit ISIC level**, following Narjoko & Hill (2007) and Aswicahyono, Hill & Narjoko (2010) — both of whom use 3-digit WPI deflators in the SI/IBS literature. In `dofiles/16_energy_intensity.do`, the 4-digit indices are first collapsed to 3-digit by taking the simple arithmetic mean across all constituent codes within each 3-digit group and year:

$$\overline{WPI}_{g,t} = \frac{1}{|C_g|} \sum_{i \in C_g} WPI^{isic4}_{i,t}$$

where $C_g$ is the set of 4-digit ISIC codes with $\lfloor isic4/10 \rfloor = g$. The resulting 3-digit $\times$ year lookup is then merged to each firm observation on `isic3 × year`. For example, ISIC codes 1511–1514 each have distinct 4-digit WPI values that are averaged into a single deflator for `isic3 = 151` (Food processing). This aggregation is appropriate because IHPB sub-sectors themselves correspond to roughly 3-digit or broader industry groups — applying a within-group mean preserves price variation across 3-digit industries while avoiding spurious within-group dispersion.

**WPI coverage.** Of the 314,574 firm-year observations in `si_energy_intensity.dta`, **314,345 (99.93%) receive a valid WPI deflator**. The 229 missing cases (0.07%) are not caused by gaps in the concordance — all 131 manufacturing ISIC4 codes in `ihpb_isic4_concordance.csv` have a valid `ihpb_sub` assignment. Instead, they arise because the raw `data8514_SI.dta` contains a small number of observations with `isic5_raw` codes outside manufacturing entirely: 227 obs coded as KBLI 93091 ("Jasa Penunjang Industri", a services activity code, present in years 2010–2014) and 2 obs coded as KBLI 10200 (coal mining). These observations produce `output_real = .` and are excluded from log-scale intensity analysis.

**IHPB–ISIC4 concordance construction.** The BPS IHPB publication organises manufacturing into 50 named sub-sectors (Table 1, e.g., sub 1 = "Industri Pengolahan dan Pengawetan Daging", sub 7 = "Industri Makanan Lainnya"). No official BPS crosswalk between these sub-sector labels and ISIC codes exists. The correspondence is therefore established via **semantic matching**: each IHPB Table 1 label (in Indonesian) was compared against the official ISIC Rev. 3 English definitions (sourced from `isic_rev3.csv`) and each ISIC4 code was assigned to the IHPB sub-sector whose description most closely corresponds in meaning. The full verified concordance is archived in `data8514_SI/ihpb_isic4_concordance.csv`, which records both the original Indonesian label (`notes` column) and the official ISIC Rev. 3 English definition (`isic4_description` column) for each code, allowing the match quality to be inspected directly.

The table below illustrates four representative match types encountered in the concordance:

| IHPB sub | BPS Table 1 label | ISIC4 code(s) | ISIC Rev.3 definition | Match type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pengolahan Daging | 1511 | Production, processing and preserving of meat | 1:1 exact |
| 7 | Makanan Lainnya | 1541–1549 | Bakery / sugar / cocoa / pasta / other food products | many:1 (broad IHPB sub covers multiple ISIC4) |
| 14+15 | Kulit & Alas Kaki | 1911–1920 | Leather goods + footwear | 1:2 — two IHPB subs jointly cover these codes; arithmetic mean used |
| 26 | Kaca & Barang dari Kaca | 2611, 2612 | Manufacture of glass and glass products (ISIC 2610) | KBLI 2000 sub-divides ISIC 2610 into two 4-digit codes; both assigned to sub 26 |
| CAGR | *(no sub available)* | 3710, 3720 | Recycling of metal / non-metal waste and scrap | No IHPB sub exists; 2013–2014 extrapolated via CAGR |

Fourteen ISIC4 codes in KBLI 2000 are finer subdivisions of ISIC Rev. 3 categories (e.g., KBLI 1521 subdivides ISIC 1520 "Dairy products"; KBLI 2611–2612 subdivide ISIC 2610 "Glass products"). These codes have no exact entry in `isic_rev3.csv` but are assigned to their parent IHPB sub-sector and their descriptions are manually supplied — this does not affect deflation since all 131 concordance rows have a valid `ihpb_sub`. The only firm-years that receive no WPI deflator are the 229 observations with `isic5_raw` codes outside the manufacturing concordance entirely (KBLI 93091 "Jasa Penunjang Industri" and 10200 "coal mining"); these produce `output_real = .` and are excluded from log-scale intensity analysis (see §[Coverage and Missing WPI](#sec-coverage-missing-wpi) above).

For ISIC 37 (Recycling — ISIC 3710, 3720), which lacks a corresponding IHPB sub-sector, the 2013–2014 values are extrapolated using a 2010–2012 compound annual growth rate (CAGR), consistent with the pre-upgrade approach. This affects a negligible share of the panel (ISIC 37 constitutes < 0.5% of firm-years).

For ISIC4 groups where two IHPB sub-sectors jointly represent the relevant industries (e.g., leather goods 1911–1912 and footwear 1920 collectively covered by IHPB sub-sectors 14 and 15), the arithmetic mean of the two IHPB indices is used. This applies to 6 groups where the original `wpio.dta` already assigned a single WPI series to codes spanning two distinct IHPB sub-sectors — confirming that the aggregation is consistent with the original data construction.

## Time-Series Comparison

Although physical (GJ) and monetary energy intensity are strongly correlated across firms (r = 0.794), Figure EI-1 reveals a divergence in how energy composition is measured under each metric. **Panel A** shows that in physical terms, fuel combustion dominates throughout the period, consistently accounting for a larger share of total GJ than purchased electricity. **Panel B**, however, shows that in monetary terms Indonesian manufacturing firms allocate an increasing share of their energy expenditure to electricity relative to fuel. This pattern may result from two mechanisms: first, it may reflect efficiency gains in production technology — whereby the monetary share of electricity rises while the physical units of energy delivered per unit of output decline; second, the falling fuel expenditure share may be driven by rising fuel prices over the past decade, which compress the quantity of fuel purchased per unit of monetary expenditure even without any change in physical fuel efficiency.

![**Figure EI-1.** Fuel vs electricity composition of energy use, 2000–2014. **Panel A (left):** Share of total physical energy (GJ) from fuel combustion (Scope 1, blue) vs purchased electricity (Scope 2, light blue). The GJ mix is stable — fuel accounts for roughly 65% of physical energy throughout the period. **Panel B (right):** Share of total nominal energy cost from fuel expenditure (red) vs electricity purchase cost (light red). Electricity's *cost share* rises noticeably after 2005–08, reflecting larger and more persistent electricity tariff increases (PLN normalization 2010–2013) relative to fuel costs. Source: `si_energy_intensity.dta` · Do-file: `dofiles/17_ei_figures.do`.](../output/figures/fig_ei_composition.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

Moreover, Figure EI-2 presents both intensity series indexed to their 2000 value (log-point deviation from the 2000 mean), allowing direct comparison of trajectories from a common baseline. The two measures move in **opposite directions**, yet reflect interrelated dynamics: **monetary intensity rises slightly (+0.1 log points, from −3.80 in 2000 to −3.69 in 2014), while real GJ intensity falls −1.3 log points (−7.4 → −8.7)**. These opposite movements are **two sides of the same structural shift** — rising energy prices increased monetary costs while firms simultaneously reduced physical energy consumption per unit of output. The price increases were not incidental: they were driven by a series of energy subsidy reform policies aimed at reducing government subsidy expenditure, including (1) the removal of the IDO (Industrial Diesel Oil) subsidy in **October 2005** (raising household fuel prices by 114%); (2) the **2008 global oil price peak**; (3) **coal price liberalization via the HBA (*Harga Batubara Acuan*, Indonesian Coal Reference Price) benchmark** from the mid-2000s, as the domestic reference price was progressively aligned toward export parity; and (4) **PLN electricity tariff normalization (2010–2013)** following the May 2008 industrial tariff reform. The declining GJ intensity is also consistent with **a structural shift in energy input mix**: the falling proportion of firms' monetary expenditure on fuel — visible in Figure EI-1 Panel B — aligns with the GJ decline, **suggesting firms progressively reduced reliance on fuel combustion and shifted toward electrification**. Without WPI deflation of the denominator, the nominal GJ intensity decline would appear roughly twice as large (approximately −2.4 log points); the extra gap reflects output price inflation absorbed by the WPI deflator rather than genuine energy efficiency improvement. The dip in GJ intensity in 2001–2002 followed by partial recovery in 2003–2005 reflects compositional changes in the survey sample and fuel-mix shifts across the post-1998 recovery.

Dashed vertical lines: 2005 IDO desubsidization; 2008 global oil price peak. Figure EI-3 decomposes the aggregate divergence into its fuel and electricity components. Panel A confirms that both physical components decline steadily — fuel GJ intensity by approximately −1.6 log points and electricity GJ intensity by approximately −1.3 log points by 2014 — consistent with the genuine physical efficiency improvement shown in the aggregate trend above. Panel B is the key novel finding: fuel *cost* per unit of output spikes sharply after 2005 (+0.4 log points at peak), reflecting IDO subsidy removal and global commodity price transmission, remaining elevated through 2008 before gradually declining. Electricity monetary intensity is comparatively stable until 2010, then rises gradually following PLN tariff normalization. The contrast isolates the price effect: physical fuel consumption per unit of real output fell, but fuel cost per unit *rose* — the two effects nearly cancel in the aggregate monetary measure visible in Figure EI-2.
